This compenY has been formed for the purpose of purchasing is a going eoneern and extending the business of bread and biscuit manufacturers and flour merchants carried on for many years with greet success. The business is in full working order. the Company taking over the existing staff of employes, and the shareholders may therefore look for an immediate return on the invested saPital. It is no doubt that there exists in the metrop.ilis a C etnand for good and pure bread, and by the request of the directors the bread has been analysed by Pro- fessor Jago, and he found it perfectly pure and wholesome bread (original rePort oan be inspected). Messrs. Whitcombe and Emson, Chartered Accountants. of 1, Gresham-buildings. Basinghall-street, EM., have carefully examined the ne.tessary accounts, and have reported that the average turn-over of the six bakery and confectionery busi- nesses, including the wholesale business, is over 300 sacks of flour per week, and that the net profit as at present is suffi- cient to yield a dividend of 10 per cent. on the proposed capi- tal of the Company' at £30,000. (Original report can be inspec- ted.) There is not the slightest doubt that the additional capital will enab:e the Company to effect a very large saving in the purchase of flour, besides reducing the expenses in the different establishments considerably, and the directors con- fidently expect a much larger dividend than 10 per cent. The directors also refer to the great success of other existing bread companies, the Aerated Bread Company, for instances, whose £1 shares are now quoted on the Stock Exchange at over £4 each. The directors have secured the services of the vendor. Mr. Geisel. as managing director, and his confidence in the concern is shown by his taking 12.000 shares in lieu of cash. further to deposit at the Clompanes bankers' sufficient cash to to secure the guaranteed if per cent, per annum for three years on the "A" shares, and his undertaking not to receive any remune- ration for his services until a dividend of if per cent. per an- num be paid to the shareholders. The only contract having reference to the fotmation of the company is one bearing date August 27th, 1886, and made be- tween John George Gelsel, of the first part, and the Trustee of the Company of the other Part, whereby the vendor agrees to assign the goodwill, plants, and effects, and the leases and agreements, together with the goodwill and his busiceis as a flour merchant, for the suM of £2O 000, payable £B,OOO ha cash, and 12,000 fully paid-up shares of the Company Alf expenses incurred in bringing out this Company up to the day of allot- ment are paid by the vendor. Copies of prospectus, articles of association, &c., can be ob- tained at the bankers', the solicitors', and at the Company's offices. Application for shares may be made in the form ac- companying the prospectus, or by letter, stating full address and the amount of shares, and sent with the deposit direct to • the Company's bankers.

ELEANOR You can see her, if you look Behind that door. 'Tis a place, I know full w3ll, • She's been before. For the sofa, small and neat, . With a cushion for her feet, _ Makes a very charming seat For Eleanor.

I have sat with her ofttimes Behind the door, For my love I told her there In days of yore. And her eyes were black as jet, While she murmured, "darling," "pet"— But she is an arch coquette, This Eleanor.
You would better leave her there Behind the door, Else your heart she'll surely make Extremely sore. So now let us drink our wine, While some other doth recline, Undergoing feelings fine For Eleanor.
PEATiCE BAILEY.

HARVEST. - Lord of the Harvest! Thee we praise In heartfelt song this day. To Thee our harvest hymn we raise, To Thee our tribute pray. Lend us, we ask, a gracious ear, And in Thy courts on high Deign with a Father's love to hear Thy children when theycry— Hear;Lord, in heaven the hymn of praise ' Which here on earth Thy servants raise! "Seed-time and harvest shall not cease," Of old Thou promised so; And, as an emblem of Thy peace, Placed in the heavens Thy bow. And, year by year, with thankfulness. When Spring and Summer flee. We, in the Autumn's balmy days, Fulfilled that promise see. Hear, Lord, in heaven the hymn of praise Which here on earth Thy servants raise! The fields have yielded up once more Their sheaves of golden grain, And with the precious harvest store Our barns are filled again. For this our songs of gratitude To Thee, 0 God! ascend; To Thee, the Giver of all good, Our best, our heavenly Friend. • Hear, Lord, in heaven the hymn of praise Which here on earth Thy servants raise! Lord, when the end of earth shall come, On Thy great harvest-day, May we by Thee be gathered home— ot cast as chaff away. Great Reaper, grant that we may rest For ever in Thy fold, And through all ages, truly blest, Thy loving face behold. Hear, then,io Lord, the endless praise Which we in heaven to Thee shall raise. Preston, Oct. 14th, 1886. EXCELSIOR.

Following is a comparative statement of the tough- ness of various woods :—Ash, 100; beech, 85; cedar of Lebanon, 84; larch, 83; sycamore and common walnut, each 68; occidental plane, 66; oak, hornbeam, and Spanish mahogany, each 62; teak and acacia, each 58; elm and young chestnut, 52. e - The following conversation occurred in the French language. It loses, we fear, none of its significance by being turned into English :—" My good woman, have you only that one cow ?" "Yes, sir, only this one." "How much milk a day does she give?" "Ten quarts." I "And how much do you sell ?" "Fifty quarts every morning." *- A gentleman once asked a little girl, an only child, I how many sisters she had, and was told "three or four." Her mother asked Mary, when they were alone, what induced her to tell such an untruth. "Why, mamma„' cried Mary, "I did not want him to think you were so poor that ycu hadn't but one child. Wouldn't he have I thought we were drefful poor ?" Mrs. B. is one of those energetic, quick-motioned women who carry their work by assault. One day she had started across the room on some errand, but mid- way forgot what it was. "What was I going for ?" she asked aloud. Two-year-old, seated on the floor, and always liable to be swept up in one of his mother's hurricane passages, asked meekly, "Was oo gem'— for me?" I,*:, • i The very recentmost agony is for a lady to have her photograph taken, full length panel, and then after hav- ing elaborately dressed the picture in silk and laces, to send it to her best young man. The true significance of this is not to be understood by the average acute young man. It means, "That's about the style I shall expect t,o dress." Whereupon he goes and gets introduced to a ntore economical girl. ;Lord M—, whith no very large portion of either wit or wisdom, had a very exalted opinion of his own powers. When once in a large company, and expatiating about himself, he made the following pointed i remarks : "When I happen to say a foolish thing, I always burst out laughing." "I envy you your happiness, my Lord, then," said Charles Townsend; "for you must certainly liwe the merriest life of any man in Europe." 'Say, mister, did you see a dog come by here that looked as if he were a year, or a year and half, or two years old ?" said a Yankee to a countryman at the road- side. "Yes," said the countryman, thinking himself quizzed; "he passed about an hour, or an hour and?a, half, or two hours ago; and is now a mile, or a mile and a half, or two miles ahead; and he had a tail about an inch, or an inch and a half, or two inches long." ".That'll do," said the Yankee.

Stammering,-sais.-Coleridge, is sometimes the cause of a pun. Some one was mentioning in Lamb'slpresence the cold-heartedness of the Duke of Cumberland in pre- venting the Duchess from rushing up to the: embrace o f her son, whom she had not seen for a considerable time, and insisted on her receiving him in state. "How horribly cold it was," said the narrator. "Yes," said Lamb, in his stuttering way, "but -•ou ;know he is the Duke of Cu-cum-her-land." Once they were talking before " Cham," the great French caricaturist, of the effect of a powerful painting upon the mind, and some one said enthusiastically, "The painter with his brush can bring tears to the eye as well as tly-i poet with his lyre." "That is, indeed, true," raffled M. de Noe; "I was in Ary Scheffer's studio yes. terdav, and he was showing me one of his pictures, and, thouili I am not usually in the melting,mood,: I fairly wept for ten minutes." "AL, I had heard that Scheffer was treating a very pathetic subject; and you found his wonderful brush " "Oh, that isn't it; he stuck his wonderful brush in my eye while gesticulating." HIGH-PRICED ART.—" Mv, nit those ere works do TIM into money," remarked a passenger whose breath smelled like a whisky distillery. "It beats all what tools some folk make over pictures. When I was in London I saw a little painting about a foot square that was valued at £l5O. 'Spect some simpleton will come along and buy it. If I had a million of money you'd never catch me paying £l5O for a little painting like that." "That's the way you talk," spoke up:a bashfulZdrummer, "but I'll bet you paid four times astimuch money for a paint- ing not a tenth part as big." "What, me?" "Yes, you." 'What kind of a paintingr "The one on the end of your nose!" Two men were disputing about their powers of en- durance. One said testily to the other, "I bet you that I can hold my right leg in boiling water longer than you en." "Done," said the other, and the steaming, bub- bling water was brought. In went the legs; number one with an air of defiance; number two with an edifying serenity. Number one began to wince; number two called Falmly for the newspaper. Number one began to find it intolerable; number two smiled at the humour of the paper. "In heaven's name," at last exclaimed num- ber one, exasperated by the heat of the water and the coolness of his antagonist, "what is your leg made of ? " " Wood," sententiously replied the other.

On the Friday of the show there was a similar competition, and as no foreigners had entered for the previous day the competitors were nearly all the same ones as before. Miss Morgan generously withdrew to give the others a chance, and the details of the work went on pretty much as before. Sixteen entries, of whom ten came forward, were divided into two lots, with a final try of six. Cream supplied at 55 deg. Fahr., cooled down with ice, the use of the latter being a new feature compared with last year's contests. In this case Miss Connell was placed first, Miss Holmes second, and Mrs. Holmes third. The two latter have been both the first prize winners in previous years. From 201 b. of cream the first-prize girl made 81b. 10oz. of butter, the second 81b. 120 z., and the third 81b. 10oz. All the competitors used barrel churns with internal dashers, with the exception of one end over end, while circular and Albany butterworkers were both used. The judges were Mr. Gibbons, Mr. Carrick, and Mr. Mark Vice ; and the marked excellence of the butter made by all the six of the final try made it a very difficult matter to decide the order of merit. A " v.h.c." was awarded to Mrs. Harman, Mrs. Stevenson, and Miss Brady. Dur- ing the contests the working dairy was visited by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress, with daughter, Lord Cork, and Lord and Lady Vernon, all of whom remained some time to see the competition. LIME AS A FERTILISER.—The most common fertiliser is lime, either burnt from limestone or oyster-shells, or in a state of sulphate commonly called gypsum or plaster of Paris. There are few soils which are not benefited by its application. It does not seem to be of very great importance whether it be added to the soil in the shape of lime direct from the 'kiln, slacked, or in the form of carbonate, as it occurs in chalk, marble, or marl. The essential point is extreme fineness. The finer it is the more easily it enters into combination and produces its effect. This purpose is always better attained by burnt lime, whatever it may be burnt from, whether limestone, marble, or shells. Lime has a great affinity for carbonic acid, which is one of the ever-present constituents of the atmosphere: so that, upon the exposure of caustic lime, it soon becomes carbonated. Caustic, or fresh-burned lime, when put in contact with organic matter, either animal or vegetable, causes immediate action and rapid decomposition. Carbonate of lime is less active; and, although it has lost its power by the absorption of car- bonic acid, still it produces important changes in soils. As we have seen, soils are mixtures of salts and or- ganic matter containing air and water in their pores. Here lime acts, decomposing the organic matter and freeing carbonic acid. It again acts upon the alkaline and earthy salts, decomposing them, and enabling them to form such combinations as' the plants require. Chemistry has rendered important services to agricul- ture in many ways, none more than by analysis of soils; not by informing us of the difference between poor and rich soils, nor by pointing out the specific wants of the farmer,,, or the particular applications to each soil so desired by him, but by showing us that certain com- binations exist in the soil ; that a simple silicate of alumina is barren, experience proving that the mere THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. application of manure to it will not give fertility; POULTRY AT THE LONDON DAIRY SHOW. though lime being added on common clay, a double The eleventh annual show of the British Dairy , added to a clay soil destroys that sticky, waxen, censist- silicate of alumina and lime will be found, which, in Farmers' Association was held last week, and, as usual, the was a large display of poultry thereat. COTTAGE GARDENING.

Bnoccom.—Winds have been blowing* with sufficient I force to loosen these and Borecole about the collars, and it would be as well to examine them and make them firm once more. When this has been neglected we have seen the cavity, 'formed by the movement of the plant, full of ice in frosty weather, and, though this may not affect the class of winter vegetables known as Borecole, it imperils the existence of the first-named. In some parts of the country gardeners are so anxious to secure the crop that they lay the plants on their sides with their heads to the north at this season of the year, in order to check succulent growth, and any excitement from sun- shine, and its destructive influence after a frost. The operation is performed by taking a spadeful of soil out in front of the plant and placing it further out, and with the spade form it into a miniature sloping bank for the head, or rather the base of it, to rest upon; then prize the plant with the spade into an inclined position, and pack soil over any roots that may be exposed. If .the plants are large it may be necessary to take more soil out in front in order to admit of the soil adhering to the root. In winters of ordinary severity the crop is toler- ably safe without being interfered with; but if a hard winter follows a mild, moist autumn, and the plants are gorged with aqueous particles, they are in the worst pos- sible condition to resist frost, which has very little effect on dry tissue, and it is a known law that the power of a plant to resist frost is in the inverse ratio of the quan- tity of water contained in its system. AULIFLOITERS.—Autumn giant, or any other variety that may be expanding at this season of the year, should have the longest leaves turned over the flower after the first night's frost, lest the next frost should be severe enough to injure them, which the first rarely is. Should some good heads be at any time found in a frozen state, they may be saved if carefully cut and placed in cold water, or they may be pulled up and taken into a dark room before the sun's rays strike upon them, for in this case it is the sudden thaw that destroys, and not the frost. August sown plants of Cauliflowers should have a few pricked in a frame, the interior of which should be nearly filled with half decayed leaves and soil, so as to bring the plants near the glass. In the absence of a frame, select a dry corner facing south, against the wall of the residence or building, where an old window sash may rest over them. These kind of articles are some- times picked up very cheap, and by making incisions in the bars the water will not lodge, if a moderate slope is given to the frame. Even an old door or shutter placed over them during heavy rains, sleet, or snow will very often save them from the action of frost. THE FRONT GARDEN.—It is not too late to insert cut- tings of such herbaceous plants as antirrhinums, pen- stemons, phloxes, rudbeekias, centranthus, and others, and if they could be provided with glass protection it would ensure their rooting 'much 'quicker than if left exposed. Calceolarias are the last to be propagated of what are termed summer bedding plants. They are best inserted in a 'frame, with the light kept moderately close for a few days. The frame is usually fixed with a north or west aspect, and if the cuttings are watered when put in they seldom require any more before the turn of the year. The chief points to be observed are firm planting, shading to prevent drooping, ventilating to prevent damping, and slight protection in severe weather. In February or March, if they have done well, they will be too thick in their nursery bed, and must be provided with more space, and for this purpose a shallow trench, a yard wide, and of any length, may be formed with boards along the side, kept in their places by cross pieces, to prevent the side of the trench falling in. Here they may be planted six or eight inches distant, after adding a liberal portion of half-decayed leaves or decayed manure to the soil, so that at the subsequent lifting there will be something that will be pretty sure to adhere to the roots. The conduct of these plants, after their re- moval into the flower beds, has been a perplexing prob- lem to gardeners of recent years, for just as they com- mence to flower they die one by one, the whole plant becoming suddenly paralysed. Various suggestions as to the cause have been thrown out, but nothing conclu- sive has been hit upon. Generally they do better in Lancashire and the north than in other parts of England. THE GREENHOUSE.—Chrysanthemums forward in bud are no longer safe in the open air, as they will only with- stand a few degrees of frost with immunity; they should consequently be housed without any further delay. But first free the plants of all dead foliage and examine them as to mildew, which will be readily seen under the leaves if the plants are turned over on their sides. The only remedy for this that we are acquainted with is flower of sulphur mixed with water, and applied with the syringe whilst the plants are on their sides. The sulphur is best mixed in a small vessel first, and when it is got into a pasty state it will readily mix with the water intended for syringing. It is perfectly harmless to the plant when thus applied, so that there is no danger in using too much, but a handful to a gallon will be as much as will pass freely through the syringe. Agitate the water each time before filling the syringe, or at the finish the sul- phur will be in the pail instead of on the plant.

Evidence of the recovery of the bodies having been given, Inspector Butcher repeated the story which the boy made when brought to the Police Station. Robert Leader, the boy, replied, when he asked him if he had a mother and brothers, " They are dead," Asked how long since they died, he replied, " Not. long." Gradually the boy told him that they had gone into the water, and that it was light when they went ill. He said his mother and little brothers went ill together, and that. his brother asked him to go in, but he was afraid. He added that his mother bought some gin.

The Coroner intimated that the lad eculd not be called, because he was too young to be sworn. The Coroner, in summing up, said tha inference from the evidence was that the man and the woman had not lived very happily. The story was extraor- dinary, and had capability of credence. The jury returned an open verdict, "Found drowned."
It is now considered certain that the body of Mrs. Leader and the infant were washed out of the lock into the river, and it is feared they will no; be recov- ered for some days.

The celebrated red Shorthorn bull calf, Lord Thirsk, has been sold by Mr. T. Strickland to go to Germany. The price has not transpired. The "Rural New Yorker," commenting upon the tor- ture of dairy cows by flies, remarks that "good farmers point with scorn at a man who keeps his cattle out in cold freezing weather," and then asks "How much more cruel is it than the usual summer treatment ?" KENT AND SUSSEX FARMERS are already reducing the number of their farm hands in view of increased depres- sion during:the coming winter. A great many labourers left their employment on Michaelmas Day, and hundreds of them, it is stated, will be unable to find fresh engage- ments. Last winter the farmers kept on only just enough men to do the actual amount of work required, and this year they will follow the same coarse. The agricultural outlook in Sussex and the Weald of Kent is especially gloomy. PIGS SUCKING COWS.-A story is told of a curious in- cident which happened in the neighbourhood of Craven Arms, Shropshire. It is as follows :-A farmer owned several cows, which until recently had been giving heavy yields of milk. Latterly the morning supply has been so sparse that it was hardly worth the trouble of fetchine the cows up to milk: Consternation prevailed in the household, and various causes were given for the de- crease. Some suggested that hedgehogs sucked the cows; others, more practical, whispered" tramps "-meanwhile a neighbouring farmer saw with wonder the increasing obesity of the pigs. Their food was of the ordinary description, but they thrived upon it as surely pigs had never thriven before. They were pictures of health- round, glossy, playful, and good-tempered. What could it be? One day the two farmers met at market, over a friendly glass. The one dilated on the story of his cows who gave no milk; the other remarked upon the grand feeding qualities of his swine. As the owner of the cows drove home a thought occurred to him. Was it possible there was some connection between his milkless cows and his neighbour's obese porkers? A watch was set, and the secret discovered. The neighbour's pigs were in the habit of sucking the cows dry every morning. No wonder they became fat and rosy. New milk evidently agreed with them, and they liked to draw it for them- selves. div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
THE STATE OF IRELAND.

-- - A Cork correspondent telegraphs that Timothy Burley, the tenant who resisted eviction at Ctotleview, near CI ona- kilty, on Tuesday, left his fortification in the evening with his band of defenders for the purpose or indulging in rejoic- ings at the victory over the bailiffs. They were all arrested by the police.

Five- men, alleged to be Moonlighters, named Coakley, McAuliffe, Bronii4an, Lane, and O'Connor, were brought into Listowel, on Sunday, under a strong escort of p3lice, from near the village of Brosna, eight miles distant, and were charged on Monday. It is alleged that when searched there were a six-chambered revolver and a num.- ber of disguises found on Coakley; and it is added that one chamber of the revolver appeared to have been recently discharged.

Mr. Dillon and other Nationalist Members of Parliament addressed a large meeting at Woodford, on t,unday. Mr. Dillon said that if the landlords refused what the tenants offered, there was no course open to the latter out to form a fund of these offered rents, to upport the struggle. He concluded a lone speech by urging the tenants to be in no hurry to use Lord Ashhourne's Land Act. The market was falling fast, and would get lower if the people carried out the determined policy of the Woodford tenants. News of a deliberate attempt to murd,r a land agent in Kerry comes from Trahie. On Wednesday night Mr. Cecil Vandeleur, agent for Captain Oliver, a landowner, was re- turning from Causeway to Tralee on a car, when three shots were tired at him from behind a hedge on the roadside. Mr. Vandeleur, who was not hit, fired several shots from his re- volver, but with what effect is not known. He drove on to Tralee, and there found that both horse and car had been struck by slugs or pebbles. No arrests have so far been made.

Archbishop Walsh, addressing the pupils of the Chris- tian Brothers' Schools, Dublin, referred to the suggestions that by conceding the demands of the Roman Catholic Hierarclsy they might be detached from the National cause. He said: The time has come to make a plain and public declaration that never with our consent shall this question of education or any other such question form the matter of any corrupt bargain or of any bargain at all, between any section Irish people, laity or clergy, priests or bishops, and any English party whether in office or in Opposi- tion. The alleged Captain Moonlight, arrested last aveek at Boherbee (Cork), was brought bafore Mr. Dunsterville, resi- dent magistrate, at Kilrush, on Saturday. He gave his name as John Keeffe, "or anything else." He was charged with raiding for arms on September 7th, and intimi- dation. In reply to the Court, he sai4 he didn't want to bother with an attorney, and told the magistrate to "hurry on with his business." Incriminating evidence as to his raiding and threatening householders on vaious occasions was given, and on the application of Inspector Wynne, the prisoner was remanded. THE BELFAST RIOTS COMMISSION. On Saturday the principal witness was Mr. Cobain, M.P., whose letter in a local newspaper, with the expression "liveried assassins," as applied to the police, has been de- clared by many witnesses to have instigated Orange violence against the constabulary. Mr. Cobain said that the old local police of Belfast were in evely respect preferable to the Irish constabulary. He knew of many cases of cruelty to prisoners taken during the riots. The constabulary had shown recklessness of consequences in firing on the people. At the sitting of the Commission, on Monday, the Rev. Dr. Hanna, examined by Mr. Jastice Day, said, speaking on behalf of the entire Protestant community of Belfast, that the attempt to introduce Home Rule and Mr. Morley's ap- pointment as Chief Secretary, roused the indignation of the Protestant community, especially as the latter had stated that the police would take care that "hot-beaded Loyalists would be brought into subjection." The feeling reached its highest pitch at the beginning of Jane, and the threats of the Catholic navvies at Queen's Island were the sparks that lighted the flame of civil war. He defended his sermon characterising the police as " uniformed mur- derers."

Mr. William Sinclair, Presbyterian missionary, was the first witness examined on Tuesday. He gave an account of the rioting on the Shanishill road, and characterised the tiring of the police as most wicked, desperate, and uncalled- for.

On Wednesday several witnesses were examined; A Catholic gentleman, a barrister by profession, recommended the alteration of the law that claims for damage during riots might be heard by arbitrators or the recorder. Catho- lics mainly suffered in the riots, and thuy got scant justice from the Corperation, which was exclusively Protestant. "In fact," he said, "a lamb before a jury of butchers had as much chance of a fair trial as a Catholic before the Cor- poration." Incendiary newspapers should be mulcted. On Thursday, the Loyalist Defence Committee called a number of witnesses at the Belfast inquiry to show that the police were influenced by party feeling, and that the re- newal of the riots on the 13th and 31st July was due to attacks on Protestants by Nationalists. Mr. Ewart, made some suggestions for preventing riots in the future, advocating among other things the reorganisation of the Police on a less military basis. He thought the bands and processions could hardly be stopped in Belfast without their being stopped elsewhere in Ireland. He was in favour of severe sentences upon stone-throwers and the flogging of persons caught attacking and looting houses. He would have two stipendiary magistrates, one a Protestant and the other a Roman Catholic. Mr. Justice Day said he feared such a system of dual appointments would only protbng the differences of the People of Belfast.

WHERE THE STRAIN Is.—Philanthropist: rOON man, the hod must indeed tire you.—Mr. Murphy: 'Tis nothing, sir, in comparison with mounting the ladder. Bebe is given two oranges because she has behaved well. "Come," said her mother, "don't be greedy. Give one of them to your little brother." Bebe, with very good grace, holds out the fruit to her brother. You may choose said she but don't take the biggest one."

George Colman was an admirable punster. Sheridan once said, when George made a successful hit, "I hate a pun; but Colman always reconciles me to the infliction." He was once asked if he knew Theadore Hook. "Oh, yes," was his reply, "Hook and I (eye) are old associates."

Bridget was called in and informed that the census- taker wished to see her. "The sinsus taker, is it? Be gora, and it is mysilf that came a thousand leages across the wather to have my anises taken from me? Howly virgin! protect a poor woman who has niver a bit of sinse to spare." On a slow-going railway recently a passenger stopped the guard and asked, "Why don't the trains go faster ?" "They run fast enough to suit us. If you don't like the speed, why don't you got out and walk," was the re- joinder. "I would," said the passenger, settling himself back in his seat, "but that my friends won't come to meet me until the train arrives, and I don't want to be waiting about the station for two hours." There was once a vessel belonged to Kirkcaldy, 'twas called " Cat-luggit Sow of Kirkcaldy." The master's name was Willie Willison and the mate's Jamie Jamieson. The master, getting drunk one day at a foreign port, was rowed out to his vessel in a state of mental obnubilation. Just upon being towed up he awoke, and, seeing his vessel without recognising it, called out, "What ship, ahoy?" "The Cat-luggit Sow of Kirkcaldy," replied a voice from the gangway. "The master's name ?" "Willie Willison." "The mate's ?" "Jamie Jamieson." "Lord keep my puir wits !" cried the amazed skipper; "twa Jamie Jamiesons, and twa Willie Willisons, and. twa Cat-luggit Sows, a' frae the lang toon o' Kirkcaldy, and me to ken naething about it—gude guide us!" How THE QUEEN DINES.—Any of her Majesty's sub- jects who may desire to know the ceremonial of Queen Victoria's dining-table can, says the Pall ifall Gazette, hear all about it from a French journalist. All the de- tails are interesting and some of them surprising. Exactly fifteen minutes before the dinner-hour the guests are ranged in a semi-circle, the band plays "The Roast Beef of Old England," and to this appropriate and characteristic music the Queen enters the presence-room; she shakes hands with the ladies and salutes the gentle- men. Then she passes to the dining-room, taking pre- cedence of all her guests. As she looks down the table she finds her own family (so Many of them as there are) all ranged on her left, and the guests of the day seated on her right hand. At this meal the Queen always wears gloves, unless it should be a State meal. On two points the rules of Court etiquette are very strict. 'No one is allowed to address a remark to her Majesty directly. If a guest thinks he has something which may interest the Royal hostess he mentions it to a fellow- guest. The latter discusses it, and so, filtered and at second-hand, it reaches the Queen. There is no rule, however, which prevents the Queen of England from asking any question she likes of any guest at the table. One other regulation bears peremptorily on the invited. Instantly the Queen has finished with a course every guest at table must also end. Curiously enough, this French chronicler gives no details of what happens when the Lord Mayor dines at Windsor.

illimisrxits--whose professional labours necessitate long in- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating. comforting, and capable of snstainina exLausted natn,e.as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure. Beware a imittitions.—Advt.

div.p: EXCITEMENT IN ROCHESTER.
TEE COMMOTION CAUSED BY THE STATEMENT
OF A PHYSICIAN.

An unusual article from the Rochcfster, -Democrat and Chronicle was published in this paper recently, and. has been the subject of much conver- sation, both in professional circles and on the street. Apparently it caused more commotion in Rochester, as the following from the same paper shows : Dr. J. B. lienion, who is well known, not only in Rochester, but in nearly every part of America sent an extended. article to this paper, a few clays since, which was duly published, detailing his re- markable experience and rescue from what seemed to be certain death. It would be impossible to enumerate the personal inquiries which have been made at our office as to the validity of the article, but they have been so numerous that further in- vestigation of the subject was deemed an editorial necessity. With this end in view a representative of this -paper called on Dr. Henion at his residence, when the following interview occurred: "That article of yours, Doctor, has ' created quite a whirlwind. Are the statements about the terrible condition you were:in, and. the way you were res- cued, such as you can sustain?" " Every one of them, and many additional nes. "I was brought so low by neglecting the first and most simple systems. I did not think I was sick. It is true I had frequent headaches; felt tired most of the time; could eat nothing one day, and was ravenous the next; felt dull, indefinite pains, and my stomach was out of order, but I did not think it meant anything serious. • The medical .profession have been treating symptoms instead of diseases for years, and it is high time it ceased. We doctors have been clipping off the twigs when we should trike at the root. The symptoms I have just men- tioned or any unusual action or irritation of the water channels indicate the approach of Bright's disease even more than a cough announces the com- ing of consumption. We do not treat the cough, but try to help the lungs. We should not waste our time trying to relieve the headache, stomach, pains about the baly or other systems, but go directly to the kidneys, the source of most of these ailments. "This, then, is what you meant when you said that more than one-half the deaths which occur arise from Bright's disease, is it, Doctor?" "Precisely. Thousands of so-called diseases are torturing people to-day, when in reality it is Brie-it's disease in some one of its many forms. It is a by monster, and the slightest symp- toms should. strike terror to every one who has them. I canlook back and recall hundreds of deaths which physicians declared at the time were caused by paralysis, apoplexy, heart disease, pneumonia, malarial fever, and other common complaints, which see now were caused by Bright's disease." "And did all these cases have simple symptoms at first ?" "very one of :them, and might have been cured as I was by the timely use of the same remedy —Warner's Safe Cure. I am getting my eyes thoroughly open in this matter, and think I am helping others to see the facts and their possible danger also." Puny satisfied of the truth and force of the Doc- tor's words, the reporter bade him good day, and toiled on Mr. Warner at his establishment, North St Paul-street. At first Mr. Warner was inclined to be reticent, but learning that the information desired was about the alarming increase of Bright's disease, his manner changed instantly, and he spoke very earnestly: "It is true that Bright's disease has increased wonderfully, and we find, by reliable statistics that in the past ten years its growth has been :250 per cent. Look at the prominent men it has car- ried off—Everett, Sumner, Chase, Wilson, Carpen- ter, Bishops Haven and Peck, and others. This is terrible, and shsws a greater growth than that of ally other known complaint. It should be plain to every one that something must be done to check this increase, or there is no knowing where it may end?' "Do you think many people are afflicted with it to-day who do not realise it, Mr. Warner ?" "Hundreds of thousands. I have a striking example of this truth, which has just come to my notice. A prominent professsor in a New Orleans medical college was lecturing before his class on the subject of Bright's disease. He had various fluids under microscopic analysis, and was showing the students what the indications of this terrible malady:were. In order to show the contrast be- tween healthy and unhealthy fluids, he had pro- vided a vial, the contents of which were drawn from his own person. And, now, gentlemen,' lie said, as we have seen the unhealthy indications, I will show you how it appears in a state of perfect health,' and he submitted his own fluid to the usual test. As he watched the results his countenance suddenly changed—his colour and command both left him, and in a trembling voice he said: Gentle- men, I have made a painful discovery: / have Bright's disease of the kidneys;' and in less than a year he was dead." "You know of Dr. Henion's case ?" " Yes, I have both read and heard of it." "It is very wonderful, is it not ?" "A very prominent case, but no more so than a great many others that have come to my notice as having been cured by the same means." " You believe, then, that Bright's.",disease can be cured ?" "I know it can. I know it from the experi- ence of hundreds, of prominent persons who were given up to die by both their physicians and friends." "You speak of your own experience, what was

it." "A fearful one. I had felt languid and unfitted for business for years. But I did not know what ailed me." When, however, I found it was kidney difficulty, I thought there was little hope, and so did the doctors. I have since learned that one of the physicians of this city pointed me out to a gen- tleman on the street one day, saying, there goes a man who will be dead within a year. I believe his words would have proven true if I had not fortu- nately secured and used the remedy now known as Warner's Safe Cure." "And this caused you to manufacture it ?'' "No, it caused me to investigate, I went to the principal cities, saw physicans prescribing and using , it, and I therefore determined, as a duty I owed MI- I manity and the suffering, to bring it within their reach, and now it is known in every part of I America, is sold in every drug store, and has become! a household necessity. The reporter left Mr. Warner, much impressed with the earnestness and. sincerity of his statement, and next paid a visit to Dr. S. A. Lattimore at his residence on Prince-street. Dr. Lattimore, al- though busily engaged upon some matters connec- ted with the State Board of Health, of which he is one of the analysts, courteously answered the ques- tions that were propounded him: " Did you make a chemical analysis of the case of Mr. H. 11. Warner some three years ago, Doctor ? ' " Yes, sir." "What did this analysis show you ? " "The presence of albumen and tube casts in great • abundance." "And what did the symptoms indicate? " " A serious disease of the kidneys." "Did you think Mr. Warner could recover?" "No, sir. I did not think it possible. It was sel- dom, indeed, that so pronounced a case had, up to that time, ever been cured." "Do you know anything about the remedy which cured him ?" "Yes, I have chemically analysed it, and upon critical examination, find it entirely free from any poisonous or deleterious substances.' We publish the foregoing statements in view of the commotion which the publicity of Dr. llenion's article has caused, and to riaet the protestations which have been made. The standing of Dr. lien- ion, Mr. Warner, and Dr. Lattimore in the com- munity is beyond question, and the statements :they make cannot for a moment be doubted. They
Iconclusively show that Bright's disease of the kidneys is one of the most deceptive and dangerous of all diseases, that it is exceedingly common, alarmingly increasing, and that it can be cured.

div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE BULGARIAN CRISIS. RUSSIAN POLICY COMPLICATIONS.—REPORTED LOAN TO BULGARIA. VIENNA, MONDAY.—An inspired communication from St. r Petersburg, forwarded to the " Politische Correspondenz," thus sets forth what purports to be the policy of the Rus- sian Government : Russian occupation would only take place in case of unfcreseen events, and providing it were de- sired by the large majority of the population, as then only would it appear legitimate and be effected without bringing on international complications. In the meantime Russia cannot do better than observe an expectant attitude, and avail herself of those rights she possesses in virtue of the Berlin Treaty in order to prevent any settlement of the Bul- garian question that is inconsistent with her interests or self-respect. This applies more particularly to the eventu- ality of Prince Alexander's re-election. The Russian Go- vernment are of opinion that. if Prince Alexander were to be re-elected he would only, accept the throne as the inde- pendent ruler of United Bulgaria, and that England would negotiate with the Sultan for the effective union ot Eastern Roumel:a with Bulgaria, probably with success. They trust, however, that Europe, in recognition of their correct and pacific attitude, will not sanction what has received the veto of the Cabinet of St. Petersburg. The Russian Govern- ment have also arrived at this decision because the antici- pate that the occupation of Bulgaria, although it might perhaps not be opposed by the other Powers, might furnish them with the pretext for a policy which would weaken Russia and exclude her from European deliberations. The Russian Government hope, by their present attitude, to remove all mistrust of their intentions, and that considera- tions resulting from the necessity of maintaining peace will triumph over any hostile disposition entertained towards them. VrEtora, MONDAY NIGHT.—I learn from an excellent source in Paris that the financial difficulties of the Bulga- rian Government have been removed by the spontaneous offer of a loan of ten million francs, which has been placed at their disposal without the smallest security being asked in return. The generous friend of Bulgaria who has thus come forward to assist a struggling nationality is a well- known and highly esteemed American of great wealth re- siding in Paris. Those who know him, or even know of his many acts of generosity, will not need to be told his name. This, however, I am not at liberty to mention, much as I , could wish to do so. GENERAL KAULBARS.

Acting upon instructions from General Kattlhars, the Rmsian Consul at Rnstchuk, on Saturday sent a note to the Prefect protesting against the elections, and declaring them to be illegal. The Prefect returned the Note, declar- ing that such a communication should be addressed to the Central Government. It is stated that General Kaulbars is engaged in drawing up a report to the Czar upon the results of his mission. It is believed that he has abandoned all intention of continu- ing his tour. A Berlin correspondent says he hears from a trustworthy source that the recently issued circular of Lord Iddesleigh on the Bulgarian question reflects the hope of a normal and peaceful issue of the crisis, but does not invite the Powers to any particular policy with regard to it. GENERAL GOUIiKO TO REPLACE GENERAL KAULBARS. VIENNA, TTlrßSDAY.—lntelligence received here from St. Petersburg states that it is proposed to replaceereneral Ka:nl- - by General Gourlm, who has been summoned to St. Petersburg from Warsaw.

OUTBREAK OF CHOLERA. IN VIENNA. The first case of cholera which has taken place in Vienna, this season, terminated fatally on Monday. A gentleman who held an important post in connection with the State Railway arrived there on Sunday, from Buda Pesth, being ill with the terrible disease ; and he died in the hos- pital. THE BULGARIAN ELECTIONS DECLARED ILLEGAL. The Prefect received on Tuesday, an official letter from the Russian Consul here, stating that General Kau!bars had requested him to inform the Prefect that the Russian Government did not recognise as leg,il the recent elections to the Sobranje. The Russian Government has received a formal assurance from all the Great Powers that they do not favour Prince Alexander's return to Bulgaria. EGYPT. ENGLISH POLICY AND INFLUENCE.

TROOPS ON THE NILE. CONSTANTINOPLII, SIINDLY. -Ru St ern Pasha recently msde certain representations to Lord Iddesleigh concerning British policy in Egypt, the tenour of which had not, how- ever, transpired. PARIS, TUESDAY,—To judge by the Egyptian correspond- ence of the "Journal des DObats," English influence in that country is being as hotly contested as ever. CAIRO, MONDAY NlGHT.—General Stephenson has or- dered another regiment to proceed to Assouan, as that sta- tion is insufficiently protected, and an advance is shortly expected. AFGHANISTAN. THE FRONTIER COM- MISSION.

ON THE SOUTHERN SLOPES OF THE HINDOO KOOSH (five marches from Cabul) OCT. B.—Sir W. Ridgeway with the main body of the Commission, has safely crossed the Hin- doo Koosh by a succession of passes varying from 10,000 to 15,000 feet in height. During the night of the sth, when encamped at an altitude of 12,000 feet, heavy snow fell, but the last pass was safely crossed the next day. The road is probably closed now. We are to be here until the detached parties under Major Holditch and Captains Maitland, Pea- cock, and Talbot, who are exploring the other passes of the Hindoo Koosh, rejoin us. We expect to reach on the 15th of October the neighbourhood of Cabul, where the Ameer will meet Sir W. Ridgeway. The people are Liendly, and wel- come us everywhere. BURMAH.—THE STATE OF THE COUNTRY. ATTACK ON A TOWN B I INSURGENTS.

RANGOON, MONDAY.—General Macpherson has arrived at Thavetmo, where he is receiving reports from various dis- tricts upon the state of the country. He is expected here ehortiv, and a general movement of troops towards Upper Burmah will it is understood be made early in December. On the 16th instant the town of Ningvan was attacked by a large body of insurgents, who were repulsed. Owing to the fact that many police arms and much ammunition have been found with the insurgents, the Burmese policemen in the Ningyan district have been disarmed. A small column under Lieutenant Coxhead, has been attacked by a large body of insurgents, an.l forced to retire. Lieutenant Cox- head was Severely wounded, and several baggage animals were lost. All the horses in the Ningyan district have been requisitioned for military purposes. ANOTHER REPULSE FOR INSURGENTS IN BURMAH.

Nyngyan was attacked on the lath instant by insurgents, who were repulsed after a sharp fight. Lieutenant Cornwall was wounded. General Macpherson is suffering severely from fever, and is journeying slowly bv wagon. DEATH OF GEN. IuIACPHERSON. RANGOON, WEormsDaY.—General Sir Herbert Macpher- son died of fever at Ernie, on the Irrawaddy, this morning. Major-General White, who is in provisional command of the trooPs, has started for Mandalay. General Macpherson favoured the establishment of martial law, bat Sir C. Ber- nard disagrees with the adoption of that course. THE QUEEN AND THE LATE GENERAL SIR H.

div.head: MACPHERSON.
div.p: MACPHERSON.

- Sum!" TIMRsDAL—At a meeting of the Viceregal Coun- cil to-day the Viceroy referred to the death of General Mac- pherson, and expressed the sorrow which he felt upon learn- ing the sad intelligence. His Excellency announeed that he had received a telegram from the Queen conveying the expression of Her Majesty's deep regret at the calamity which had thus suddenly overtaken the country. div.p: COMMAND.

BOMBAY, THURSDAY--.-LGTe-11-0-I:aT - Sir Frederick Roberts. Commander.in-Chief in India, will amine the command of the Army In l3armah, rendered vacant by the death of Gen. Sir H. Macpherson. FRANCE.—THREATENED RESIGNATIONS.

PARIS, MoerpsY.—The conflict between the Finance Minister and the Commission of ' the Budget has reached an acute stage. Resign or not resign, that is the question put by Bourse men and boulevardiers who interest them- selves in the state of the money market. M. Sadi Carnot is at hopeless variance with M. Wilson and others of that persevering purseholder's way of thinking about the imposi- tion of an incoMe-tax and the best modes of stopping the gap in the deficit of over two millions sterling. PARIS, TuEsnaY.—ln the Chamber of Deputies yester- day, M. Maret addressed an interpellation to the Govern- ment respecting the recent riots at Vierzon, and blamed the attitude taken up by' the authorit,es in the matter. several other Radical men3bers also spoke in a similar sense. M. Sarrein, Minister of the Interior, in reply, justified the action of the Government. who, he declared, had confined them- selves to preserving order and ensuring freedom of labour. The Radical members then laid upon the table a motion ex- pressing regret that the authorities had resorted to force, whereupon M. Prod 1 brought forward a motion of confidence in the Government. The Chamber. notwithstanding the opposition of the Minister of the Interior, agreed to pass to the order of the day pure and simple. M. Sarrein thereupon left the:House, intirsitlng his intention to tender his resig- nation. PARIS, TITESDA.Y.--"At a Cabinet Council, to-daV. M. Sarrein, Minister of the Interior, and M. Sadi Carnot, Minis- ter of Finance, withdrew their resignations. CITY DESTROYED BY CHOLERA.-1,000 DEATHS DAILY.

NEW YORK, SUNDAY.--A telegram which has been' re- ceived here, via San Francisco, givesi:a dreadful account of the outbreak of cholera at Seoul, the capital of Corea. The deaths average 1,000 daill• The bodies of many of the dead are abandoned owing.; tO the difficulty and danger of in. interment. The absolute extinction of the city is threatened.

div.head: EARTHQUAKE IN INDIA.
div.p: EARTHQUAKE IN INDIA.

- BOMBAY, WEDNESDAY. A telegram from Srinagar, Cashmere, states that a severe and prolonged earthquake was felt there early this morning. The damage caused is net yet known. A number of brilliant meteors were observed at the time, and continued until sunrise. Great alarm pre- vails among the inhabitants. THE VATICAN AND CHINA.
