div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of F )otball Clubs gre requested to note tbat reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent tc the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY RULES. WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES V. LATCHFORD 2No.—Played on the ground of the former, and after a good game, victory rested with the True Blues by two tries, three minors to two minors. SANKEY RANGERS V. GANDY'S WALK RANGERS.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Satur- day, and after a rough game ended in a draw in favour of Sankey Rangers by 1 try (Savage) 6 minors to 3 minors (Clare). COCKHEDGE MISSION STAR OF HOPE (2ND TEAM) V. ST. JAMES', LATCHFORD —Played at Latchford on Saturday, the game resulting in a win for the "Star" by one goal anti four minors to nil. For the winners Harrop. Blackmore, and Adcroft played well. SUTTON FREE WANDERERS V. WARRINGTON RANGERS.— These opponents met for the first tinee this season on the ground of the former, at Sutton. An excellent game was played, resulting in a win for Sutton, the score being Sutton on gmal two tries, and three minors to Warrington one try and two minor points. ST. HELENS ALBIONV. SKELMERSDALE ROYAL (2nd team) —These clubs met for the first time on Saturday last,on the ground of the Albionites. The visitors, winning the toss, played with the wind in their favour, and during the first half scored two goals. On changing ends, however, the home team equalised matters, and the game therefore ended in a draw—two goals each. FRODSHAM ROVERS Y. WIDNES HORNETS. This match was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, and, after an evenly-contested game, ended in a victory for the visitors by one goal and five minors to the Hornets three minors. Darlington dropped the goal for the visitors in grand style. Briscoe, Mercer, and Dimelow played a good forward game for the visitors. The becks on both sides played well. WARRINGTON ST. PAUL'S V. SANKEY IST.—This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the latter, and re- sulted in a draw, Sankey scoring three miners to St. Paul's nil. In another account of this match which we have re- ceived. it is stated that Sankey won by one try and three minors to nil. The try was objected to by St. Paul's, but the referee gave in in favour of the home team, and the visitors then walked of the field. LA.TCHFORD V. SALE "A " TEAM—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday last, and after a very fast game ended in a victory for the home team by one try and one minor to one minor. The try was obtained by Joseph Boardman, John Barber taking the place, but failing. For Latchford J Acton and Jos Board- man were the pick of the backs, T Wright, Barnes, J Bar- ber, and W Taylor, forwards. For Sale Coleman and Baker played well. RUNCORN RECREATION (2ND TEAM) V. WESTON.--A match was played between the above teams on Saturday last on the Recreation ground, resulting in an easy victory for the home team by one goal, two tries, eight minors, to nil. In addition to the above, ths Recreation players crossed the visitors' lines three times, but each time had to be brought back owing to Weston disputing the points. Tries obtained by H Grounds, R Hailwood, and W Beckett. Goal kicked by J H Crompton. LOWE Horn TRUE BLUES V. UPHBLLAND.—These clubs met at Upholland, on Saturday last, and a very fast game was played. The Blues were placed at a very oreat disad- vantage,Pilkingten, their centre three-quarter back, getting hurt in the first half,and he had to be assisted off the field. Despite this, they played a very good game, their passing, and especially that of Liptrot'e, being very good. Frodsham (captain) and Unsworth played well for the Blues. The result was—Upholland 1 try and 1 minor to True Blues 4 minors. After the game the Upholland team entertained the True Blues to a knife and fork tea, to which they did ample justice. WIDNES RECREATION (14 MEN) V. RINGLEY.—PIaved at Ringley. The Recreation were without the services of Grundy, Wailing, Norris, Sumner, Tonkies, and Brad- shaw, and the team that they had only consisted of 3A players. The game was well fought, and resulted in a win for the home team, the result being—Ringley 1 try, 3 minors to 1 minor. For the home team Wilkinson was safe at full back, and the brothers Seddon at three-quarters and half played well. The forwards were best represented by Barlow, Chadwick, and Smith. For the Recreation Smith and the McCriries were the pick of the backs, the whole of the forwards striving hard to avert defeat. COCKHEDGE MISSION STAR OF HOPE V. GOOSE GREEN (WIGAN).—Played OR Saturday on the ground of the former, under the new rules. The home captain won the toss and the visitors kicked off. The ball was instantly returned to half-way into touch. After the line out some tough scrim- mages took place, the visitors working the ball into the home quarters The home team, however, managed to get loose and dribbled back to half way, where other tight scrimmages ensued. Some good kicks were then put in by the respective backs, the ball at last being worked over the home line, where it was kicked dead. After dropping out, the home team worked loose and paid a visit to the Wigan territory, but the good defensive nlay of the latter backs prevented any scoring. At the close of a hard game, the result was a draw, neither side scoring a point. ST. HELENS V. SALFORD (A TEAM.) St. Helens club sent a team to try conclusions with the strong "A " team of the Salford club, on Saturday. There was a large num- ber of spectators. The game during the first half was well- contested, the visitors having a slight advantage, but in the second half the home team scored heavily. The score at the close of the game was—Salford three goals, two tries ; St. Helens one goal and one try. Anders and Halton gained the tries, the former kicking the goal. The decision of the referee caused great dissatisfaction amongst the St. Hele 38 team. The St. Helens team was :—J J McLaughlin, full back; E Foreman, J Halton, and A Tickle, three- quarter backs ; A Borthwick (captain) and W Green, half- backs ; C Anders, D McLaughlin, H Varley, J Besnett, R Ellison, T Green, J Leatherbarrow, L Kersh tw, and T Pen- nington, forwards. ST. HELENS RECREATION V. LEIGIL—This match was played at Leigh en Saturday, Leigh winning by one goal, one try (which was disputed), and four minor points to St. Helens Recreation one goal. Great interest was attached to this encounter, as the Recreation were in the semi-final tie for the West Lancashire Cup. From the commencement both sides did their utmost, but Leigh gradually assumed the offensive, and for a time scored nothing but minor points. At length, after a scrimmage near the visitors' goal, Smith, the Leigh captain, got possession, and sent the ball over the crossbar. At half time Leigh had scored one goal and four minors to one minor. After changing Pyke dropped a goal. Leigh now pressed the visitors, and after some finely-contested play James Hurst got possession, and, knocking off his opponents, gained a try, but the place kick failed. This point was disputed, and three of the Re- creation players left the field, and, though repeatedly called back by the Recreation captain, they refused to return, and the game thus came to an abrupt termination. The Recrea- tion captain, along with others conscientiously remained on the field until time had expired. WIDNES V. ASPULL (" A" TEeets.)—Thess teams met on the Aspull ground on Saturday, but owing to the late arrival of the Widnes men they were only able to play a game of 40 minutes' duration, the latter 30 minutes being played in semi-darkness. Aspull winning the toss chose to play down hill with the wind in their favour. Sampson kicked off for Widnes, the bill being well returned and rushed over the Widnes line, Aspull scoring their only minor point. Upon Wilkinson dropping out the Widnes forwards worked the ball to the Aspull line, and compelled them to touch down. Nothing of importance occurred up to half time, with the exception of Gandy crossing the Aspull line, Wid- nes claiming a try, which the referee overruled. In the second part of the game Widnes continually pressed their opponents, the game eventually ending in a draw—Widnes six minors, Aspull one minor. The Widnes backs played a good game considering the slippery state of the ball, whilst of the forwards Foster, Woods, and Cornea were the pick. The following was the Widnes team :—Full back, F. Wii- kinson ; three-quarter backs. E. Pannington, R. Johnson, and J. Wright; half backs, R. Barker and G. Wright; for- wards, Woods, Gandy, Spencer, Comes, Williams, Foster, Sampson, Locke, and Bingham. RUNCORN RECREATION V. 4TH BRIGADE LANCASHIRE ARTILLERY VoLCNTEERS.—The above teams met on the latter's ground on Saturday last, being the opening game of the Brigade club. Acton kicked off for the visitors, the home team having chosen to play with the wind. For a short time the " Rees " pressed their opponents. Woodward relieving by a short run to the centre. A McGeachin soon after got the ball from a scrimmage, and, running round his opponents, gained a splendid try under the posts, which was not improved upon. On change of ends the game stood in favour of the Volunteers by one try to nil. The " Rees " now played up well together, taking flee bell over the home line, but only a touch-in-goal resulted. On the drop-out, the ball was taken back, the Brigade saving close to their line, a scrimmage being formed, from which S Abrams dropped a neat goal. The oval being again started, A Mc- Geachin and Woodward put in some good play, and for a short time the ball was kept in the visitors' half, until John- son put a long kick into touch. From a line-out S Booth dribbled to the Brigade line, and, in trying to pick up, missed a good try, a touchdown only being scored. The play was then carried on in the centre until the cell of time, a good game ending in favour of Ruecorre by one goal and two minor points to one try. A McGeachin and T Wood- ward played grandly in the backs, and D Parr and W Parry forward, for the Volunteers; Abrams and Pendlebury be- hind, with Worrell and Pennington in the front, being best for the " Recs." RUNCORN (2ND TEAM) V. LIVERPOOL ATHLETIC.—This match was played at Fairfield, on Saturday, and resulted in an easy win for the visitors by two goals, six tries, and eight minors, to their opponents' one minor. Wilcock kicked off for the home team, and Runcorn soon showed their superiority. Play for some time took place in the visitors' twenty-five, when Griffiths came through the scrimmage with the ball, and made a splendid dribble to the
THE EXAMENEP, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 23, 1886.

home line, but, kicking too hard, lost possession. Shortly after the drop out Stubs got over, no goal resulting. A little later Morton put in a nice run to the visitors' quar- ters, but Abrams replied with a dribble t. the home line, and picking up passed to Bowyer, which enabled the latter to cross the line, the kick at goal again failing. After the drop out Shingler got away to the visitors' quarters with the ball, only to be returned by Jones, and this player, fol- lowing his kick well up, gained the third try closs to touch, Brazendale making a grand attempt at goal. Wilcock dropped out. and Peters, Dodd, age Morton followed well up and took the ball to the visitors' line and tried hard to score, but were prevented by the splendid back play of the visitors. The visitors' forwards' headed by Stubbs, Han- cock, and Dolan, now removed danger, and from some loose play Whitley soon got over, but Brazendale failed to add to its value. This brought half time, with the score four tries and six minors to nil. On changing ends Andrews restarted. Peters and Wilcock experienced some hard lines, making several attempts to get in, but were foiled by the excellent tackling of Clare, Davies, and Whitley. Davies soon after got away to the home quarters, when Whitley got hold and dropped a really clever goal. The Runcorn krerards kept the ball well in the Athletic quarters, and during some quick exchanges Davies got hold and secured a clever try behind the posts, from which Brazondale placed a goal. From now till the call of time. the ball was con- stantly in the home quarters. Whitley and Andrews gaining tries, which, however, were not improved upon. On behalf of Runcorn all the backs played well, and the forwards showed rare combined form. The home team backs were

rather weak, Wilcock, Thomas, Jones, and Greenfield being the pick of the forwards. The Athletic played with four- teen men. Teams :—Runcorn Brazendale, back; E Lunt, T Davies, and T Whinyates. three-quarter backs; A Clare and G Whitley, half backs ; Dunbavand (captain), W Jones, W Stubbs, F Hancock, T Abrams, E Andrews, J Bowyer, R Dolan, and J Gittins, forwards. Athletic: W Morton, back ; P Morton, G Haines, and J Morton, three-quarter backs; C F Dodd and W Peters, half backs; It Wil- cock (capekin), J H Jones, T Greenfield, J Fraser, J lrow, Thomas, H Porter, and W Lawton-Goodman, for., wards. WARMERGTON " A. " v. LYIIIII iST.—These teams met at Warrington on Saturday last. Whittle opened the game by kicking off for the home team, and in less than three minutes Appleton, from a pass by the former, secured a try. The attempt at goal, which was made by Ashurst, however proved fruitless. Oct resuming the game the play was kept in neutral ground for a short time, when Appleton, again securing the ball, essayed at goal, but the leather was charged down by the visitors' forwards, and immediately afterwards the visitors were compelled to touch down. Gleave dropped out, bet owing to an infringement of the off-side rule the ball was called back and a scrimmage formed, from which Ashby obtained possession and relieved his side with a powerful kick, but all to no effect, as it was returned with equal precision by the never-failing Randal's. Speakman now gave Appleton a beautiful pass, which en- abled the latter to drop a splendid goal. The visitors now slightly pressed the home team, when Jones came to the rescue by a grand dribble and was only prevented scoring by Ashby, who was subsequently compelled to touch down. The game had net grown much older when Appleton secured the ball from Whittle and dropped another goal, to the de- light of some most enthusiastic spectators, when directly afterwards half time was called. On resuming the game, the Warrington forwards, who, by the way, are now noted for their fine dribbling rowers, took possession of the ball and dribbled down the field, which resulted in Lymm touch- ing down, and in less than five minutes afterwards they were again compelled to act in a similar manner. The drop out by Wilson was charged down by Eyes, and from a scrimmage which followed Speakman obtained a capital try, which he converted into a goal. The visitors were now completely overplayed, and Boardman, from a pass by Appleton, managed to ground the ball over the line, which Speakman improved upon. This try was quickly followed by another from Randal's, Speakman again doing the need- ful. Oct the game being recommenced Boardman got in the best run of the day, and was only collared near the goal line after having run from within his'own 25, and Appleton, gaining possession, finally deposited it over the goal line, but Speakman was not so fortunate as in his previous attempts. Nothing further after this was scored, and when time was called Warrington were declared the winners by five goals, two tries, and four minors, to nothing. Teams: Warrington—Full back, Randalls ; three-quarter backs, Boardman, Appleton, and Unsworth ' • half backs, Whittle (captain) and Speakman ; forwards, Jones, Molyneux, Nevins, Littlewood, Walsh, Cragan, Eyes, Ashurst, and Tel- ford. Lymm—Full back, Ashby ; three•quarter backs, Wil- son, Neil and Holt ; half backs, Chantler and H A Clegg ; forwards, Gleave, Kirk, Addenbrooke, Masters, Morris, Per- rin, Gibbons, Hatton, and Davies WIDNES V. ASPULL.

The second match this season on the Widnes ground was played on Saturday. The opposing team was Aspull, the runners-up in the West Lancashire and Border Towns Rug- by Union Cup Competition. Widnes had their full team, while Aspull were short of Roberts and Cartwright. Play commenced at half-past three, a large number of spectators lining the ropes. Owing to the recent rains the ground was very wet and sloppy, but notwithstanding this some good play was shown. Aspull won the toss, and elected to play up hill. Kiddie accordingly kicked off, and one of Aspull's backs Mulling, Widnes rushed the ball over, a minor result- ing. After the line out the ball was taken into the Widnes half, where some good loose play was indulged in. Widnes were being pressed, when Bingham nicely relieved. Morris obtained hold in the Widnes half, and by a splendid run transferred play to Aspull quarters. The ball getting into the hands of Hulme, that player made a fine run in, to the delight of the Aspull votaries. Pilkington tried the kick at goal, but failed to register the premier point. Shortly after being brought out the ball was on the loose in the home team's quarters, when Harding obtained hold and transferred play a considerable way down the fold by a fine run. He passed to Plumpton when collared, and that player sent the ball flying over the heads of his opponents, Pilkington re- turning. Widnes rushed the ball down to Aspull's quarters, where Haddock saved in fine style. Widnes again pressed Aspull, an Pilkington this time prevented operations, the ball being afterwards taken into Widnes territory. Morris here obtained possession, and put in a fine run to the visi- tors' 25, and had he retained the ball instead of attempting to kick, he would no doubt have scored a point. Half- time was shortly afterwards called. On resuming Widnes played with renewed zeal and vigour. From the kick-off the ball was carried into Widnes territor* Howard, by a piece of good running, transferred the scene of play, and was within an ace of getting over the line whoa he was brought down. Avert then rushed the ball into the Widnes quar- ter, where Bullough gave a long kick, a minor resulting. Some very fine loose play was again engaged in, each side striving hard to score, but play was confined principally to about the centre. Fogg obtained hold in the visitors' half, and by a fine ran grounded the ball over the line, amidst the vociferous cheers of the Widnesians. Morris kicked a splen- did goal from the place. Immediately after the re-kick off Harding put in a splendid run, but unfortunately slipped near the goal line, and was thus prevented scoring. After the scrimmage Aspull placed the Widnes goal in jeopardy. A minor shortly afterwards resulted, and this was immedi- ately followed by another. No other major point was scored up to call of time, the game finally resulting in a win for Widnes by one goal and one minor to a try and six minors. The following were the teams : Full back, S Bingham ' • three-quarter backs, Plumprou, Harding. and Morris- half-backs, J E Farrell and Howard; forwards, Pervin, Meagher, Kiddie, Smith, Fogg, Bingham, Wilkinson, Hardman, and Hughes. Aspull: Fall back, Pilkington; three-quarter backs, Bullough, Seddon, and Haddock; half backs, Hulme and Cross; forwards, Lawson, Linsey, Brookes, Monks, Bramble, Baxendale, Roberts,• Hesketh, and another. Mr. Latham was umpire for Widnes, and Mr. Brindle for Aspull. Mr. Allen, of Salford, was referee. LIVERPOOL OLD BOYS V. RUNCORN.

__ • _ _ Thi-, one of the most popular fixtures on the Runcorn cards, was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and produced one of the most enjoyable and exciting games witnessed on the Irwell ground for a long period. About 2,000 spectators circled, and they were frequently excited to hearty cheering loy the excellency of the form displayed. The weather, al- though threatening. continued fine, but the ground was slip- pery and sloppy. Chapman started the ball for the Old Boys. to which Cawley replied, kicking back to centre,when the Old Boys' forwards carried the ball into the home 25, where H. Hughes, being pressed, touched down. From the drop out the play increased to a very fast pace, and from a scrimmage about centre Faulkner came through, when Crosby saved well. After a succession of scrimmages a well- timed pass was made by Riley to Cawley, the latter kicking on towards the visitors' line, and following up smartly se- cured the ball over the line and scored the first try, from which Lewis kicked a goal. Starting again from centre, some smart play was witnessed in the Old Boys' quarters Clarke made a short run, giving the ball to Wainwright, who in turn passed to H. Hughes, and Renshaw and Wain- wright (Old Boys) coming up the movement was checked. Chambers and Edmunds got ir a nice dribble, which W. Hughes and Cawley successfully checked, when the home fora arils made another raid on the ':Old Boys' line. Wain- wright's kick being charged by Andrews, the ball travelled across the ground, where a smart attempt to get in was made by Cawley and Riley. H. Hughes got possession of the ball from a scrimmage, and smartly eluding Munn scored the sennd try, Lewis failing to increase the value of the point. Chapman put the ball in play again, when Faulkner kicked into touch, and following some loose play Wriiht commenced a dribble near the half-.way flag, pilot-

lug the ball safely past his opponents and kicked aver the line, when he secured the third try after a very smart piece of play, which was heartily acknowledged by the spectators. Lewis made a good, though not successful, kick at goal. The Qld Boys again restarted the ball, when the slay still rested'in their half, H. Hughes trying repeatedly to get round, and finally sending the ball into touch. Munn ex- changed to Jones, who tried for an opening, but the back play was too safe for him to get away. Nothing more was sc-red to half time, the total being—Runcorn, one goals two tries, to one touch down. Wright kicked off after the usual interval, to which Crosby returned, when some long kicks were indulged in by W. Hughes, Crosby, and Jones, who was tackled by Riley, spoiling his efforts, and shortly the Old Boys touched down, the result of a strong forward effort on the part of Runcorn. Some tight scrim- maging was next engaged in, when Cawley moved towards the Old Boys' quarter, receiving the ball from Riley. Jones ; succeeded in stopping Cawley, but the forwards took on the ball, Broady and Joule crossing the line, and Broady drop- ping on the ball a shade inside touch in goal- The ball be- ing again put into play, some good passing by Chapman, Chambers, and Jones was nicely intercepted by H. Hughes, who was pushed into touch from the line out. The ball - travelled to mid-field, where Riley threw to W. Hughes,

who made a strong ran along the touch line, and passing to centre, the latter player trade subsequently a fair bid at goal, the ball going dead. Following the drop out the ball fell to the forwards, Clarke and Faulkner making a 'good dribble towards the Old Boys' line, which was, however, neutralised by Jones and Chambers, who by smart exchanges got in close proximity to the home goal, where by a well- timed pass by Munn to Crosby the latter ran in strongly, , scoring the first try for the visitors, though an easy kick at goal was missed. W. Hughes dropped out again, when the Old Boys rousing up got toe ball back into the home half, Brodie forcing Wood to kick dead. Some excellent kicking was then engaged in •by Wainwright and Cawley, the ball finally going into touch about the centre. Play was even for a time, until Crosby got hold, and taking a huge drop at goal the ball sailed over the bar. This change put fresh vigour into the Liverpool men, who played up well trying to avert defeat, but up to the close of the match no other point of value was scored, a magnificent game ending in Run- corn's favour by five points to four. Teams :—Runcorn : T. Wools, back; W. Hughes, W. Riley. and H. Cawley, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes an-I H. Andrews, half backs; W. Wright, J. Lewis, J. Barns, W. H. Broaly, J. Clarke, J. Gatley, W. Faulkner, G. Wainwright, and F. Joule, forwards. Liverpool Old Boys: F. Wainwright, back; F. Crosby. A. D. Jones, and E. Henshaw, three-quar- ter backs ; A. G. Munn and E. Leitch, half backs; H. C. Chapman, F. Chambers, E. Bullen, F. Edmunds, J. A. Brodie, R. Lockwood, B. Whyte, Stephenson, and R. Gould, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. CASTLEFORD.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. CASTLEFORD.

The Warrington team on Saturday went to Castleford to meet the club of that name. The journey was an exceed- ingly slow one, as the team started from Warrington at 10-30 and diJ not arrive at Normanton till four o'clock. They then had to walk a distance of five miles to Castleford, when they were completely exhausted with the journey. The first halt was made at Hudderefield, where a stay was made for an hour, the team having dinner there. The station- master told them that the best route was by Nor manton in- stead of by Leeds. The team now thought there would ba no more stoppages until they reached their destination, but to their surprise they were run into a siding at Mirfield, and had another hour to wait. When they reached Normanton they were told to change, and on asking for the next train were told it would not leave till a quarter to six. They. therefore, set out to walk the distance, arriving at Castle. ford a little before five, the Castleford men having given them up, and had just commenced to play a scratch match for the benefit of the spectators. The visitors speedily made themselves ready for action, and were soon on the field of play, some 2,000 persons being present, although some hun- dreds had gone home, being tired of waiting, as the kick- off had been advertised for 2-15. At a glance it could be seen that the home team were a much heavier lot than their opponents, and well they looked in their white dress. _

_ Two twenty minutes being decided upon, I'. Dickenson kicked off for the home team, Frank Turner made a good return, and Rigby following well up secured the ball and looked like scoring; but, unfortunately, did not part with it at the right moment, as Frank Turner or Ashton could easily have got over. Hanson, after a few scrimmages had taken place, put in a huge kick to half way, but W. Dillon and Fair. Turner took the ball back again. Hai tley dodged Barnes. but Antrobus coming up in the nick of time stoPped his progress. A good run by Massey was the next item, and then Jolley, by a pass from the same player, looked like going over, but was tackled by Wilkinson. Ham- mond put on a fine kick to touch, the oval row being about the centre of the field. W. Dillon, Fair. Turner, and Povey next made themselves conspicuous by a cembined dribble to 'the home 25, whAre Clarkson put in a good pass to Hartley, and the latter player to Hammond, who punted the ball to the visitors' territory. P. Dickinson, Asquith, and Brooke were instrumental in taking the ball to the line, a minor shortly afterwards being the result. Frank Turner got in a good dribble from the kick out, Harrison returning a kick from Barnes. Some good passing was witnessed at this period of the game between Jones, Dickinson, and Castle, ;the consequence being that the ball was taken to the visi- tors' quarters. Walsh now cleverly saved a dangerous rush by the Castleford forwards, and Massey put in a good screw kick, and again lianson got in a tremendous kick half the I length of the field. Fair. Turner now broke out with a I dribble, Gilbert and Jolley aiding him to the 25, and Clark- son replying by a kick to touch. Antrobus now passed in his own 25, and the ball falling short of either Massey or Barnes it cost the visitors the only try of the match, as the Castleford men took advantage of this slight mistake, and went on with a rush. P. Dickinson claimed a try, which was allowed, the same player kicking a neat goal. The visitors, instead of being disheartened at this, seemed to , play up with more energy, several times in quick successien being within an ace of scoring; and shortly afterwards a I lonr, tiat Ftbstin bl'Ought about half time, with the ball in the visitors' 25. _ _

Frank Turner kicked off on resuming play, and there be- ing little or no return the first scrimmage took place in the home quarters. Gilbert put in a %ice pass to Barnes, who in turn passed to Massey, a touchamen shortly afterwards being registered to the credit of the visitors. Jolley next got in a strong kick, bat the home forwards by a beautiful dribble took the ball to the line, scoring another minor. Some good play by the home forwards, headed by P: Dick- inson, Asquith, and Booth, placed another minor to their credit. From the kick out Ashton Came through with the best dribble of the day, being only stopped by Clarkson dropping on the ball in the home 25. Barnes, whilst in this position, obtained possession, and nearly dropped a goal, the ball only falling a few yards short, and straight as an arrow. From the kick out P. Dickinson and Castle took the ball to the visitors' 25, Fair. Turner, Heyes, and Povey bringing it back again. Some lively scrimmages next ensued, until Morton broke away with the ball at his toes, a minor result- ing in favour of the home team. Barnes next got in a good run, and Antrobus saved well when a try seemed a csrtainty. The ball now burst, but as only two minutes were wanted to finish the game, they played it out with the same ball. Fair. Turner caused no end of amusement by collaring the ball like a piece of rag, and ran with it from one 25 to the other, bringing the game to a termination with the ball in the home 25. Thus Castleford were declared the victors by one goal and four minors to one minor.

The Warrington team, one and all, under the circum- stances, played well, Massey, Jolley, and Gilbert being the shining lights behind the pack, and H. Ashton, W. Dillon, and the brothers Turner in the front ranks. Hanson played a brilliant. game at back for the hone team, his long kicks being of the greatest service to his side, and well they knew this, for they waited off side to tackle the Warrington back, as they felt confluent of his returning almost to Walsh, who had a lively time of it. Hartley and Clarkson also played a good game behind the pack, whilst P. Dickinson, Asquith, and Brooke were the best in the scrimmages. After the match ,the visitors were entertained to a substan- tial repast.

_ , Teams :—Warrington: Back, Walsh; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey; half backs, Antrobus and Gil- bert forwards, E. Dillon, W. Dillon, F. Turner, Fair. Tur- ner, Hers, Rigby, Povey, Davies, and Ashton (captain). Castleford : Back, R. Hanson; three-quarter backs, Hartley, Hammond, and Wilkinson; half backs, Clarkson and Brooke; forwards, P. Dickinssn, Adams, Castle, Booth, Jones, Cockcroft, Brooke, Asquith, and W. Dickinson. Um- pires, Messrs. Barnes and Lightfoot. Referee, Mr. Goodhall, Wakefield Trinity.

NOTES BY THE WAY. The contest on Saturday between Lymm and Warrington "A " teams was a rattier hollow affair. To look at the two teams before play commenced one might have supposed that the juniors would Le completely overwhelmed, the visitors having to a considerable extent tha advantages of height and weight. But the first ten minutes' play was enough to convince any one that "quality" is of more value than "quantity" in football as in most other things. There was a complete contrast between the styles of the two teams. Whittle's followers were always on the alert, quick to perceive an opportunity and sure to take advantage of it, while the play of the visitors, with one or two exceptions, IN as heavy and nnpblished. Hence the result. _ .

The 'hon. sec. of the St. Paul's Football Club writes with regard to the match between St. Paul's and Sankey Ist, on the ground of the latter on Saturday, that "owing to a dis- turbance caused by the home team, the St. Paul's captain was obliged to withdraw hrs men from the field five minutes before call of time." On the other hand, one of the three reports of the match sent to us states that St. Paul's left the field becatve a disputed try was decided in favour of their opponents by the referee. It is further alleged that "St. Pauls' repeatedly lay on the ball, being completely out- played." Manchester met Liverpool at Aigbarth on Saturday, when a splendid game was played, during a great part of which Manchester were a goal in hand—an advantage they re- tained until the very last minute, when the home team, amid great excitement, equalised the score and made the game a drawn one.

_ The following ties in the first round of the Football Asso- ciation Challenge Cup Competition have been decided : Bootle v. Great Lever: At Bootle. The Bolton players had the best of the game, and at half time were a goal ahead, the score standing at three to two. In the second half Bootle failed to add to their score, whilst the Great Layer players gained another paint and won by four to two. Higher Walton (Preston) v. 3rd Lanark: At Glasgow. The Scotchmen outplayed their opponents in the first half and scored five goals to none. Neither side gained a point in the second. The usual Cheshire County trial match, East N. West, was to have taken place on Saturday, at Birkenhead, but was abandoned through the inability of the East to raise a team. Runcorn once more displayed the first-class ability to which they have attained, by making the Old Boys' for the first time this season, taste the bitters of defeat. But the pride of victory and the chagrin of defeat were alike lost in the praises of so gallant a struggle. 1 gopl and 2 tries to 1 goal and 1 try betray an evenness to be desired by all who wish to see the game played as it should be. Wright was prominent amongst the Runcorn forwards, and scored from a splendid dribble, whilst Hugh Hughes, the Runcorn cap- tain, showed sterling form at half. Dr. Chapman, Brodie, and Stevenson, forwards, and all the Old Boys' backs dis- played creditable form. " Crosby "at last came ont of his shell, and in addition to dropping a fime goal he obtained an equally meritorious try.—Liverpool ilereury.

A Rugby correspondent states that Dr. Jex Blake, head master of Rugby School, has accepted the living of Alm Church, Worcester, and will leave Rugby next Easter. The Directors of the Bank of England on Thursday advanced their rate of discount from 31 to 4 per cent. , The rate has stood at the former figure from the 26th Au- gust.
GENERAL NEWS

Lord Aberdeen has consented to inaugurate the Liberal Association lately formed at Leith, with Mr. Gladstone as hon. president. Sir Michael Shaw Stewart, of Ardgowan, Renfrewshire, has promised a donation of .E 2,000 towards the work for the

relief of the unemployed in Greenotk. Lord Hartington, who has returned to London from Hol- ker Hall, Lancashire, received at Devonshire House on Mon- day a visit from Mr. Goschen, who remained with his lord-

ship seme time. Robbers broke into a Catholic Church at Notre Dame, Ind., and stole from the altar two golden crowns of great value—one the votive offering of the ex-Empress Eugenie, the other the devotional gift of Mrs. General Sherman. _
From the report, published on Monday, of the Executive of the Irish National League of Great Britain, it appears
_ that the organisation has now 420 branches, and that the annual receipts have increaeed from £391 in 1884 to £2.21T.

The Very Rev. Dr. Kitchen, Dean of Winchester, has promised to find a niche for a statue of Izaak Walton in the great screen of the cathedral, which is now being repaired, if anglers will provide the statue. A subscription list has been opened. Mr. Gladstone walked through the village to the Parish Church of Hawarden on Monday morning. He also took afternoon exercise. There is a marked improvement in Mrs. Drew's, conelition. Sir Andrew Clarke left the Castle on Sunday night. EXTRAORDINARY " FIND " IN A ring with four pearls and three ruby stones has been found in the back of a herring caught at Dunbar. The herring was cooked and being eaten at breakfast by a woman in Edin- burgh when the discovery was made. COSTLY SEWERAGE SCREME.—On Monday the new sewer- age works at Hacken, which have been constructed for Bol- ton at a cost of £30,000, were formally opened. The new works are to supplement those at present in use at Burnden, and have been under oonetruction since 1884.

_ A telegram from Chambery states that a panther escaped from a menagerie there and created a panic in the town. It attacked several person, a policeman being literally scalped by one blow of its paw, and has since died in the hospital. Another policeman was seriously bitt:n. The animal WAS eventually captured. Lord Iddesleigh arrived at the Foreign Office early on Monday afternoon, where there were awaiting him a large number of despatches, which had been previously under the consideration of Lord Salisbury. Later in the day his lordship had prolonged intereiews with Rustem Pasha, Tur- kish Ambassador, and Herr B.engell Maller,Austrian Charge d'Affaires.

THE REV. H. WARD BEECHER.—This preacher, who is now bringing his visit to England to a close, was present on Monday at a meeting of the Liverpool Congregational Board, sod in the evening lectured in Hengler's Circus on "Evolution and Religion." His conclusion was that evolu- tion, well explored and understood, tended to the unfolding Of the wisdom of the age. THE GREAT EASTERN STEAMSHIP AGAIN IN TROUBLE.—A dispute has arison between the owners of the Great Eastern steamship and the Dublin Port and Harbour authorities. The latter body protest against the huge vessel retaining her present berth for a prolonged period, and have rEqaested her removal from the port. The owners of the vessel, however, decline to alter their arrangements. THE LIVERPOOL EXHIBITION.—The Mayor of Liverpool, Sir David Radcliffe, has received from the French Govern- ment the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour. This hon- our, it is stated, was conferred upon Sir David in recogni- tion of his work in promoting and carrying out the Liverpool International Exhibition, and of his hospitality and kindness to the foreign visitors during his two years' mayoralty. FATAL ATTACK ON A FARMER BY A BOAR.—A small far- mer residing at Clashmore, county Waterford, met with a most shocking death on Tuesday morning. For some days past a boar had been unmanageable, and this necessitated frequent applications of a whip. On Tuesday Leahy en- tered the boar's shed without his whip, and tin animal im- mediately rushed at him, seized him by the thigh. and severed the emoral artery. Death occurred in a few minutes. _ _

KENTisH FAumens CLAMOURING.—The East Kent far- mers met on Saturday to csnsi.ler the question of the de- pression in agriculture and trade, with special reference to the threatened ruin of the hop industry. It was understood that the meeting was really the inauguration of a cam- paign which the Fair Trade League propose to catty on in the southern counties during the winter. A resolution was passed in favour of "some alteration in our fiscal system." TERRIBLE DEATH--Mrs. John R. Sutcliffe, of Mytholm- royd, and her husband were. retiring to rest on Saturday night, when Mrs Sutcliffe attempted to distinguish a pare- fin lamp by blowing down the chimney. The oil suddenly exploded with a loud report, enveloping the unfortunate woman in flames, and setting fire to the bedding. The whole surface of Mrs. Sutcliffe's body was severely burnt. Dr. Thompson was promptly called, but, in spite of his aid, she expired after intense suffering. SERIOUS FIRE AT MESSRS. BRIGHT? MILL, ROCHDALE.— About eleven o'clock a.m., on Tuesday, a fire broke out in Messrs. John Bright Brothers cotton mill, Rochdale, in the mixing-room, through some hard substance gertieg into the breaker. The room is about twenty yards long and ten wide, aud contained about 70 bales of cotton. The room, however, is fire-proof, and the flames were confined to it ; the firm's fire brigade soon succeeded in extinguish- ing the fire. The damage is roughly estimated at £5OO. THE CHILDREN'S SUNDAY.—Sunday was specially ob- served by the Nonconformist Churches throughout the coun- try as the Children's Sunday. Ministers and Sunday school officials threw themselves with great heartiness into the movement. The Wesleyan Methodists, whose schools num- ber over a million teachers and scholars, followed But the direction of the recent Conference in London, and, espe- cially in the northern districts, they have prefected their arrangements for drawing the serious into membership of the Methodist Church. THE SUPPOSED WIFE MURDER AT WOLVERHAMPTON.— At the resumption of the Coroner's inquiry on Monday, at Wolverhampton, touching the death of a young married woman named Harriet Narrimr)re, a witness gave evidence that on the night previous to her death he heard her hus- band say, "I caught thee again last night with that fellow, Tom Atkinson, and I'll stand it no longer. I'll either drown her or knife her." Her body was found in the canal a few hours afterwards. The inquest was again adjourned, and the husband still remains in cdstody. THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACTS.—NEW DEPARTURE.— A letter issued by the War Office to the generals command- ing military districts, suggests that, having regard to the benefit reaped by the civilian population in garrison towns from the Contagious Diseases AMP, local authorities may desire to provide hospital accommodation for venereal dis- eases. In any such effort the Secretary of State would gladly co-operate, and instructs the above-mentioned officers to communicate with the Mayors in their districts to ascer- tain whether, with assistance from the War Office, they will undertake such provisions. A NOVELTY IN BANKRITPrec.—SAmueI Gershon, who recently carried on business in Liverpool under the style of the Liverpool Furnishing Company, gave himself a very bad character at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court on Mon- day. He described a number of statements made by himself at a former examination as untrue, and others as pure fao- rications, and altogether comported himself in such a manner that the Registrar finally came to the conclusion that his whole statement was untrue from beginning to end. It would be difficult to frame a bankruptcy law that would deal properly with a case of this kind. A Bath paper says: Miss Emma Arthur, Burlington House, Burllngton-street, the well-known medical rubber, has treated over thirty cases of rheumatism and neuralgia with Bt. Jacobs oil, and says that it has given the greatest satisfaotion and that prominent medical men are recommending it for these complaints. Sold by all druggists at 2s 6d a bottle, or by post 2s 9d, from the Charles A. Vogeler Company. sole 'proprietors, 45, Farrlngdon-road. London.

Nelson's flagship, the Vfctory, was decorated with gar- lands at the masthead in Portsmouth Harbour on Thursday, in commemoration of the battle of Trafalgar. Two goods trainfccaine into .col!ision on Wednesday at Hartlebury, on the Great Western Railway. A great amount of rolling stock was destroyed, and one man seriously in- jured.

Consequent upon the continued depression in the manu- factured iron trades, the proprietors of the Forge Works, einderford, Forest of Dan. have given a week's notice to those they employ to terminate all contracts. _

The" Rev.'; Mr. Keatinge, whose an wart Intable assump- tion of clerical character amd functions has created so much sensation in Dublin, wil: not, it is stated, be prosecuted. His period of police supervision expired More he went to the Irish coital, and it seems to be the wish of his dupes and ex-admirers to allow Lim quietly to drop out of sight and mind.

Loss OF A VESSEL AND .Nrgn LITES.—A PerVinee cor- respondent telegraphs that all hopes ef the safety of the Boswedden, of and for Penzance, have now been abandoned. the Pilgrim having arrived at Perzance on Thursday morn- ing with the boat of the Boswedden, bearing its name an address, it having bsEn picked up 12 miles from land. The crew of the Boswedden consisted of Captain John Dusting and six men, and in addition there were two passengers on board. 'I he Botwedden, which was bound from lieath to Penzance with coals, is believed to have fonndered off Tn. vose Head during the recent heavy gales. FLECTION PETITION.—An election petition inquiry began at L-mdonderry on Wednesday. The petition was presented against the teturn of Mr. Charles Lewis, M.P., by his op- ponent, Mr. Justin M•Carthy, who alleges that five minors, Eight non-resident freemen, and eight unnaturalised aliens voted for Mr. Lewis, and that 23 cases of bribery and one of personation occurred. The respondent's rebutting case alleges one case of bribery by a Roman Catholic clergyman, and that two minors, four aliens, and six persons in receipt of poor-law relief voted for Mr. M.CartbV. MR. BRIGHT AND THE LIBERAL Pa:tem—Mr. Bright has written to the Secretary of the Birmingham Liberal Associa- tion, giving his reasons for declining to accept an invitation to attend the meeting next week to present a parting address to Mr. Schnadhorst. Referring to the schism in the Liberal party, Mr. Bright says he does not wish to attack his former

friends, and to cast lame where he thinks grievous error has been committed. He can only hope the present clouds may be dispelled, and that the former harmony of the party may be restored. To promote this he thinks silence for the time is better than speaking, and he therefore prefers to be absent from any public meeting where criticism might be expected from him.

THE FEMALE PORTER—At the Marlborough-street (Lon- don) Police Court, on Wedne.day, Lois Schwich, 21, the young woman who for some months, attired as a boy, served as porter to Mr. Noble Jones, a glover in Burlington Arcade, was further examined chargA with the robbery of various articles to a large amount from her employer. The accused again appeared in m%le attire, and maintained a passive de- meanour. Mr. Bernard Abrams, who defended, stated that contributions which had been received for the prisoner and her family amounted to over £lO. Several pawnbrokers'

assistants proved receiving pairs of silk hose, fans, &c., in pledge in the names of Day and Mansfield. The prisoner was again remanded. THE WAGES IN NORTH AND NORTH-EAST LANCASHIRE.— A. meeting of the Joint Committee, composed of six repro sentatives of the manufacturers and six of the operative weavers, appointed to consider wages and other questions in their preliminary stage, was held at the Mitre Hotel, Man- chester, on Tuesday afternoon. The meeting had under its consideration the proposed universal list of wages—s list fairly applicable to all the districts. When the qnestion was up some time ago before the Joint Committee, the master's section heartily concurred in the proposition of the vreavers,but saw serious difficulties in the fair application of the list. The operatives' officials state that the adoption of an equitable list will settle most of the wages difficulties in the district. THE CONVICTION OF A MANCHESTER MINISTER.—MtICh
sympathy is expressed towards the Rev. J. Mackie, of Manchester, who has been condemned to three months' hard

labour for assaulting a deacon. and who, it is thought, must have been in a pitiable condition of mind when he committed the assault, seeing that he hid a family to maintain, and was unable to get his salary paid. The Recorder has been asked to reconsider hiq sentence, but after doing so declared that
he could not rethlce it. P'etitions to tha— Home Secretary
praying for a remission ef the remainder of the sentence

LORD RIPON ON THE POLITICAL SITUATION. The Marquis of Ripon. speaking at a mayoral banquet at Ripon on Thursday night, sard that, so far as he knew, the course which was being pursued by her Majesty's Government in i regard to affairs n south-eastern Europe was very much in acccrdance with what his own judgment would approve. Whatever might have been the case in the past. England had in this matter no greater interest than the other great Powers. nay, she very dis- tinctly had a smaller ir:terest in it thin some of those. The key to the questions of external policy which affected our In lian Empire was in these days to be found not at Constantinople, but in Central Asia. What we had to do Was IO find some mode of dealing with Russia which was suited to tte changed circumstances, and he thought the solution of the problem would not be so c4iilicult as some people might expect if it was only spproached in a frank and honest spirit by both parties concerned. LIST WEEK'S GALES.—TiIe shipwrecks reonrted last week rose to 52, in consequence of the gales. British-owned ves- sels numbered 3S, of which 35 were lost off the British !sits, as well as three Norwegian vessels. Collision cases 34, but only two vessels sunk by collision. Seven steamers were wrecked. Lives lost rose to 6'J. Four Bri!ish sailers were reported lost with all hands, and a Glasgow barque with 16 hands. Total wrecks for the year, 1,109._ A telegram was _ _

. . received on Wednesday by Messrs. Renard and Sons, ship- owners, Middleshurgh, from Truro, stating that wreckase bearing the name of the steamer Harriet Shiel, and part of a clothes box marked " Ward, Middlesbrough" (the name of the master of the vessel). had been washed ashore a' Ferran Beach, Cornwall. The Harriet Shiel left Cardiff on the 13th inst, with a crew of eleven hinds, and itis feared she, has been wrecked. The China wail, received at P;ymouth on Wednesday, brings news of the loss of the British steamer Ferntower, with 50 lives, during a typhoon off the mouth of the Saipan river. THE TRIAL OF "Dee. VIVIAN."—At Shropshire Quarter Sessions on Tuesday "Dr. Vivian," who is known tinder several aliases, was indicted for stealing a purse, £B, and a number of old Boman coins, the property of a commercial traveller named Charles Henry Prowse, who was staying at the Victoria Hotel, Whitcburch. In May, shortly before his apprehension, the prisoner, representing himself to be an American doctor, married a young lady at Birmingham, and large sums were spent upon the wedding.—Mr. Spearenarek for the prisoner, applied that a portion of the money (about L'27) found on the prizoner might be handed over for the pure. poses of the defence, but notice in regard to it not having been served upon the police, the application was refused.— Mr. Plowden, in opening the case, said teat although it was one of extreme simplicity, yet the circumstances attending the previoas life of the prisoner bad ma& it one of con- siderable notoriety.—The defence was that it was a case of mistaken identity. A verdict of guilty was returned, and the prisoner pleatled guilty to a previous conviction at Liverpool in 1876, when he was sentenc3d to ten years' penal servitude. There were other cmvictioas also.—The Chairman then sentenced the Prisoner to ten years' penal servitude.

LORD ROSEBERY AT NEWCASTLE.—Lord Rosebery pre- sided on Tuesday night at the annual dinner of the New- castle-on-Tyne Liberal Club, and said that at the present time there were three important topics before the country. The first and greatest was that of Ireland. The second and the most pressing one was that of currency; and the third was the question of the position we should take regarding affairs in the East of Europe. He did not propose to deal with these subjects, but would confine himself to the neces- sity of re-uuitiag the Liberal party, w',ich was at present in such a position as it bad never been within his recollection. If this state of things was not dealt with immediately it would become irrevocable. Looking to the causes of schism, be said the Liberal majority from various cans( s had been decreasing since 1880, and the downward progress culmina— ted in the objections to Mr. Gladstone's Irish proposals.He did n,,t believe the judgment of the country was against those proposals, but only showed a desire for more time to consider them. Mr. Gladstone and his friends stood fi,-mly to their policy, and he trusted means would be found by which the Unionist Liberals would be brought back to the main body, and to that end he advocated a policy of faith, hope, and charity. DEATH 017 THE MARQUIS 017 AILESBURY.--The Martini" of Ailesbury died, almost suddenly, on Monday, at Saver- nake House. Wilts. The deceased Marquis (Ernest Augus- tus Charles Brudenell Bruce), who was the third of his lin,, was born on Jan nary Bth, 1811, and succeeded to the title in 1878. He was educated at Eton and at Trinity Colleze, Cambridge, where he took the degree of M.A. in 1831. He was Vice Chamberlain from 1341 to 1816, and again feen 1852 to 1858. The deceased peer was a Conservative in politics, and represented Marlborough in that interest frem 1832, till be ceased to be a Commissioner. He was a magis- trate for Middlesex, Westminster, and Wilts, in the latter of which localities he possessed extensive estates, as also in Bedfordshire, Yorkshire, and other counties. He was married in 1834 to the Hon. Louisa Elizabeth Beresford, daughter of the second Baron Decies, and had three sons and two daughters, all of whom are Heine. The Mare:yds of Ailesbury had been in ailing health some time, though on Sunday he seemed fairly well. At ten minutos to ten on Monday night his lordship was suddenly seized with faint- ness whilst sitting in a chair, and on being carried to his private room he expired almost immediatAy, from failure of the heart's action.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 23, 1886.

The rank and file of the Tory party in I -Warrington seem to have lost their heads over ' the prospect of a victory at the forthcoming Municipal Elections. Seeing that five Conser- vatives and four Liberals retire in November next by effluxion of time, it was suggested by the Liberals as a reasonable basis of com- promise that a contest should be avoided by each party being allowed to nominate as many candidates as they had members retir- ing.. This would leave the representation of each ward practically undisturbed, with the majority as heretofore, on the side of the Conservatives, who are at present repre- seated in the Council by 21 members, as against Is Libetals. A meeting of the Tory pariy was held, and the heedless and reckless were in the ascendant. Had they not twice won in a Parliamentary contest, and why should they not have all their own way municipally? It was in vain to point out them that the large majoriies obtained at the General Elections were in each case secured by "a fluke " by the votes of Liberal Irishmen being given to the Tory candidate in the first instance, and, in the second, by Liberal Unionists either voting Tory or altogether abstaining. The bats of the Tory Caucus were blind to'any such considerations, and the result was—much to the annoyance of better-minded Conservatives a pro- ' _ posal to compromise the Municipal Elections on the basis of seven Conservatives to two Liberals! Need we say that the Liberals. treated the suggestion with disdain? They right‘y regarded it as an insult which called for a striking and practical protest; and to this end it was decided, at an aggregate meeting of the Ward Committees, that, if the Tory pronosition was persisted in the whole of the Liberal members of the Town Council ' should be requested to resign. This intima- tioa caused t something like a scare amongst the Conservatives, who were not prepared for like begetting like in the way of extreme action. There were not a few of the Tory members of the Town Council who did not hesitate to say that they would be no party to forcing experienced Liberal mem- bers out of the Town Council if their places had to be occupied—as seemed inevitable—by an indifferent class of can- didates on their own side. Having preached the advisability of keeping party poli- tics as far as possible aloof from munici- pal -matters, they were not going to stultify themselves by being party to a most insolent party proposal. The result has been that the decision of the Tory Caucus has been con- sidered and re considered at meetings which have been held during the past week. Two of the extra four Conservatives have re- tired, but the other two refuse, as yet, to listen to the advice of their friends. It is to be hoped that before the nominations are sent in, on Monday, they will put their leaders in a position to say that the 4-taus quo shall be maintaine-d—in other words that the Municipal Elections shall be compro- mised on the basis of five Conservatives to four Liberals. • .Otherwise the Liberals in the Council will be under the necessity of retir- ing in a body, leaving the Conservatives to make the best of an unenviable situation.

THERE can be no do-libt about it; the foe of the human race is the bacillus. The bacillus is the fly in amber; the rift within the lute, which widens till it makes the music mute. We are not sure—at least, if we were to believe all the doctors tell us we should not be sure—that the story of the serpent in the Garden of Eden is not a piece of elabor- ate symbolism concerning the bacillus. It is obvious, therefore, that if we are to get the golden age back again our first endeavours must be concentrated on the extirpation of bacillus. It seems doubtful, however, whe- ther we can extirpate bacillus. What we can do is to attenuate him. This, again, is good philosophy as well as good science. We can't turn evil neck and, crop out of doors, but we can keep it at a reasonable distance,

and modify some of its most serious tenden-1 W. Rawlins. The cry must be cies and developments. So with the bacillus.i" Register, register, register," but But before we can do this we must, as Dr. I educate, educate." PAVY, the new Fiarveian lecturer, points out, do full justice to his existence and powers of mischief. "They had to deal with something that lived :and grew by virtue of a power pertaining to itself; and if this living growth —this parasite, in fact—were permitted to become dispersed and to enter the system of a living person, presuming that it had lodged upon a soil supplying suitable conditions for its development, it would thiive and multiply, and give rise to a series of phenomena which the physician had no power to resist. Once the bacillus implanted aid the disease estab- lished, all the physicians could do was to see that the patient was kept under the most favourable conditions for battling successfully lagainst his enemy." Having now caught our bacillus we proceed not to cook but to attenu- ate him. "It had been found that the bacillus required virgin soil for its growth, and by certain means it might be brought into such a weakened state as only to occasion, when introduced into the system of an animal, an effect of a mild nature, not *dan- gerous to life, instead of the ordinary form of disease; but the effect produced—and this was the great point of prac!ical import- ance—was as protective against a subse- quent attack as the fully-developed dis- ease." This method, of course, is simply an application of the inoculation theory of which M. PASTEUR is the most distinguished repre- sentative. The aim is, in a word, to sepatate bacillus from his favourite environment, to deprive him of the conditions which best stimulate his growth, and, in a word, to make him as uncomfortable as possible. Bacillus may in this way grow to be less and less formidable, and in the end may come to such a state of attenuation and mental and bodily feebleness, that his advent may be a matter of perfect indifference to us. He will then be a proper object for contempt and derision, and our grandchildren will look at him under a microscope with much the same feelings as BUNYAN'S pilgrims experienced at the sight of Giant Pope helplessly gnashing his teeth by the wayside.

To the new and cheap edition of his pam- phlet on the Irish question, published by the National Press Agency, 11-. GLADSTONE has added a final postcript which completes his indictment of the Union. His great point is that the Irish cannot be expected to rest con- tent with a political arrangement which has never received their moral sanction. "From the time of the first Reform Act it will not be questioned that there has been no such ac- ceptance by the Irish nation as could ratify an act morally invalid at the outset. With the increase of political prestige and power, the attitude of that nation has become more and more pronounced, and it is now, in the highest consititutional sense, demanding not indeed the repeal, but an important and pro- found modification of the Incorporating Par- liamentary Union." There is really no answer to this except the blunt assertion of a resolve to maintain the Union without any change, whether the Irish like it or not. But let this be clearly understood. Let us have an end of the hypocrisy which tells us that the J-ish are "two nations," that Mr. PARNELL obtained a majority at the last election by unfair means, and the rest of the stuff with which many Englishmen blind themselves to She fact that under a democratic C;onstitution they are deliberately ignoring the wishes of the great mass of the Irish people. It is absurd to talk of placing the government of Ireland in the hands of her duly-elected representatives when you refuse to restore the Parliament which alone she is willing to accept as the symbol of local authority under the Crown and the supremacy of the Imperial Legislature.

WHETHER or no Irishmen will ever be able to acme about their own government, it is i.olerably certain that they cannot agree about their own brogue. The new number of the Quarterly Review" contains specimens of the Irish brogue as it is used in Parliament by Mr. MATT. HARRIS 2.nd:other clistinguisked members of the Irish party. On this a Mr. O'HARA politely intimates that if the writer knows no more about Irish politics than he does about the Irish dialect, he had better be silent on both subjects. In particular, said ' Mr. O'HARA, the word freedom was never pronounced " fraydom," as the " Quarterly" scribe wrote it. Well, this seemed conclusive enough, but a gentleman who signs himself " Corkonian," and writes to the "Standard" as a " rale Irishman, frequently ridiculed for my extreme brogue," declares that Mr. O'HARA is all wrong and the Quarterly" all right. " I can assure him," writes '• Corkonian," "that in the South the word 'freedom' always pronounced fraydom ' by those, of course, who cannot boast of a first-class edu- cation. This also is the case with the word greedy which, when the brogue is applied, is pronounced grady,' " As with " free- dom," so with " these " and "seize," and a score other words which the Irish peasant pronounces with a broad Doric "a." Well, whom are we tD believe? The evidence is as conflicting as that on Home Rule, and we have no doubt the controversy has in it those capacities of development which attach to every Irish theme with which we are. ac- quainted. For ourselves, we make no pretence of adjudicating in the matter. We simply sit on the rail and invite Mr. O'HARA and " Corkonian " to produce their evidence— or their shillelaghs. When the controversy is over, we will see that the surgeon is called in.

The Queen of Spain has issued a decree conferring immediate freedom upon all the slaves in Cuba who have not already been emancipated under the provisions of the Moret law. This is better than patronising bull fights; it is queenly, and when she has passed from the scene it will halo her memory.

Russia haying failed to break or bend Bulgaria, directly, through General Kaulbars is now trying .what can be done, indirectly, through Turkey; and so far with better as- suranc of success, for it is now announced that the conspirators are to be released. It looks *a little odd, this joint action of th-. wolf and the lamb, and one wonders how long it will last. It is a pity Bulgiria is not strong enough to be independent alike of .Russian and Turk.

There isn't room in our little island, it would seem, for two great preachers, and so Spurgeon has been appealing to the Lord as against Beecher. It is a hard saying to call a man a blasphemer; but it is just possible Henry Ward Beecher may have heard some- thing of the kind before. In that case he may take the " beating " as the big navvy took the thrashing from his little wife. "It doesn't matter," he said, "it pleases she and it don't hurt me."

At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, a young fellow named Marsh was brought before the magistrates for alleged desertion of his wife. His plea was that his life was made miserable by his mother-in- law, and the Bench, sympathising with him, dismissed the case, on his promising to take his wife to his parencs' home. So far, so good; but what of the wife? Does it matter nothing that her life may now be made miserable by a mother-in-law ? Of course not. What is the use of having a wife if you cannot abuse her?

Warrington is considerably behind sur- rounding towns in the matter of Starr-Bowkett Building Societies; but a start has been made, and there is every prospect of a suc- cessful society being established. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided over a well attended meeting on Monday evening, and made some practical remarks on self-help and thrift. The Starr-Bowkett is essentially the working-man's building society, and it is to be hoped the new venture will be well patron- ised by those who wish to have an umbrella for the proverbial rainy day.

St. Helens, on Wednesday, Mr. Seton- Karr, M.P., presided over a meeting to in- augurate a branch of the " Counties Conser- vative Permanent Benefit Building Society." He, too, spoke of such societies as en- couraging thrift, hut he didn't explain why they should be associated with politics. Why "Conservative ? " Politics, pure and simple, cause quite sufficient division in communities without introducing them into Building So- cieties. Mr. Seton-Karr thinks the name of the society in question is a long one ; let him use his influence to get the word "Conserva- tive" struck out, and thus shorten and im- prove the title.

The Dean of St. Paul's has made it pretty clear that he has no sympathy with the fussy bigots who have complained to him that certain Roman Catholics had been al- lowed to pray at the tomb of Edward the Confessor in Westminster Abbey. Dean Bradley says it is not the practice to dis- courage private prayer in the Abbey, or to question those who assume the attitude of devotion as to the nature and object of their personal petition. If one Roman Catholic can in the ordinary way visit and pray at one of the Abbey tombs, why not two, or twenty?

" Sorry ! you wretched woman," exclaimed the Liveroool Stipendiary on Monday, "go- ing about with this .child—your own child— so drunk that you actually smothered it. You might be living in a savage country." This wasn't sufficiently hard on the woman, but it was a hard hit on the " savage country." As a matter of fact, it is only in civilised coun- tries that human beings, brutalised by drink, thus smother their offspring. -" Oh that men (and women) should put an enemy .in their mouths to steal away their brains !" Wretched women and wretched drink—what a pity we cannot banish both!!

Bishop Nulty. has been indulging in a little plain speaking to " Moonlighters " and other outrage-mongers. Their wickedness is only equalled, he thinks, by their folly. He says: —" Some of them want to take revenge on some persons, and by burning their houses, stores, or haggards they think they do so. The stupidity as well as the wickedness of that proceeding is incalculable. They en- deavour to wreak their vengeance on their enemies, but they do nothing of the kind. On the contrary, they confer great favour on them, because in every one of these instances the party whose property is burnt receives fari more for it than it is worth." This is a nut tor "Captain Moonlight" to crack, and it is to be hoped he will find the kernel.

The hall had been tastefull!e decorated for the occasion. INFANT MORTALITY AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Worsley, the depsty coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest at Runcorn on the infant child of T. Hughes, warehouseman, 11, Bris- Coe-greet. The child had only lived an hour and thirty-five minutes after birth, haying been born prematurely. A ver- dict to that effect was returned.—Mr. Worsley also held an inquest upon an infant three months old, the son of John Bazley, labourer, of Gas-street. When the father got up to go to his work on Tuesday morning the child was appar- ently all right, but an hour afterwards the mother found it lying by her side dead. Dr. McDougall deposed that the child died from asiehysda, and the jury returned a verdict accordingly. DITTON PARISIL—At the recent Church Congress held at Wakefield, Ditton Church was mentioned by Canon Lefroy in his speech as an instance of extremely unfair endowment. All the tither, it appears. go Out of the parish, the majority of them to King's College, Cambridge, and the rest to Pros- cot. In order, if possible, to remedy this state o affairs, we understand that the Vicar (the Rev. C. W. Wool!) and his parishioners are memorializing the Provost and Fellows of King's College on the subject. RUGBY FOOTBALL JUNIOR CHALLENGE CuP COMPETI- TION.—A number of local football clubs have entered for the competition which was instituted at the annual general meeting of the West Lancashire Union, held last month. These comprise Runcorn Recreation, Widnes Recreation, Farnwortb, and Warrington Hornets. Over twenty clubs have notified their intention of taking part in the competi- tion, which bids fair, like the senior one, to be a great success. Clubs will be allowed to join up to the end of De- cember. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT FARNWORTH —A shocking acci• dent occurred on the L. and N.-W. Railway, near Fern. worth station, on Wednesday evening. Wm. Platt, a young man, who was employed as a goods porter, and lival at Farnworth, was found terribly injared about five o'clock. His back was broken, ,and he had also a compound fracture of the tight arm. It is supposed that he fell whilst attempt- ing to alight from a moving mineral train and injured him- self to such an extent that he could not move, and that a blink engine that followed along the line shortly afterwards struck him on the back and broke it. DYSON'S DIORAMA. AND GIPSY CHOIR.—This admirable entertainment, which has been elven in the Widnes Drill Hall during this week, will commeme a week's engagement at Runcorn to-morrow (Sunday) by two Sacred concerts. The entertainment, both pictorial and musical, is of the most enjoyable and artistic character, and crowded and delighted audiences have gathered in the Widnes Drill Hall. Mr. Dyson has introduced a novelty in the system of ad- reission. In place of the ordinary fixed charges made for witnessing such performances, Mr. Dyson makes a collec- tion on entrance, and apparently the method is a success. PROPOSED LIBERAL CLUB AT RUNCORN. The forma- tion of a Liberal Club for Runcorn gradually draws near realisation. At a well attended meeting of intending mem- bers this week, it was all but definitely decided that a limi- ted comp iny should be incorporated with a capital of £5OO in 1,000 shares of 103 each, and already promises equal ,to 300 shares have been made. In the exceedingly probable event that the company is floated, only half the caeital will be called up for the purpose of furnisliine 14-,e premises,l which are to be taken at an annual rent. All Liberals: ought to show their interest in the cause by becoming shareholders.

SODDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—A very sudden death took place at Runcorn yesterday. Mr. William Moores, who was employed as a clerk by the Bridgewater Nav;gation Co. at the Old Quay, went with a telegram to John Buckley, the warehouseman at the canal side, High-street. Whilst he was talking to Mr. Bucaley. Mr. Moores gave a moan, fell to the ground, and immedia:ely expired. Dr. Robinson was on the spot a few minutes later and gave his opinion that death resulted from dropsy. The body was conveyed to his home at Ashmocr Bridge in tlim care of P.C. Harvey. Mr. Moores had attained the age of 73 years. THE LIBRARY OF THE RUNCORN Y.M.C.A.—After very careful consideration, the committee of the Young Men's Christian Association have decided to sell the library of that institution. Since the establishment of the Free Library the books of the association have been but little called for, in fact it may be said to have fulfilled its purpose when no other library existed in the town,. The Frge Library Com- mittee, who had the first offer, have decided to purchase 208 of the volumes, at a cost of £l9 12s 63, and the result will be of advantage to the town, and the Y.M.C.A. It is estimated that the first cost of the library to the Y.M.C.A. was no less than £l5O. B SOCIETY MEETING AT RUNCORN.—The annual meeting of the Rune rn Branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in Bethesda School-room, on Thurs- day evening, under the presidency of Mr. W. Hankinson. Thete was a fair attendance. Mr. J. Humphreys rea4 the treasurer's report. which stated that the total receipts for the year amounted to £49 lOs id. including subscriptions and collections. The sum of £33 10s lid had been banded over to the Parent Society. The Rev. W. Preston, MA., the chairman, and the Rev. D. JOSEPII LITTLER, OF WIDNP,S.—The mortal remains of Mr. Joseph Littler, of Midwood-street, Simni's Cross. were interred at Farnwortb, on Monday after- noon. The deceased gentleman, who had only attained the age of 36 years, was a Wesleyan local preacher, and many members of that body honoured the funeral with their pre- sence. The procession, which included many of the de- ceased's fellow workmen, proceeded to Victoria-read Chapel, where the burial service was read by the Rev. R. Burdon, to a large assemblage of persons. Afterwards the coeteae wended its way to Farnworth churchyard, where Mr. Bur- don again officiated. Mr. Littler, who was much respected, succumbed on Friday last to a brief but painful malady— cancer of the brain—and he leaves a wife and family of three to mourn his loss. WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WESTON.—This chapel was re-open- ed on Sunday, after being closed for several weeks for deco- ration. The interior, which has been decorated by Mr. George Yarwood, Church-street, Runcorn, has undergone greet imerovement. Advantage was taken of the occasion to open the organ which bee been placed in the chapel The instrument is the one which for many years occupied an honourable position in the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel.and has been re-erected at considerahletnet by Messrs. A. Young am 6 Sons, of Manchester. There were large congregali'm at the opening services, and sermons were preached by the Rev. 'John Shipham, of St. Helens. Mr. George Hazlehurst officiated at the (wean, and its power and tone greatly en- hanced the interest of the service. A collection was made on 'behalf of the expenses incurred, and the sum of £2O was realized. PIA.LTON PARISH Ceireten.—This sacred ediLce was elaborately and beautifully decorated for the annual harvest thanksgiving services, which were held on Friday and Sun- day. The col- lections amounted to the total of £l4. ASSAULT 'ON A BOY AT WIDNES. Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. J. Merewood aseed Red why he AVAA deire that, he replied " You young deeil." and humped his head against the wall. He then got hold of him bythe eo,t end reeve him a kneck on the side of the head.
