A VIONT AUNCORN BOA.TWOMAN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Hannah Hickson was charged with as=aulting Margaret Farrell.—Defendant pleadLd guilty. —The women travel with canal boats, and it was alleged that on the 28th September, at Norton, the defendant knocked the complainant senseless, and kicked her as she lay on the ground. The defendant's daughter, it was stated, incited her mother to kill her.—Deferalant : lam guilty, but I did not giver .half enough. She denied the kicking.— In reply to the magistrates the complainant said she was not afraid of the defendant.—A fine of 10. e and costs, 94 63, was therefore imposed.—The defendant, vrko wea in a very excited condition, looked with fury upon the complainant, and said she was the worst woman on the canal. She would give her more, she threatened, even if it cost her £lOO. Superintendent Hollirsworth sent an officer after the woman into the street to see that she committed no offence. ASSAULT BY A ST. HELENS MAN AT WIDNES.—At Wid- nes Police Court, on Monday, Joseph Hampson, plomber, St. Helens, was charged on a warrant with having assaulted Peter Carr, deputy-oßanager of the Model Lodging-house, Lugsdale-road. Complainant alleged that on the 3rd October, about ten o'clock at night, lie was standing at the door of the Model Lodging-house, when the .prisoner and two other men came by. Without any provocation what- ever, the prisoner struck limn with his fist, knocking him down, and then kicked him. He got up, but immediately he did so pristiner struck with a bat, and he again fell to tilt, ground. He did not know the prisoner, and had never given hint any provocation. He was badly hurt, and had been under the care of Dr. Cooper.—A woman corroborated. —Prisoner said there was a general fight going on amongst some men who had come out of the fairground, and he was watching them, When he raw a man go up to complainant and strike him. He then went up and tried to separate them. He did not strike a blow.—A young man who was passing gave evidence in support of prisoner's statement.— The Bench conside-ed him guilty, and he was fined 203 and costs, or one month in default. COURSING MATCH AT Sr. HELENS.—There was a very good attendance at the Star Inn Grounds, St. Helens, grounds on Saturday, to witness the Fox- Terrier Coursing Match between Milne's dog Ben- cligo, of St. Helens, and Speck's dog Spot, of Sutton, who contested the best of 21 courses, for .£l5 aside. Spot won the match by catching 11 to 0. Betting: 6t04 on Bendigo. Cask, of Pocket Nook, was the referee, while Win. Smith was pistol-firer. The wound was then cleared for the foot race between. ltedden's novice and Curley's novice, both of Earles- town, distance 100 yards, for a silver cup and a bet of £lO a side. The pistol was fired to a very good start, but Redden's novice, coming away after they had run 30 yards, won veiy easily by three yards. VICTORIA BREAD AND BISCUIT COMPANY.—We would direct the attention of our readers to this new Limited Company, an abridged prospectus of which will be found in our advertising columns. The company propose to take over the flourishing business of Mr. J. G. Geisel, who shows his own confidence in the undertaking by accepting 12,000 shares in lieu of cash, while engaging not to receive anything for his services as managing director until a dividend of 71 per cent. per annum be paid t 3 the shareholders. For three years, too, he guarantees a dividend of 71- per cent. A London Company that can produce good bread is sure of a profitable -busi- ness. The Aerated Bread Company has been very successful, the .£1 shares being at the present time quoted at over .E 4 each. Mn. GLADSTONE. AS A lIORSEMAN.—A London correspondent says :—" The news that Mr. Glad- stone used the oar very frequently in his boyish , days will come as a surprise to many people who suppose that his only form of exercise is tree-fell- ing. This is a mistake. Mr. Gladstone at one time was a splendid and fearless horseman. There is a well-known instance of his having a fierce contest With an animal of bad temper and high spirits in Hyde Park, before all fashionable London. He 'made the horse jump and jump and jump yet again ,over the railings until he subdued its temper, and made it as obedient as a lamb. ?Ir. Gladstone ought certainly to have been a splendid oarsman. He has not remarkably strong arms, but his back and legs are very muscular. This accounts for the extra- ordinary fact that even to this day he holds his back more straight than any man, .old or young, in the House of Commons." NEWTON LIBERAL DIVISIONLECTURES.The first of a series of public lectures throughout the New- ton Division of South-West Lancashire, under the auspices of the Liberal "3C03" was given in the Methodist schoolroom, Billinge-Chapel-End, on Tuesday evening. There was a very good attend- ance. The lecturer was Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rain- hill, who chose for his subject "The English land laws," Mr. James Hamilton, of Ilirehley Hall, and one of the vice-presidents of the Newton Liberal Association, presided. In the course of an address Mr. Rawlins traced the origin of the present land laws with reference to pnmogcniture, settlement, and entail, showing how they acted detrimentally to the interests not only of the land owning classes, but of the people who had to live on the land. He in- sisted that no satisfactory legislation was to be ex- pected from the Conservatives, and it was only by uniting together to return a Liberal majority that they could hope to amend the existing laws.—The Chairman, in according the thanks of the meeting to Mr. Rawlins, briefly commented upon the land laws, and complimented the lecturer upon the abi- lity displayed in the add.ress.—Mr. P. Ai. Camp- bell moved, and Mr. Challoner seconded, a vote of -thanks to the Chairman, which was accorded, and the meeting terminated.

div.p: 'TOUCH AND GO."

Widnes School Board election takes place to-day. The leading Nonconformists are working hard to secure the return of their candidates, Messrs. Davis, Robinson, and Fogg. Let the bulk of the Nonconformists do their duty—vote straight-3.d they will return all three.

--- Under the pretence of having a regard for order, the Tory members of the Runcorn Free Library Committee have been seeking to put some restriction on the discretion of the Librarian in accepting pamphlets and leaflets of va,rious kinds. Education is not in their line; but the move failed, as it deserved to do,

The Northwich Rural Sanitary Authority acted wisely and promptly, on hearing of a scarlet fever patient in a room where ,cheese- making was carried on, in passing a bye-law making it compulsory to notify an infectious disease. It may be alliterative to associate Cheshire cheese with scarlet fever, but it isn't nice.

The "Liberal 300 " of Newton are acting wisely in resolving ona course of political lec- tures during the ensuing winter. The first of the series was on the Land Laws, .and was given on Tuesday evening by Mr. J.

MR. T. C. EDWARDS-MOSS, M.P., ON EDUCATION. The annual entertainment of the Wesleyan Day School, Garston, was held- on Monday eyenine, in the Reeding- room, under the presidency of Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for Widnes Division. There was a large attendance, amongst whom were the Rey. P. M. Parkinenn, Dr. Cayser, Messes. W. J. Stewart, E. Pierpoint, W. Newell, E. W. Turner, T. Lemmens, and W. T. Husband. During an in- terval in the programme Mr. Edwards-Moss spoke upun education. He said no education fully met their require- ments that did not include religions training, and upon tbe system of education they adopted would depend the future of the country. It was now some sixteen years since it had been decided by law that evely child in the country, no • matter of what class it was, should receive a certain degree of education. The question then came what sort of educa- tion should be adopted. It was his opinion that , the principles of religion should be instilled into every child, not only en its mother's knee, but also in the school where it att,rideci, and it was because he held that opinion tbat he would welcome any legislation that would iii any way tend to inere tee the efficiency or to add to the popularity of such schools as the one they were supporting that nieht. Alluding to dif- ferences between the cost per head of each child in Ward schools and voluntary schools, he said the latter were in- finitely cheaper than the former. From statistics which had been supplied to him it appeared the cost of educating each child in Board schools. was £3 7s 11-1 per annum, whereas in the voluntary schools it only cost £1 15s 41. He objected to Board schools on two points—because they did not do the work so well as voluntary schools, and that they did not teach religion. In conclusion, he hoped the
ladies and gentlemen of the district would do al: they c3l:ld to help the promoters of that school in the noble work th:y were doing.
DISTURBANCE AT RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOL.
A lIISTRE.`,S ASSArI,TED.

Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Miss Frances Letitia Hutchinson, mistress of the Board School in Cireenway- road, was summoned to answer a charge of assaulting Betsy Lydiate, a scholar eight years of age —Mr. W. H. Linaker, instructed by the School Board, appeared for the defendant, and stated that the girl would not perform a task of writing set her by Miss Hutchinson, and with other girls she was set apart until the writing was done. The other girls per- formed the task, but the complainant began to cry and would not touch the slate. Mss Hutchinson punished the girl by s';iking her on each hand with a cane.—ln reply to questions put by Mr. Reynolds the girl stated that she could not do the sums given her by Miss Hutchinson, who besides striking her on the hand slapped her face. "It did not hurt very much."—This was the case for the complain- ant.—Phcebe Sutton, eight years of ao.;e, said the complain- ant would not do her writing at all, and Miss Hutchinson caned her, but did not slap her on the face.—Sarah Broad- bent cerrohorated.—Mrs Lvdiate, mother of the girl, said theta were finger marks upen the child's face when she came home "heart broken" at noon.—Mr. Linaker said this was impossible as the alleged offence took place at half-past nine.—Mr. Reynolds said the summons was dismissed. The Bench did not consider there had been any undue punish- ment. He always considered it foolish to use the hands about the bead of a child; and he advised Miss Hutchin- son never to do so. Probably the cane was u.ed often enough, but order must be maintained. A stupid child must be corrected, and he did not see any hardship or c-mlty in the way the complainant had been treated.—Mary Ellen Lydiate, mother of the complainant in the last case, was now charged with assaulting Miss Hutchinson.—Miss Hutchineon's evidence was to the effect that on the 30th September she had occasion to punish the defendant's child, and about*led f-past twelve the de.fendant came to her lodg- ings followed oy a large crowd of children. She shouted and made use of bad names to Miss Hutchinson, who told her she would see her at the school and then closed the door of the house. At half-past one Mrs Ly,4iate entered the school, and walking up to Miss Hutchieson'3 chsk began shouting and calling that young lady "names." In conse- quence of her abusive leriguatze and the disturbance she created, Miss Hutchinson had to turn the children out, and keep them out for half-an hour. Miss Hutchinson ordered the defendant out several times. Defendant replied that she had "as much right there as her," and put her fist to Miss Hutchinson's nose and threatened to knock her to the feu. Miss Hutchinson raised her hand with the intention of putting 'tie deendant out, but the defendant seized hold of her and scratched her hands until blood came. The care- taker, Inglesfield, was sent for, but leefore his arrival the defendant had departed. In a short time, however, she re- turned, and created a second disturbance, and was at length put out by the caretaker.—Evidence of a confirmatory char- acter was given by Beatrice Smith, 13 years of age, a moni- tor, and by Samuel Inglesfield, the caretaker.—The defend- ant stated that she went to the school in order to ask Miss Hutchinson what she had laseu " " her daughter for. She was at the desk, and would not make any :answer, but put her hands on her (defendant's) shoulders to push i her out. She resisted. Miss Hutchineen told her to ' go out and take her child with her, and threw the school fees on the table. She took the child home.—ln answer to the Bench, Miss Hutchinson said the child had since at- tended the school.—Mr. Reynold-. said Miss Hutchinson was quite within her rights in ordering the defendant to leave the schoolroom, when she kicked up a row there; and the case was fully proved.—Mr. Linaker said the School Board did not wish to press the case, but merely to show parents that they could not interfere with the canduct of the school.—Mr. Reynolds said such conduct as the defend- ant's was destructive of all discipline in a school.—A tine of is and costs was imposed.
WIDNES AMATEUR ELOCUTIONARY AND DRAMATIC SOCIETY.

The annual meetiug of this society was held on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. G. E. Say-ce. There was a good attendance of members.—The report of the com- mittee stated that the membership at present consisted of 1 president, 20 vice-presidents, 15 acting and 61 honorary members, making a total of 97. Alluding to the performan- ces given in February last, the report stated that the repre- sentations were given without professional all, the society relying entirely upon its own members, a thing which very few societies attempted, especially when rendering such a high-claso comedy as "Our Boys.' The committee took that opportunity of thanking the leading metril.•;ers for their valuable assistance, and congratulated them upon their cefe- ful reading, and the intelligent manner in which they im- personated their several characters. The sum of £l.l 19s 2d was handed over to the treasurer of the Widnes Cricket Club as the net proceeds of the entertainment. The season closed with a balance in hand of Lid 9s 11d, and a few more subscriptions for the last season might yet come in. The committee stated that since the performances the so- ciety had sustained a severe loss by the death of one of its most capable acting memlnrs, Mr D. W. Hunter, whose clever impersonation of Sir Geoffrey Champneys, in Our BVs," would long be remembered. In concluding the report, the committee thanked the members for their support during the past season, and expressed a hope that it might be extended to the new officers sad committee, and that the general feeling at the annual meeting might be of such a character as to encourage the acting members to , push on vigorously with the coming season's dramatic work. —The report was unanimously adopted on the motion of Mr. H. Rawclifie, seconded by Dr. McCambridge. It was unanimously decided that Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., be in- vited to fill the post of president for the ensuing year, on the motion of Mr. Lewis, seconded by Mr. C. Nixon.— The vice-presidents were reappointed, with the addition of Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., and Major Williams. Mr. R. Lewis was re-elected treasurer. On the motion of Mr. Lewis, seconded by Mr. H. Yates, Mr. E. M. Davies was unanimously re-appointed hon. sec. Mr. Davies was highly euleg4e.d for the valuable services which he has rendered to the club during the past year.—Mr. James White was ap- pointed stage manager, and Mr. H. W. Cookson acting manager. The committee was re-appointed. Votes of thanks to the various officers for the services which they had rendered to the society during the past year were ac- corded.—An early meeting of the committee will be called to decide upon the pieces to be played during the forth- coming winter.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

To-day the ratepayers of Widnes are called upon to elect eleven gentlemen to represent them on the School Board. Since the adoption of the Education Act, 12 years ago there has caly been one contested election, the three sec- tions of the inhabitants, broadly defined as Church, Catholic, and Nonconformist, have usually effected a com- promise that so far worked satisfactorily, as the town pos- sesses three magnificent schools,Which are in a very efficient state. The efforts to avoid an election on the present occa- sion, however, failed, mainly through a split in the church , arty, and 21 candidates were nominated. By withdrawals, the number has been reduced to 15, divided as follows Church of England: Messrs. T. S. Timmis, J.P., H. W. Deacon, J. B. Imison, and J. W. Wareing. Roman Catholic: Revs. Father Clarke and Father Finegan, Messrs. R. Brad- shaw, F. Heyes, and Dr. O'Keeffe. Nonconformist: Messrs. R. Holden, Davis, Roger. Ciogg. and Joseph Robinson. In- dependent: Rev. aireerge Bond, Mr. G. H. Bolton, and Mr. ' E. Martlev. The candidates who have withdrawn arc the Rev. J. Wright Williams, Messrs. J. Brock, J.P., A. McClele land. S. K. Muspratt, George Pilkington, J.P., and George Pryde. The three organised parties have isened addresses advocating the claims of their nominees, but no meetings have been held by the Catholic and Church parties. Can- vassing has, however, been briskly carried on, and con- ' siderable interest is felt in the result. Mr. S. H. Hartley, the returning officer, has completed the arrangement for the polling. THE NONCONFORMIST CAMPAIGN. The Nonconformist party have conducted their:contest with great vigour. Each evening during the past week a meet- ing has been held in some part of the district, and the can- didates have delivered addresses. On Tuesday evening a uneet!ng was held in Oakland-street Wesleyan Schoolroom, under the presidency of Mr. B. Brown, who ex- plained that the candidates had been selected by a repre- sentative meeting of the Nonconformists of Widnes._ Mr. Roger Fogg (Wesleyan) one of the candidates, de- livered a long address, in which he said the contest was not a men nut principles, and to test the strength of Noncon- formity in Widnes. The Nonconformist candidates had no selfish interests to serve. Their only aim was to get the , best possible results for the Board schools at the lea 4 pos- sible expense. Their Church and Roman Catholic friends were makings strong point ef the fact that they had to I maintain their own schools and also pay a School Board rate ; but these persons did not object to rceiving the Government grant, although they objected to Government Interference. These gentlemen were anxious to get on the Board with the object as far as possible to clots the wheels of the education movement in the town—(hear. hear,)—and as far as possible to keep down the Board schools to the I level of their own schools. (Applause.) The object of the ratepayers ought to be to send representatives who would , have the Board cbools in as efficient manner as possible, and at the least possible cost. There was one section of the , church in the town which in particular made a strong point of having to support their own schools. He should like to point out this fact that there were very fey; Nonconformist children who had to apply to the Education Committe• for their school fees to he oid—(hear, hear,)—but he. b. hewed, that 75 percent. of the school foes paid were paid to Catho- lic children in that town. He contended that the clenotni- national schools had been very much improved through the influence of the School Board. Nearly tv,ry denominational school had had to be enlarged, owing to the good wwl, done by the attenal•nc, officers in driving eltildeen into schools. Therefore the general ratepayers paid to some extent through the Government grant, and the School Board for Denominational Education. Alluding to religieus educa- tion. Mr. Fogg said the religious teaching in the Board Schools was quite as efficient, if not much better than the education given in Donominational Schools. The ground for complaint by the Church people was that the Church Catechism and dlogmatic theology were not taught ; but why aid not the clergy avail themselves of the opportunity of attending the schools to giv:, spocitie ins motion ii the dogmas they taught. The Nonconformists hold thit the

religious observances in the Boerd achoels were quite right, bat the religious beliets they held dear were .taught in the Sunday scheols,oneof the tinaet hlessinge of the land. He how- ever,maintained that parents could not delegate the teaching of reiiaion either to the Sunday school or the day school; they must be responsible alone. (Hear, hear.) This cry of religious education was simply a red herring drawn across the track for the purpose of damaging the chances of the Nonconformist candidates. He tr ustei that Nonconformists would be true to their principles, and not only elect the three ca#didates, but show that there was a strong element of Nonconformity in Widnes. The Nonconformists were entitled to a greater representation than they had had in the past, and he trusted that they would be more strongly repro- eented when another election CAMS round. (Applause.) The Rev. R. Burdon moved a resolution pledging the meet- ing to support the candidature of Messrs. R. H. Davis, joeeph Robinson, and Roger Fogg. He remarked that the Nonconformists were not afraid of pure Bible teaching.— Mr. T. S. Swale seconded the motion. An attempt, he said, was being made to make people think that the Congregationalists, Baptists, and Wesleyans did not care for religion. He should like to know where Widnes would have been in its early days, " When there was no eye to pity," if it had not been for the efforts put forth by devoted Nonconformists. He believed that if a poll of the town were taken there would be found to be more Nonconferrnists than any other denomination.—Ma. Martin Taylor supported the motion. He said the Church party were forcntz this contest upon the ratepayers. No c, Mr. Timmis and Mr. Deacon were both gentlemen who had stood up for the Board Schools quite as much as any Non- conformist candida;e. He should therefore be sorry to see these men put off the Board, but they c sold not allew their synapathies to interfere with this position, that they were trying to show what was the pceition of Nonconformity in the town. (Hear, hear.) He advised all to vote with that idea fixed in their minds, and put .Messrs. Davis, Robin- son, and Fogg at the head of the poll. (Applause.) What- ever the clerical element of the Board might be, he hoped it would not be that Mr. Bend would be elected. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had a greater respect for the Church of England—(laughter and applause)—tkan to think that Widnes was so depraved that it could return a clergyman whose character was so well known in the town. (datug,hter.) He argued that the struggles for education bed been in the teeth of the clergy of the Church of England, cud that whatever strides had been made in England during the present century there ware no thanks due te'thein. It ha I been the spirit of Non- conformists that had fought and won the battle, and he ehould be astonished if they did not have Nonconformity shovva in its true positien when the result of the election was made known.—The mation was carried uasnimously.— Mr. John Jackson moved, and Mr. John Wise seconded, a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was carried. Mr. Wise hoped that the Nonconformist candidates would Put down the dreadful state of corporal punishment that existed in the Board schools.
RUNCJRN FREE LIBRARY.
TORY MEMBERS AND POLITICAL PAMPHLETS.

At the monthly meeting of the Runcorn Free Library Committee on Wednesday evening, there were present Messrs. F. A. Lake (chairman), .T. Simoson, W. Haedley, T. Rile-, J. R. Frith, Geo. Moss, F. J. Norman, W. J. Shore, E. Marwood, and J. D. Jones (librarian). Mr. Shore moved the following resolution, of Which he had given notice :—" That no literature he placed on the reading room tables without the sanction of the Book Selection Committee." Mr. Shore declaimed that his reso- lution was not intended to cause offence to Liberal or Tory, Churchman or Dissenter. Their space in the reading room was far too lialited, and as at various times of the:year when elections were on a groat mass of political literature was sent down by political organisations for distribution, be thought such a rescOution would take away from the librar- ian the responsibility of probably giving offence by refusing what he might consider unnecessary. Mr. Simpson expressed the astonishment he felt when he received notice of such a motion to be proposed in these days of light by any member of the Free Library Commit- tee: He understood at once that it was because of the Liberal literature that hed been sent down to be placed on the tables of the reading room that such it motion as that was proposed by a Tory member of the committee. He would not place any retriction upon Conservative or Liberal publications, nor upon either side of any other ques- tion. He thoullit that in these days they oueht to allow people to judge for themselves. and he opposed most strongly the motion. Mr. Shore stated his willingness to.withdraw the motion after this expression of opinion. Mr. Simpson said he liked the readers to have the oppor- tunity of seeing and of criticising for themselves. Mr. Ma.rwood said he thought that the real objection was against the elips and dy leaves that were placed on the tables, and not against the pamphlets. The Chairmen said the motion of Mr. Shore certainly could not have been made from a political mo:ive. The Liberals were in a majority on that committee, as well as on the Book Selection Committee. He did net believe in the reading-room being made into a sort of battle ground or an advertising board for different parties and crotchet mon- gers. All that was asked for was that the matter should be put in something like order, and he would second the motion with pleasure if Kr. Shore would not withdraw it. Mr. Shore intimated that he was quite willing the motion should go before the meeting. Mr. Moss was of opinion the resolution would form a bar- rier to any literature le:ing placed on the tables. Mr. Handley said they must remember that all the litera- ture of whatever political party wee of a very evanescent character. He was quite sure that no member of the Board, least of all Mr. Simpson, would send anthing but what might safely be read by anyone. At the suggestion of the Chairman, Mr. Shore made his motion read—" That no literature he placed on the reading tables without the sanction of the Book Selection Committee or the Librarian on their behalf."

Mr. Simpson moved that as the Librarian already pos- si,t,sad the rower proposed to be given to him by that reso- lutinn, it was altogether unnecessary. Mr. Frith seconded the motion. He said it was pretty zenerally known what the opinions of Mr. Jones were, but be was proverbially fair, and no one could raise a finger against him. Mr. Norman said it was singular that the motion should, be brought forward by a Conservative, that a Conservative should second it, and that the only gentleman who had yen-- tared to say a word in its support was their friend Mr. Marwood, who seemed to see some wid.3 distinction between a leaflet and a pamphlet For the amendment there voted Messrs. John Simpson, J. R. Frith, George Moss, W. Handley, T. Riley, and F. J... Norman. For the motion : The Chairman, and Messrs. W. J. Shore, and E. Marwood. The motion was therefore de- • feated.

FRODSHAM.

MUTUAL IMPTIOrEMENT CLASS.—A meeting of tha Frod- - sham Wesleyan Mutual' Improvement Class was held on Friday, Mr. Samuel Walker in the chair. The mestinL: was devoted entirely to readings from the poets by nine mem- bers of the class.

DROWNING FATALITv.—A sad fatality occurred at Frod- sham on Wednesday morning. A middle-aged woman named Unsworth, wife of a farm labourer, was hanging out clothes oppo,ite her dwelling when she went into a fir, ta which she was subject, and fell into a running stream that passes along the road. Although the water is only a few inches deep, she was suffocated before aid arrived. From the posi- tion and condition of the body, it was evident that the woman's struggles had been very severe. LETTER FRON! ABROAD.—(Advt.)—Detroit, Sept. 13th, MM.—Dear Mother,—As soon as Annie has left give this to Mr. and then ha will know that he has to put that in the paper that he promised me; and aive all Frod-- sham a public invitation to our wedding, which will take place on the 20th Oct., ISM, at my own residence, 176,. Franklin-street, Detroit, Michigan, U.S., where I will pro- vide a great feast for them. So now, dear friend, I must conclude with much loye.—l remain, yours truly, A. HOU() RTON.

'WRY I All LIBERAL."—Mr. B. KniYeton, of Runcorn.. attended ?t the Liberal Committee Room, Frodsharn, on Saturday evening, and read a paper entitled "Why I am a Liberal," in which he impressed upon young men in par- ticular the necessity of being able to give satisfactory reasc,ns why they were Liberals. He brought under their notice several interesting statistics with reference to that working classes, comparing their earnings and food at the present time with what they were fifty years ago. He also mentioned various Acts the Liberal Governments bad passed which benefited this class of people in this country.

A FRODSHANI PUBLICAN AND TEIE HUCKSTER. Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn P,ttv Sessions, en Menday, William Youd, landlord of the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsham. appeared to answer a nharga of assaulting Ann Littler.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.— The camplainant said she lived at 36, Bridge-street, Ran- MD. She had also a house at Kingsley, near Frodsham. She had been a huckster for 20 years, and travelled four dsys a week between Frodshatm and Runcorn. On the Bth inst. she travelled in a second-class compartmeut from Frodsham. The defendant was in the same compartment. She never Came across such a man in her life. On the journey he struck her twice on the knees, and at Runcorn she saw him taking pears out of her basket. She told him to "leave them alone," and he replied, "What the -- is a pear or two?" She snatched the pears out of his band, and told him he was stealing them. He shook his hand at her face, and touched her chin. Ile then shook his finger at her, and said, "This is your master; I will make you suss for taking these pears out of iny band." Site avas never 10 in- sulted in her life.—ln reply to the defendant, the com- plainant said she never spoke to bin) onc.? in her life about trade or any other matte,.—The defendant said in travelling cue miaht easily put hie la 1 anc. on a knee quietly when talk- ing. He did not kuow that he insulted the woman at all. He hid talked to her many a tinie about business Ho never put his band to bc!r chia et :01, and he knew n9thi7g about the nears.—The complainant: You filled your pockets. ,-Neither complainant nor defendant had any witnesses.— Mr. Reynolds characterised it as a trumpery case, and fine defendant 5s and costs, 12s Oil.

Lord R. Churchill returned to London on Thursday A meeting in favour of Home Rule was held at on Wednesday night, and addressed by Mr J A Pic - A resolution in favour of Mr. Wadstoue'a measa, Rule was adopted.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

div.head: COST OF THE SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE COST OF THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

Among the Parliamentary papers issued on Sat- urday was the return moved for by Mr. Craig-Sellar showing the expenses incurred by local authorities and public companies in connection with private Bill legislation from 1883 to 1885 inclusive, this period having been fixed upon primarily with the object of publishing the enormous sum spent by the promoters and opponents of the Manchester Ship. Canal Bill. The return, however, gives no conclu- sive information on this subject. It simply records the fact that in 1883 the promoters spent £62,484, in 1884, £42,422, and in 1885 £41,504, or a total of. £146,500 in their Parliamentary proceedings. Even these figures do not represent all that was ex- pended in conducting the first and principal Bill of the Company through Parliament, inasmuch as they include no allowance to Mr. Daniel Adamson and other individual promoters in regard to the expense to which they were put in attending the sittings of the different committees. These expenses are roughly estimated at £26,000, 80 that up to the end of 1885 the outlay upon the scheme did not fall short of £172,500, and to this will have to be added the expflases of promoting the Bill of last Session seeking power to pay in- terest out of capital during the construction of the canal. Nor would the total then arrived at repre- sent the full account for 1884 and 1885. The town of Warrington spent £2,522 in opposing the scheme, while a considerable share of the £5,584 incurred in ParAiamentary expenses by the Manchester Cor- poration was in connection with it in " watching " or promoting charges. The return gives no infor- mation whatever as to the amount expended by the different petitioners in opposing the bill; but it is well understood that the costs of the promoters were not one whit heavier than those of the oppo- nents and upon this basis the mere proposal to make the canal cost the enormous sum of £345,000 before it finally received the approval of Parlia- ment.

div.head: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening, when there were present—Mr. W. L. Evans (in the chair). Messrs. T. P. Hewitt, H. Fogg, W. Goldsworth, H. Cross (clerk), and T. Cowherd (assistant clerk).—The Now-payment of School Fees: Mr. Hewitt sug- gested that the teachers el the various schools should sub- mit each month statements and particulars of each case in which the school fees had not been paid during the month. He thought the arrears would be easily dealt with if they were taken each month before they had accumulated to a large amount, when it was impossible for them to deal with them. If they attacked the arrears when they were young they would be able to get in some of the arrears, and then they could at once strike out the arrears which were irre- coverable. He moved that each teacher be requested to submit a statement as to the arrears at each fortnightly meeting of the Attendance Committee, and that the com- mittee have instructions to deal with the arrears as sugges- ted.—The Chairman said he thought that course would be a very good one to adopt.—Mr. Goldsworth seconded the motion, which was adopted.—Mr. Biyliss (school attendance officer) remarked that some of the arrears were owing in re- gard to children whose parents resided outside the Board's district.—The Chairman stated that in future all children should be refused admittance to the school who resided out- side of Prescot, unless they brought their school fees, or came by recommendation of the school attendance officer or the guardians.—Mr. Hewitt said the question would come before the committee according to the resolution just passed. —The matter then dropped.—ei Promotion : Miss Harris, head mistress of the girls' school, reported that about a fort- night ago Miss Doak, one of the assistants, had received an appointment as an assistant it: a large school at Walton-on- the-Hill, and she left at once, by arrangement with the clerk.—The Chairman considered the promotion a satisfac- tory one.—Mr. Goldsworth (to Miss Harris) : Is your pre- Beet staff sufficient ? Miss Harris : Yes, sir.—School Attendance Report : Mr. Bayliss (school attendance officer) reported that siece the last meeting 226 children had been reported as irregular in their attendance at school. Thirty- three parents, representing 4fBoroef the Attendancethemostirregcuolmarmaitttteene: dances, had been brought and three summonses had been issued. Remissions of fees had been granted as follows :—Boys 27. girls 25, iefants 15, total 6L During the quarter ending 15th inet 28 children living in the School Board district had reached the age of five years, and were attending school as follows :—Church schools 9, Board schools 7, Yew Tree 6, private Tests- neonial : A letter was read from Mr. William Baylise, school attendance officer, stating that, as he wee desirous of apply. ing for the post of school attendance officer under the St. Helens Corporation, he asked the Board to kindly grant him a testimonial in support of the applieation.—Mr. Hewitt moved that the clerk draw up a testimonial on behalf of the Board, and that the seal of the Board be attached to such testimonial.—Mr. Fogg seconded the motion, which was adopted. the Chairman stating that they would be sorry to part with Mr. Bayliss, and they regretted they were not able to pay him sufficient to retain his services.

div.head: WILLIAM TYNDALE AND HIS WORK.
div.p: WILLIAM TYNDALE AND HIS WORK.

Sunday being the 350th anniversary of the martyrdom of William Tyndale, the Rev. James Johnston preached in the Congregational Church, Prescot, with reference to the sub- iect from the words." My faithful martyr," Revelation ii., 13. The rev, gentleman said they commemorated that day

div.p: TEE EXAMINER, S XTURDAY, OCTOBER 23. 1886.

the death of an Illustrious English scholar, confessor, and martyr. Early in the year 1535 at the instigation of Henry VIII. Tyndale was basely arreseed in Antwerp, tried at Augsburg, imprisoned for eighteen months, and burned at Vilvorde, near Brussels, on the 17th October, 1538. As a chivalrous end conapicuoue leader of the English Reforma- tion, and as a divineukshed translator of the New Testa- ment, he was entitled tel rank with the foremost reformers of France, Germany, Switzerland. and Italy. Born in the West of Englend in 1454, Tyndale was first educated in Oxford. where he came in contact with Lutheran teaching, and, afterwards, at Cambridge threw himself heartily into the burnine question of the times, viz., the revival of pure religion according to the scriptures. At an earlier day Wycliffe. Huss, Jerome, and Weasel, "reformers before the 'Reformation," had opposed Remish•innovations, and won many adherente who were ultimate.ly suppressed by the overwhelmieg power of the Church. With the dawn of the ldth century the movement was spreading steadily over the face of Europe. Savonarola had perished in Italy in 1498, while there remained in the vanguard of the cause Luther in Germany, Zwingli in a Nwitzerland,Geetavus Vasa in Sweden, Ferri end Calvin in France, and If trnilton in Scotland. England was under special obligations to the visits of Eras- mus which gave immense impulee to the s'udy of the Scrip- tures among the educated clessee, the citizens of London, and peaeamts of Lincolnshire. His edition of the Greek Testament was earnestly studied at Cambridge and its con- tents expounded by 'llyndale, Bilney, Freth, and others. Failing to receive adequate patronage in London, and ex- posed to persecutions, Tyndale left England for the con- tinent in 1523 after having made an earnest vow that ‘• if God would spare his life, ere many years he would cause the boy 'she driveth the plough to knew more of the scriptures th an did all the priests." Landing at Ham- burgh he completed the first fruits of his noble enterprise— , the translation and printing of the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. In 1525 he is believed to have visfted Luther and other reformers at Wittemberg and, at his sext city of refuge, Cologite, made rapid strides with his great task. His whereabouts being niscoyered he was banished front the city and immediately sailed up the Rhine to the ancient city of Worms, already celebrated by the memorable defence of Luther, and where Tyndale was destined to accomplish his entire translation and printing of the New Testament in the English tongue. This first edition, numbering 3,000 conies, was carried tea England in 1520 lw some pious Hanseatic merchants and secretly circulated. In addition to him lebniars on the Pentateuch, which was finished in the year 1531, he eubeequently acted in the capacity of chaplain to the British merchants in Antwerp. His saj mm n in the venerable commercial metropolis had not extended over three years when it WAS abruntly closed by a successful conspiracy formed between the Emperor and the English monarch for hie seizere. After nigh upon two years' confinement ttae so-called enemy of the faith died at the stake in the same year that his erudite attester, Erasmus, had peseedetway. Tyndale unquestionably laid the feunda- tion of treat New Testament which for upwards of four centuries has been the bulwark of England's strength and prestige. It ham substantially formed the baeis of our pre- sent modern version. Although Wyclitt'e translation had been made 150 years before, it was not published in printed form until 1731. Whether lyndale had acquaintance with Wycliffe's version or the German translation of Luther is untletertnined, though it is admitted that, with respect to perspiceitv, noble simplicity, propriety of idiom, and purity of style, as r,nglieh version has yet surpassed it. In ten years 30,000 copies were printed, and by the year 1611. when our authorivel version was put forth, no less than 273 edi- tions of the Bible and New Testament in English issued from the press. How incalculably precious the services of Tyndale have been on behalf of Christendom and the heathen world nsay be faintly estimated by the figures of the British and Foreign Bible Seciety, which alone has pub- lished the Scriptures in 303 languages and dialects, and dis- tributed 170 millions of copiee.

had been filled up for £7, and cashed at Parr's Bank. The forgery was a very clever one.—Mr. William Silcock, cashier at Parr's Bank, said that on the 12th inst. prisoner presented a cheque (produced) for £7, which witness cashed. The cheque purported to be signed by Major Brown. Witness knew Major Brown's signature, and the signature of the cheque produced appeared to be a fac simile. Witness paid prisoner £7, and afterwards the cheque was given to Inspector Spinks.—Major Brown, in his evidence, said that on the 13th inst. he discovered that a a blank cheque had been torn out of his cheque book on Parr's Bank. The cheque was numbered C 438163. Witness, on mak- ing inquiries at the bank, found that a cheque had been cashed for £7. The signature and endorsement of the cheque were forged. Prisoner was a mess waiter at the barracks, and could get into witness's quarters, as the door was not locked.. —lnspector Spinks, who received prisoner into cus- tody on the 14th inst., said that prisoner, when charged with forging and uttering the cheque pro- duced, replied "It is quite true : I opened Major Brown's portmanteau with his keys, took the, blank cheque from the cheque book. The writing upon it is mine ; I cashed it at Parr's Bank on Tuesday the 12th. The money found upon me (£5 odd) is part of the money I received from the bank."—Prisoner was then further charged with stealing a letter containing a cheque for the value of £7, also the property of Major Brown.—Evidence was given by Major Brown to the effect that he made out a cheque on the 10th inst., dated the 9th inst., on Messrs. Cox and Co., which he put in an I envelope. He inadvertently left the envelope on. a I table in the ante-room. Evidence given by several soldiers from the barracks shewed that on the 12th inst. Major Brown's servant went into that officer's quarters, and discovered prisoner under the bed:. The officers were at mess, and Major Brown was I called out, and prisoner was given into custody,and I. taken to the guard-room. When he was being searched a paper was seen to fall to tho ground, which on being picked up was found to be the i cheque that had been placed by the Major in the 'envelope. Prisoner had endorsed the cheque. Pri- soner, on being subsequently charged by Inspector ; Spinks, admitted that he was guilty of the second offence.—Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool ; Assizes on both charges.

LIBERAL CLUB DISCUSSION. THIC DUTY OF LIBERALS,. The first discussion of the season in connection with the Earlestown Liberal Discussion Class was held in the Earles- town and District Liberal Club. Fairclongh-street, on Thursday evening, when Mr. W. D. Burdis, of Newton. read a paper on "The political duties of Liberals in this Divi- sion." There was a good attendance, and Mr. Wilson pre- sided. Mr. F. A. R. Neill, of Bold, had been announced to preside, but forwarded a letter expressing his eutreme regret that he was unable to be present, and remarking that he trusted the meetings during the winter would be crowned with success, as he believed a thorough education was the only way to have Liberal principles brought to the front. Among the gentlemen present were Messrs. W. D. Burdis, L. T. Foulkes, J Bryce (Newton), Smethurst, X. Davies, C. Kelly, W. MbEvoy, T. Morris (honorary secretary), atc. The Chairman, in introducing the subject, remarked that he thought the Liberals of the division bad well found out what were their duties, hut they were rather in the back- grownd at present. He honed they would be more to the front in the future. (Applause.) Mr. W. D. Burdis, on rising to read'his paper, was warmly received. After remarking that the granting ot the fran- chise to county householders, thanks to the efforts of the Liberal party and their great leader, Mr. W. E. Gladstone would lead them to a closer study of politics, he urged that it was important that such institutions as their Liberal Club and Debating Society should become not only centres for pleasure at social intercourse and recreation, but schools were men were educated in the highestof all duties—that of true patriotism. Believing, as Liberals, that their creed was the one hest calculated' to carry out the idea of true patriotism, he wished to show how they in the riewton Division could best do their duty and hasten the time when they shonld be represented in Parliament by a man who would speak and vote for the principles they espoused. He then proceeded to urge that the first duty of every Liberal, if he was duly qualified, was to get his name placed upon the register of voters, for many votes were lost to them through a lack of a feeling of personal responsi- bility. The second duty he • considered was that every Liberal should join the Liberal Association for the purposes of securing a strong aid united organisation, while third/y there should be a careful selection of persons selected to act upon the executive and Three Hundred. Liberalism wanted workers and not ornaments. upon their executive committees. As -a'fourth duty he itn- pressed upon Liberals the study of history, esp,.eially the history of the present century, and he asked if the Tory party could produce such a list of measures for the public weal as the abolition of slavery, the free- dom of trade, the cheap press, the "free breakfast table," as it was called ; the abolition of religious tests, the various bills for-providing a cheap and good education, the ballot, the enfranchisement of the residents in counties, and the many other great and good measures secured by the Liberal party. He said no.. (Applause.) As a fifth duty he asked all Liberals to perform with care. and zeal the education of the young in political knowledge, and he thought further it was the duty of all Liberals in the division to agitate for more polling places. He urged they should also agitate to have the expenses of the election very much reduced, and the appointment by the Govern- ment of a special registration agent for each division, and he believed that the one man one vote franchise was the only just and proper one. (Applause.) He next contended that it was the duty of every Liberal to advocate the total abolition of canvassing, and he thought it was particularly the duty of the Liberals of that division to have as many lectures and meetings in the small 'places and outlying dis- tricts as was possible, and in conclusion he urged all Liber- als to fight fair and be generous to their opponents. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. T. Morris then proposed that the discussion upon the subject sheald be postponed until that day fort- night, and Mr. McEvoy seconded.the motion, which was passed.—On the motion of Mr. Smethurst, seconded by Mr. Morris, cordial thanks were tendered to Mr. Burdia, and a similar compliment to,the Chairman closed the meeting.

ST. HELENS. THE CONGREG,‘TIONAL CHAPEL —On Sunday evenin the Rey. R. J. Ward, pastor, preached in the Congregational Chapel, Ormskirk-street, a special sermon to young men and women, on "The parting of the ways." There was a large congregation. NUTGROVE WESLI3YA SUNDAY 15CLICOL —A Bind of Hope Entertainment was given on Saturday evening, when a programme of songs, greem, recitations, and dialogues was gore through by the members, assisted by a few friends. Mr. William Hitchen presided and delivered an appropriate address. There was a good attendance. Cirimar ORGANISATION SOCIETY. On Tuesday, a meeting of t:e general committee of the promoters of the Charity Organisation Society mat by permission of the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman T. Cook), in the Mayor's com- mittee-room, Town Hall, for the purpose of taking steps to start the organisation. Colonel Gamble presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. C. Pigot, James Brown, G. Lakeman, Fr: Mordannt, J. Shipham, C. H. Bradbury, Mr. George Webster, etc., etc. .It wao resolved to present a requisition, after being duly signed, to the Mayor, request- ing him to call a, meeting early, in November, for the pur- pose of formally inaugurating the society, adopting rules, and electing oilTters..

SEQUEL TO A L0V3.13.8 QUAREEL.--It the Town Hill, on Friday, Thomas Byrne. a respectable looking young man, living in College-street, was summoned for setting fire to the dress of a young woman, named Sarah Kay of Ashcroft-at, thereby doing damalor to the extent of las 9d.—The plainant stated that the defendant recently lived at the house of her mother, hut be left about a fortnight ago. On the night of the 9th inst. he appeared at the house in a drunken condition. Hia fell asleep in the kitchen, and as he did not seem inclined to more all the members of the family left him. He was afterwards heard walking 3 p and down the house, and striking a large quantity of matches. He went out about midnight;; immediately after which her mother got up and found her (witness') dresslying upon the kitchen table. It was all burnt and completely spoiled. She had kept company with the defendant for the last two years, but she had refused to have anything more to do with him —Mrs. Kay confirmed her daughter's statement. The magistrates adjourned the case for a week in order that an additional witness could be summoned.

THE CHARGE OF DECOYING A GIRL. At the Police Court, on Friday, before Mr. J. C. Gamble (chairman) and Dr. Gaskall, a married man named Richard Halton, described as a traveller for Mr. Lowry, wine and spirit merchant, St. Anti's, Manchester, was charged under remand with assaulting Police-constables Reeves and INPElenry, and further with assaulting Margaret Myles, a girl thirteen years of age, while she was travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Ribchester to Chester, on the 7th inst. Mr. Preston prosecuted on be- half of the London and North-Western Company; and Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, defended.—Mr. Preston de- tailed the circumstances as previously published, and said the age of the girl should have protected her from insalt, and such proceedings on the railway were a menace to other passengers.—Margaret Myles was then called. She said she was thirteen years of age and an orphan. When she was not in service she lived with her aunt, Mrs. Morals, at Stephen- son-street, Chester. She hot been in service at Stydmanor Farm, Ribchester, but left in the afternoon of the 7th inst. She took a ticket from Longridge Station to Preston, and there got out and took another ticket for Chester. On the platform at Preston she saw prisoner, and he said," Where are von going ? " She said, "To Chester." He said, " Will you go to Manchester with me and I will make a lady of you ?" She said she would not, as she. was going home to Chester. Shortly afterwards she got into the train in a compartment in which there was a gentleman, and prisoner got in just hefors the train started. At Wigan be asked her to go with him and he would get her lodgings. She refused, until he said there was no train to Chester, upon which she went with him to a refreehenent room in the town. He asked a woman in charge if he could have lodgings for himself and wife, and the woman asked witness if she was his wife. Witness said " No," and the woman said she could see that, and added that she had no room. Witness and prisoner then cante back to the station and went into a wait- ing-room, where prisoner assaulted her. Witness then went en the platform, and he followed and requested her again to go to Manchester. Witness got into a t..Helens train, prisoner again follows , and they were the oily two per- sons in the compartment. When nearing St. Helens be re- peated the offence. She threatened to call the guard. On reaching St. Helens they got out, and he took- he took her to Mrs. Johnson's lodging- house in Market-street, where he represented that she was his wife. Witness denied the state- ment. Before going to the lodging-house prisoner took her and the guard of the train into a public-house. He offere her a glass of beer but she refused it. Prisoner then took her to Mr. Cowan's cookshoo in Market-street, where he asked for accommodation, but being refused they went to Johnson's.—ln reply to Mr. Swift, witness said she had been in service at Ribchester for three janonths. She was sent away because she was untidy and not very clean. There was no other reason. She had to wait an hour and a half at Preston station. Between Preston and Wigan the other gentleman spoke to her, and said he had seen her as she went to Ribchester. Both prisener and a porter told her there was no train for Chester that night. She thought she had got into a Warrington train, but it name to st. Helens. She had no money when she got to Win at eight o'clock. Prisoner had had some drink, and at. St. Helens he said he thought they were at Warrington. She told prisoner she had no money for lodgings, and prisoner said he would get her a lodging. In a public-house near the station he said she was his sister, but she said she was not.—Matthew Hurst, fore- man porter at St. Helens station, said he witnessed th 6 ar- rival of the train from Wigan at 9-7. Prisoner and the girl were afterwards on the platform. Prisoner said be and his sister from Manchester had got astray, and they wanted to know when the next train was, he said 10-20. Prisoner then said he was going for refreshments, and asked witness if he could drink a glass. Witness went with him to the Royal Alfred. He heard nothing mentioned about Chester. He thought they were brother and sister, bat they were shy and quiet.—William Fraser, cabdriver, said he was in the Royal Alfred when the three persons were there. The girl refused to drink, and the prisoner threw some of the beer, on the girl's shoulders, saying nobody should travel with him who had nothing to drink. Prisoner asked for the ad- dress of a house of ill -fame. He sometimes called the girl his wife and sometimes his sister.—Robert Cowan, proprie- tor of an eating house in Market-street, deposed to his hav- ing declined to provide apartments for prisoner and "his sis- er."—Charlotte Johnson said the prisoner introduced the girl to her as his wife. Witness, suspecting that she was not his wife, told him to go. He refused, and she sent for the police. Witness detained the girl.—Police-consiables Reeves and Milburn deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who, when taken into custody, said be would not go without his wife. He was very stupid. He appeared to have had some drink, but wts not drunk.—Mrs. Johnson, recalled, said the girl told her that while passing through a tunnel another gentleman assaulted ber.—Mr. Swift, for the defence pointed out that the girl did not make any effort at Wigan to ascertain the time fixed for the departure of the next train for Chester, nor did she avail herselrof the numerous opportunities thrown in her way of complaining of the prisoner's conduct.—ln reply to the charge, the prisoner said : "I am not guilty. I never assaulted her. I will give my evidence at the sessions."—The prisoner was committed for trial at the sessions, being admitted to bail—hfmself in £6O and two sureties each of £3o.—Two informations for assaulting the police were not proceeded with.

div.head: ROBBERIfS AT WA7tPINGTON.
div.p: ROBBERIfS AT WA7tPINGTON.

At the 'Warrington Borough -C-ourt,--on-Wednesday morning, Frances liley, hawker, of Morris-court, off Silver-street, was brought up in custody on charges of being drunk and disorderly in Silver-st. on the previous night, and of stealing a silver geneva watch, value 30s, from the person of Rd. Willcock (70), who lives in Rose and Crown-street. Early on Tuesday afternoon the two, who have known each other for a long time, met in Horse- market-street, and afterwards had some beer to- gether in publichouses in that neighbourhood. They then went to where prisoner lives, and she wanted prosecutor to pawn his watch. This he declined to do and she then, according to evidence given by the prosecutor, snatched his watch, and after some altercation ran into the house of a neighbour with it was alleged, the watch in her possession. Will- cock gave information to the police, and prisoner was apprehended. As the watch had not been re- covered the magistrates granted a remand.—Yester- day morning prisoner Frances Riley was brought up on remand, charged with stealing, on the pre- vious Tuesday, a silver geneva watch, value 305., from the person of Richard Willcock. The magi- strates explained that the case had been remanded so that endeavours might be made to recover the missing watch; it had not. however, been recovered. The magistrates, after hearing evidence, said that there was a suspicion in regard to the watch, but as there was a doubt in the case they should dis- miss it. For being drunk, however, she would be fined 10s. and costs. Mr. John White, who presided, added that the magistrates thought that the com- plainant was rightly served in loAing his watch, it having been given in evidence that the two had been drinking together for some time.

At the same skiing of the court, Sarah Kanocross, formerly a domestic servant, but now a widow, was charged with stealing on the previous day a black jacket, a vest, a skirt, and other articles, value £1 19a., the property of James Green, tanner's labourer, Beatrice-street, and of his wife, Agnes Green. She was also charged with stealing a sheet and child's nightdress on the 12th inst. When asked if she. would elect to be dealt with summarily she made reply "I want you to send me as far as ever you can." In explaining the case to the magistrates on the Bench, Chief Constable Hunt said that James Green was prisoner's brother, and had been staying with him and his wife. Mrs. Greene left her in charge of the house and on returning home missed a number of articles, and, on information being given to the police, inquiries were made which led to the discovery that prisoner had pawned them in the names of Sarah Green and Mary Green. She pleaded guilty, and the magistrates sent her to prison for three months, with hard labour. Norah Hems, described as the wife of a comic singer, was at the same court, on Wednesday, charged with stealing a bed sheec belonging to Mrs. McDermott, at whose lodging-house in Dolman's- lane she had been staying. Prisoner, who had pledged the sheet for a shilling, now told the magistrates that she intended to redeem it, but was wailing until she received a letter from her hus- band. The was sent to prison for fourteen days. At the Warrington. County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday morning, a young girl named Alice. Goulding was brought before Mr. It. Houghton on a charge of stealing wearing apparel from the house of John Smith, of Sankey.—Superintendent Weir said that the case was not one of actual theft. Prisoner, who knew Mrs, Smith, borrowed the articles in question from her on the 4th inst., saying that she wanted to wear them to go to Warrington with, and would give her them back on her return. She did not keep that promise, and was, when sub- sequently apprehended, wearing the articles, which were a hat, a jacket, and a pair of boots, value 30s. —The charge was not pressed and prisoner was dismissed, the recoveredproperty being handed over to the rightful owner. _

At the— Borough Court, on Thursday morning Thomas Jones, who said that he was an ironworker from Wolverhampton, was brought up in custody on a charge of stealing a waterproof overcoat, -value 355, the property of Thomas Taylor, farmer, of Grappenhall, from the Norton Arms. Wilderspool- road, on the previous evening. Prisoner, who, when arrested, gave his name as George Roberts, also said that he had been travelling with a boxing booth. On Wednesday evening he was seen loiter- ing about the hotel premises, and the macintosh was afterwards missed. He attempted to pawn it, and Constable Singleton was informed and ques- tioned prisoner, who became abusive and was then handcuffed and taken to the police station. He behaved himself in a disorderly manner during the night, and damaged the cell in which he was con- fined. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for three months with hard labour. Emma Jackson, a stranger, who said that she was a native of Dublin, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Thursday morning with stealing a woollen shawl, the property of Mary Galvin, of 10, Priars Green. Prosecutor keeps a lodging- house, and prisoner went there on Wednesday after- noon and engaged lodgings for the night. While Mrs. Galain was upstairs prisoner stole the shawl, and pledged it in Winwick-street for is. 6d. She pleaded guilty, and was sent to prison for two months with hard labour.

FORGERY AND ROBBERY AT ORFORD BARRACKS. At the Borough Police Court, yesterday morning, Charles Plannagan, a private in the South Lancashire Regiment, was brought up on remand on a charge of forging and uttering a cheque, for the sum of £7, purported to be signed by Major Brown, of the King's Liverpool Regiment, with intent to defraud Parr's Bankinc, Compahy, or the said Major Brown. —Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk) appeared to prosecute, and said that on the 12th of the present month Major Brown had occasion to examine his cheque book, and discovered that a blank cheque had been extracted. It was found that a cheque

div.head: EARLEsToWN.
div.p: EARLEsToWN.

HAND BELL RINGERS.—In aid of the organ fund of the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, Cross-lane, an enjoyable entertainmer.t was given in the Lecture Hall, beneath the chapel on Tuesday evening. This consisted of a selection of pleasing airs on hand b4lls by the " Metropolitan Hand Bell Ringers," interspersed with selections of vocal music by the performers. There was a good attendance._ _ .

THE SHOOTING AFFAIR AT EARLESTOWN.—Up to last night (Thursday) the man James McKinsey, who attempted to commit suicide by shootiug. himself in Earle-street, on Thursday week, was still lying in an injured condition. He ir.s made rapid progress towards recovery, and on his leav- ing the institution, it is said, he will be apprehended by the police, and will be brought before the magistrates on a charge of attempting to commit suicide. GOLI3ORNE COTTON MILLS.—A Golborne correspon- dent says :—I beer from several reliable sources that, after prolonged negotiations, the extensive cottsn spinning and weaving premises, known as Parkside Mills, liolborne, be- longing to Messrs. S. Brewis, and Co., havu just been sold by private treaty. The news respecting the sale is hailed : with great delight, as it is believed the entire concern will ere long again be in fall swing. A Wigan firm are believed te be the purchasers.

GOOD IHEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Temlars was held on Monday evewina under the presidency of Brother George Warburton, P.W.C.T. After two members had been initiated several items of lodge bueinesa were considered, and arrangements for the celebration of the 14th anniversary of the lodge wore completed. The evening's programme, was, "Enter- tainment—all to take part." In accordance therewith an excellent selection of songs, readings, recitations, &c., was rendered.

GARDEN ROBBERIES AT BOLD.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday,. b.fore Mr. J. C. Gamble, two boys, named John Kenwright (8) and Richard Highoock (9), were summoned for damaging plum, apple, and pear trees, at Bold on the 2nd September, the property of John Stead, nurseryman and seedsman.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the complainant and stated that on the date named James Lord, manager for Mr. Stead, observed the lads in the gar- den and found them loaded with apples, &c. He then dis- covered that the trees in the garden had been seriously damagsd.—The Bench fined each boy 6d and costs, 7s 6d, and ordered thew to pay 31 as damages. Famt LABOURERS' QUARREL.— Before Dr. E. P. Twyford and Mr. J. C. Gamble at the St. Helens County Police Court, on Monday, James Broughton, a farm labourer at Bold, was summoned fer assaulting William Pat- terson,. ale a farm labourer, on the 20th ult.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the complainant, who said he was a teamsman in the employ of 31r. Stead at Bold. The defend- ant was also employed by Mr. stead. On the date named they had some words and complainant told the defendant that he did not understand cutting hay any more than a pia did. The defendant afterwards struck him and knocked hiD down.—A fine of 2s 6d and costs was imposed upon the defendant

THE UNITED EVA.NGELICAL MISkION.—The series of gatherings in connection with the United Evangelical Mission in Earlestown were cammenced on Monday evening with a prayer meeting, which was well attended, in the Dis- trict Infants' School, Market-street. The leaders were Oe Rev. T. R. Matthews' (vicar) and the Rev. J Allatt (Con- gregational). On Tuesday evening a prayer meeting was held in the Baptist Chapel. Market-street, under the leader- ship of the Rev. R. Carr (Primitive Methodist). On Wed- nesday evening a similar gathering was held in the Lecture Hall below the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, Cross-lane, and here the leaders were the Rev. James Kent (Wesleyan) and Mr. G. Dring the Town Missionary. No meeting was held on Thursday evening. PRIMITIVE METIICEMST SERMONS AND CONFERENCE.— On Sunday afternoon, throughout the Primitive Methodist Connexion, the servises in all places of worship were to- wards the furtherance of Sunday school work. In the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, Earlestown, the preacher, both morning and evening was Mr. R Johnson, of Golborne and in the afternoon a meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. James Woods, superintendent. In- teresting addresses on Sunday school work were delivered by Messrs. R Johnson (Golborne) and G. Drieg (Earles- town Town Missionary). On Monday evening a conference of teachers and Sunday school workers in the Earlestown circuit was held in the chapel. Prior to the discussion an en- joyable tea was served to about 40 friends, At the subse- quent proceedings the chair was occupied by Mr. James Pears, of Earlestown, and the Rev. Ro:ert Carr, the resident minister, read.an instructive paper on "The end to be aimed at in Sunday school work." The essayst urged that the end they should have in view was the perfecting of a re- ligions character in the young children committed to their charge. In the discussion which followed Messrs. T. Clarke, J. Holyocke, F. Bagnall, E. Dickens, J. Jackson, ITravis, and others took part. MISSIONARY MEETING AT WARGRAVE.—The Rev. E. C. Spicer, a returned missionary from Melbourne, Aus- tralia, preached in aid of the Society for the Propogation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, in the Parish Church, War- grave, on Sunday, and attended a public meeting in aid of the same object, held in Wargrave School, on Monday evening. The room was well filled, and the chair was oc- cupied by the Rev. Canon Whitley, rector, who was also supported by the Rev. J. Carson, of Winwick, and Mr. Wm. Thompson The Chairman remarked that he had been a member and supporter of the society since 1837, but hitherto lie had never asked the congregation to support it, and they had never held a meeting in its support. The society had claims on their support, and had done a great deal of good.—The Rev. J. Carson (Winwick) then explained the objects of the society as being to convey the ministrations of the Church of England to the subjects of the Queen in our colonies, both to the white men in Australia and to the black men in India. —The Rev. E. C. Spicer followed with a lengthy and in- teresting address on missionary labours, and the difficulties encountered by them in their works.—A collection in aid of the funds of the society was afterwards made. On the motion of Mr. W. Thompson, seconded by Mr. J. Catherall, a vote of thanks to the Rev. E. C. Spicer and the chairman. ciosed the proceedings.

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL SALE OF WORK.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL SALE OF WORK.

A two days sale of work to serve the double purpose of raising funds to defray certain alterations at the Congrega- tional Church, Crow-lane, and to celebrate the reopening of the Sunday school, was opened in the schoolroom adjoining the church on Wednesday afternoon. The school has been closed for several week, while the interior has been painted and decorated by Mr. George Wareing, of Earlestown, at a cost of about £4O. While this work was being carried out one of the beams supporting the roof was found to be in a faulty state, and the repairs necessitated a further outlay of about £3O. With the view of clearing off the decoration expenses Mr. Thomas Thompson has laboured energetically, and over £25 was realised by a concert held some months since, and a second similar gathering is expected to be held, during the 'lest few weeks. In addition to the schoel alte- rations, the front of the organ loft in the chapel has under- gone certain improvements and repair, and thereby a further expenditure of about £6O or £7O was incurred. To clear off the balances remaining the present sale of work was sug- gested, and the arrangements have been carried out under the directions of an energetic committee of ladies, under the presidency of Mrs. Allatt, wife of the Rev. James Allatt, the resident minister.

The schoolroom recently beautified, and arranged for the sale of work looked extremdv pretty. The efforts of the Ladies' Committee had met with a great shore of success,. and the seven stalls, exclusive of two refreshment stalls, were each well stocked with choice articles, both useful and ornamental. The ladies in charge of the stalls were :-Ist, Mrs. Glover, Ye% Stelfort, Mrs, Orridge, Mrs. Craw- ford; 2nd, Mrs. Holmes, Mrs. Dobson, Mrs. Hunt, Mrs. Pritchard; 3rd, Mrs. Lomas, Mrs. Duncalf, Mrs. Daniel Owen, Mrs. Dr. Patterson ; 4th, Mrs. Bryce, Mrs. Burdis, Mrs. Urquhart, Mrs. Bcdmer ; sth, Mrs. i3irks, Mrs. Tate, Mrs. Campbell; 6th (Young Ladies' Stall), Mrs. Arnold,

div.head: MARRIAGE OF DR-. VALENTINE.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF DR-. VALENTINE.

A large number of persons assembled in Wargrave Church, Wargrave, on Saturday forenoon, to witness the marriage of Mr. William Valentine, surgeon, of Haydock-st, Earlestown, to Miss Ellen Thompson, eldest daughter of Mr. William Thompson, of the Sankey Sugar Company. The interesting ceremony was performed by the Rev. Ca.non Whitley. rector. The bride was given away by her father, and the bride's gister, Miss Mary Thompson, was the brides- maid, while Mr. Thomas G. Dobb, of Leigh, was the grooms- man. s the happy couple left the church they were greeted with showers of rice, while flowers were strewn along the path from the church, • The presents were of a costly character and included a suite of drawing-roam furniture, including a pianoforte, from Mr. William Thompson, senr ; plaques and painted brackets, frem Miss Mary Thompson ; brackets, &e,Mr. Her- bert Thompson ; wine glasses and tumblers. Mr. William Thompson, junr ; timepiece,. Mr. John Thomson; carvers and case, Captain Thomson ; silver mounted bis- cuit barrel, Mr. John Henry Thompson and Miss Emily Thompson ;, set of knives and carvers, Mr. James Thompson;. a splendid silver cruet stand from a few employes of the Sankey Sugar Company; a sewing machine, Mr Edward C Turner; cases of silver tea spoons and sugar spoons, Captain Seton ; pair of Venetian glass vases, Mrs Seton ; dinner and tea services, Rev Canon Whitley; fish carvers in case and Aynqley tea. service, Mr Thomas Molyneaux ; toast and egg rack, Mr Slee ; preserve sprons in case, Mr TG Dobb ; card tray, Miss-King ; Eider- down quilt, Miss Wateaough ; cruet, egg and toast stand. Miss,Adair ; jelly dish, Miss Warburton;. knife and fork rests; Mr and Mrs James Davies; marmalade spoon, Miss Jessie Davies;. brass pan, Mr and Mrs Bretelle ; breakfast cruet stand, the Misses Bretelle ; cookery book and butter knife, Mr S Bretelle ; pickle fork, Mr Pimblett ; breakfast cruet and crumb dish and tray, Miss and Mr W Johnson; claret jug, Mr and Mrs Waloasley (Blackpool) ; glass vases and dishes, Miss Bates; Indian table covers, mantle border, white cashmere shawl and tea cosy, Mr Robert Wrigley ; American rocking chair, Mr and Mrs Worsley ; flower stand and set of tidies, Miss Noble; two toilet bottles, Mr A Peake; glass dishes and toast rack. Mrs Birkhead ; covered jugs, kettle, and other articles, Mr John Walker ; leather bracket, Mrs Buckley; cushion, Miss Dora Buckley; antimacassar and mats, Miss Caunt; crumb brush and tray, Miss Nor- bury; antique brass candlesticks, Mr and Mrs. C T Whitley; water jug, Master W Thompson ; silk cushion, Miss D Buck- ley ; large Shetland shawl, Mr P Buckley ; silver mounted claret jag, Mr and Mrs Walmaley ; Bohemian engraved flower vase, Miss Cloudsdale ; sugar spoon, Miss Danbury; smelling salt bottle, Miss Hill ; glass vase, Mr Haden ; and pair of spittoons, Mr T Sedoskie ; card tray. Miss King.
The dispute between colliery employes and employers in North Wales was amicably adjusted on Wednesday, and work has been resumed at all the pits.

At a meeting on Tuesday of the delegates representing the wrought nail-makers of Worcestershire and Stafforu- shire. it was decided to accept the advance of 10 per cent. offered by the employers. This will probably avert a strike.

CODERS.-At the Birmingham Police Court on Monday, William Oram and Eliza Thompson were charged with the manufacture of counterfeit coins. The police made a raid on Thompson's house on tho 9th inst., and found the prison- ers plating counterfeit coins. Nearly 200 base coins„ and a battery and other articles requisite in the manufacture of base coins were found in the house. They were both com- mitted to the assizes.

MR. SETON-KAaR, M P., AND BUILDING SOCLETIES.—On Wednesday evening, Mr. H. Seton-Karr, M.P., presided at a meeting at the Conservative Club, Hall-street, to inaugurate a branch of the Counties Conservative Permanent Benefit Building Society. Mr. Seton-Karr said they were gathered together for what seemed to him a very practical and business-like object. As far as he understood, it was a society which was certainly worthy of all support, because it was a society to encourage thrift amongst the working classes, and to enable working men to reap, in the best pos- sible manner, the fruits of their own industry, and become their own landlords, which he thought, under present cir- cumstances, a very desirable thing, and to become ulti- mately, by the very least possible amount of expenditure, the owners of their own boom

SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT'S HOYSR-DEALING.

He bought a horse for one hundred guineas from adealer in Oxfordshire, After the meeting of Parliament he got immersed in his briefs (he was then a Parliamentary lawyer, not an M.P.), and forgot all about the park hack waiting for his orders at Bicester. In the month of August, just before starting for Scotland, his memory came back to him, and he sent off in a hurry to his agent, explaining that, perhaps, as he had DO longer any use for it, t 11), horse could be sold without coming to town. " CertainlY, was the reply, "but not now, in the autumn, for the sum you gave in the spring." Thu hundred guinea horse-el:11Y fetched seventy guineas, and yet Harcourt thought him- self well out of the business. But, alas 1 when he applied for his money he was met with this courteous rejoinder, "Pardon me, but you have forgotten the keep of the horse, you have forgotten various other items, not to men- tion a farrier's bill or two. In point of fact, you owe obe thirty shillings, but, under the circumstances, I will not insist upon that."—Beminiscences and Opinione of Sir .t7rancis Hastings Doyle, 181,1-1885.
