To ask for a bath is to create the greatest alarm as to the state of your health; and I roused such a commotion by the request that I soon found out the enormity of it. An old man who werkod about the premises, being asked if he had ever been washed, reflected some time, and then said he thought some one had washed lira when he was a, small child. The only clean inhabitant of our village 19 a returned convict, who, on coming back to the bosom of his family after twenty yea.rs at the 13s,gni, immediately' set his wife to scrub and scour the premises, remarking that he was accustomed to clean dwellings, and could on no' account put up with dirt and untidiness, so fastidious had he become during his residence at the expense of the' Government. —Our Hoene by the Adriatic. By the Hon. Margaret Collier* (Madutne Galletti di Cadilhac.)

div.head: YANKED IN A LONDON REDTAUP.ANT.
div.p: A YANKED IN A LONDON REDTAUP.ANT.

He arrived in the rertaurant at five o'clock, and called for a bill of fare. It was printed on a sheet of paper the size of a page of an ordinary newspaper. Half the items: were in red ink. This indicated that they were special: dishes for that day. Ho had soup, and ordered boiled, mutton in red ink. The waiter consulted the cook, ancl said the- mutton would be done in three minutes. The stranger waited. In ten minutes the waiter came back' and said the cook had concluded not to serve any more mutton that day. The American said he would have a i ' lamb chop—also n red ink. Another consultation and another disappointment. There were no lamb chops. Would he try a "fillet "of beef, rare? Yes, he would. The waiter looked rather ashamed as he came back this time. He had no need to speak; the truth was written in his face—there was no "fillet." The American was hungry, but calm. He said: "Briny me anything you've got ni the ranch, I don't care what it is, only don't keep me in suspense. I dcat't want to make up my mouth for • any more things and not get them. Praduce anything you have." He received a fair sort of a dinner, Int he wa.s out of sorts all the time. When it came to making out his bill, you, may imagine how carefully he watched his man put down 'be items. As the waiter wrote he talked. This is how it ran. "One soup, one radishes and butter, one new potatoes, one turbot, one steak, one asparag-us, one peas, one Bars'—how many breads?" "What ? " "How many breads?" "None of your d—d butiness." "Well, I'll have to charge far two." " Charge? You don't charge for bread ? " "Yes, sir. A penny for each piece." " Humph ! Well, I had one." This very sulkily. "How scatty butters?" "Eh ?" "How many butters?" "Butters! Oh, you charge for butter? Ah ! I seo. Two butters. There's nothing mean about you. Oh, no. Hold on there, don't add her up yet; you've forgotten the salt. I had some on my radishes." No charge for salt." "What ? Is there anything you don't eharge for in this pleasing eountry. Perhaps you want to tuck it on for tilat glass of water. No? Well, this is simply paralysina liberality." And he went out muttering. This act/zany occurred in a restaurant where fully 500 people dine erer7 day. I know, because I have seen the masa. I sae him in the mirror every morning.— ..4s the Yankees See Us; or, rile Customs of the Cockneys. By Leander Biehardswt.

Referring to a neighbour he (Mr. W. H. Vanderbilt.) would say; "HQ isn't worth a hundredth part as much as I am, but he has rnoro of the reel pleasures ofglife than I have. His house is, as et-rnfortabla as mine, even if it didn't cost so much;, his team is about as c.,,-ood as mine; his opera-box is next, to mine; his health Is better than mine, and he will probably outlive ma. And he can trust his friends." W. H. Vanderbilt never handled his money. He never saw it. Ho was never in its presence. In fact, he never had it. It was, is the ikAlld3 of strangers, and was used by them for their 01171 ‘,-)esie.fit, they paying him five or six million dollars a year for the privilege. But even of this five or -six millions he never saw a tithe. Ninety-nine cents out•of every dollar he " owned " were in the hands and coffers, of others, employed mainly for , their exclusive advantage. In ministering to his own real and imaginary wants,.he could not use more than a small fraction of his income. He constantly over-worked, and violated many of the laws of heal* in order to get and keep his fortune; and for wages, Jae received, as Stephen Girard grimly put it, .only his "board and clothes," un- less we count among his imponderable assets the reputa- tion of being an avaricious and dangerous man. The Vanderliilts and the- Story of their _Fortune By W. A:. Crolut.

div.head: TATTOOED LEAUTIES.
div.p: TATTOOED LEAUTIES.

One Oaba, woman had alight blue pattern traced over her throat and bust like a scarf. This had been done with a shark's tooth when she was a young child. Others had their skins blistered up into the similitude of flowers and ferns,carneos in living flesh, really pretty. Others, again, were ornamented with fish and lizards. To bring these to perfection must be a very difficult task, and very painful to the one about to be made beautiful for ever. The skin is cut, and earth and hot ashes placed inside, when the flesh grows over into the forms into which the artist dresses the sores. Certainly after suffering so much these women must have felt mad at having to cover their beauties to please our squeamish tastes.—Cannibals and Convicts. By Julian Thomas.

div.head: NUMBER OF THE EEAST.
div.p: THE NUMBER OF THE EEAST.

It compels our very great respect, that one evidently so ready with a trenchant blade, so fond of indulging even in the very jocularity of lively humour, should with such severity discriminate between things that differ. Perhaps our readers will remember his imaginary lecture on John in which ho shews, certainly by a most justifiable, and not altogether unastonishing ad hontinein, in reply to those who are .so ready to prove that Rome has the number of the beast in Revelation, that, in reality, Queen Victoria has that number. Of course the whole thing is a joke. He says: "Gentlemen, can it surprise you to be told, after such an exposition of the blasphemies of England, that, astonishing to say, Queen Victoria is dis- tinctly- pointed out, in the Book of the Revelation, as having the number ofthe beast? You will recollect that that number is 666. Now she came to the throne in the Year '37, at which, date she was eighteen years old; multiply, then, thirty-seven by eighteen, and you have the very number, 666, which is the mystical emblem of the lawless king." A volume might be compiled upon' the almost innumerable persons to whom has been attached the theory of the mystic number, 666. Edward with cogent learning, fitted it on to the Papacy in his " Horm Apocalyptica." Lord Macaulay, when in India, was suddenly attacked by an Englishman, to whom he had never spoken, and whom he did not know, exclaiming: "Pray, Mr. Macaulay, do you not think that Buonziparte was the beast?" "ho, sir, I cannot say that I do." "Sir, he was the beast; I can prove it; I have found the number 666 in his name; why, sir, if he was not the beast, who was ? " " TEs was a puzzling question," says Macaulay, "and I am not a little vain of my answer. 'Sir,' said I, 'toe House of Commons is the beast. There are six hundred aud fifty-eight members of the House; and these, with their chief officers—the three clerks, the Serjeant and his deputy, the chaplain, the doorkeeper, and the librarian—make six hundred and sixty-six !'" His interlocutor, however, would pursue his demonstra- tion, and Macaulay thought he regarded him as a very wicked fellow, and believed that he went away determined to write Macaulay's name in Tamul, leaving out T in Thomas, B in Babington, and M in Macaulay, which he says would give to himself the number of this unfortunate beast, and which was exactly the process by which he had fixed • the number on Napoleon, spelling the name in Arabic, and leaving out two letters.—The Vocation of the Preacher. By F. Paxton Hood.

I saw a. girl some sixteen years old, at the railway statior • or rather " Deepot," as it is named and pro- nounce-1d there. She was evidently waiting or a train, seated near her trunk. There was no one cicse by, and she came up, to me. She was a particularly pretty. looking girl, nicely dressed, and seemed to be of a better class than the usual inhabitants in that somewhat out- of-the-way part of the country. I expected, • therefore, when she addressed me, she would do it nicely. The following passed: Girl: "I cannot fix try box—you do it..." The rope had come off. Myself: • Yes, ni help you. Are you -waiting for the train ? " Girl: "Guess you are right. How stupid you are, don't fix it in that way. Can't you see the rope is long entaigh to go twice . round? " Myself : "All right, I'll du it so." • Having completed the job, as the young lady was sitting on the one chair available, I sat on her box, which was a,large and strong one. Girl: "You fixed it well, thank you, but don't sit on my box." Alyself : "Why not?" Girl ; "Because I don't like it.. • Can't you sit on the steps?" Myself : "No, thank you, 11l s,tand." Girl : "Tell me when is the train d 65." Myselt ; Immediately. There it is coining now." Girl: "Guess, the box is too:I-wavy for one man. Will you help to fix it upon the car ? " She did not wait for a reply, but ran and took her place. No. more thanks. I looked round :;or some one ta help with her box, and as I did so she put her head out of the window, and called to a man who was sitting in a cart,, and had probably brought her and the trunk. " can't you see my box? Help that man standing by it to. ship it on the car." Jimmy did kindly help me, and so the difficulty was got over, but I saw or heard no more of the American lassie.—The Truth about America. By Edward Money.

WIT AND. HUMOUR. The first of the family circle.—The wedding-ring. The rule of three.—For the third party to clear out. Item from the beach.—A parasol often hides a pair o' spoons. When does the captain of a ship commit self-mutila- tion?—When he goes on shore and leaves his hands ' behind him. A certain clergyman, a great athlete and lover of cricket, forgot himself recently by saying, "Here endeth the first innings. Let us pray." A relenting father recently signified his desire for reconciliation with the family prodigal by the following curt telegram :—" Mr. —, Pueblo, Col.—The veal I spread is ready when you are." At a recent banquet given to a writer of comedies in honour of his latest work, one of the guests proposed the ; following toast—" The author's very good health May lie live to be as old as his jokes !" ' 1 "Bailiff," said an Arkansas judge one day last week to ; the officer in charge of the jury, "will you please inform ' the jury that there will be a horse race in Merrick's pasture at 3 o'clock?" The jury had been out for forty- eight hours, but in less than thirty minutes they came into court with a verdict. MONEY FOR A RAINY DAY.—Elderly gentleman, to I little boy who is buying toffee: My young friend, don't you think that, instead of spending all the pennies you I get, it would be better to put some of them away for a j rainy day ?—Little boy: Oh, no! What's the good of 1 money on a rainy day? Ma never lets me stir out of the house.' • HIGH-PRICED ART.—" My, but those ere works do run into money," remarked a passenger whose breath smelled like a whisky distillery. "It beats all what fools some folk make over pictures. When I was in London I saw a little Painting about a foot square that was valued at £l5O. 'Spect some simpleton will come along and buy it. If I had a million of money you'd never catch me paying £l5O for a little painting like that." "That's the way you talk," spoke up a bashful drummer, "but I'll bet you paid four times as m*uch money for a paint- ing not a tenth part as big." "What, me?" "Yes, you." "What kind of a painting ?" "The one on the end of your nose !" MATRIMONIAL RISKS.—" So you are going to marry that small, wheezy, consumptive-looking specimen of a man, are you?" said one girl to another. "I really don't see what you can see in him to love." "Mary," said her friend, "your father is a small man, isn't he ?" "Yes," was the reply; "but what of that ?" "Nothing,. except that if he wasn't small it would be doubtful if your mother would be boss. I'm going to marry that small man because I'm fond of having my own way and won't accept any risks." An old Georgian judge had been a fierce Secessionist, and the fact was not forgotten when, after the war, he re-entered the political arena of his native State. Speaking at a certain place one evening in the interest of his own candidate for Congress, some one in the audience who evidently had a good memory inquired, "Didn't you speak here just before the war?" "1 did," proudly responded the judge. "And didn't you say we could whip the durned Yankees with pop-guns?' "I did," replied the unabashed judge; "but, confound 'em, they wouldn't fight that way!" "Now, sir, I hope we shall have no difficulty in getting you to speak up ! ' said a Boston attorney, in a very loud commanding voice. "I hope not, sir !" shouted the wit- ness at the top of his lungs. "How dare you speak to me in that way ?" "I can't speak no louder !" screamed the witness. Have you been drinking ?" " Corfee, sir !" hoarsely vociferated the witness. "Something be- sides coffee, sir, you've been using! Don't look at me like that, sir !"—furiously. "Look at the jury, sir! Did you have something in your coffee, sir ?" "Yes, sir !" "What was it ?" "Sugar!' "This man is no fool, your honour—he is worse!' stormed the counsel. "Now, sirrah"—turning to the witness—" look at me! What besides sugar did you take in your coffee this morning ?" The witness collected his forces, drew a deep breath, and, in a voice that could have been heard half a mile away, bellowed out, "A spune— a spune, an' nothin- else, sir !" A " RASPER."—A certain old gentleman at Tewkes- bury who rode a blind horse for many years had taught his steed the feat of jumping when he received a hint that he was desired to do so. erobably he had been a good fencer once; anyhow, when his master wished it, he could always make the animal clear some feet of space at a bound. After a day's hunting, some return- ing sportsmen were talking in the bar of an hotel about big jumps and fencing generally, when the owner of this horse offered to bet that his blind hunter would jump over a single obstacle which none of their hunters would leap, and he put down a five-pound note, daring them to cover it. The result was that four took the bet to save their reputations. On going outside, the sly old sportsman put down a straw in the street. He road up to it, when the blind steed rose at the "rasper," clearing it with a bound four feet in the air, and covering twelve feet of ground at least. None of the other four horses would nss at a straw, and the old gentleman pocketed he money. FIXED !—An English traveller who had often heard that the Venetian gondoliers were remarkable for their , perfect acquaintance with ever," building and locality, however obscure, in their beautiful city, determined to put their knowledge to the test, and with this view stepped into a gondola, saying to the boatman who awaited his orders, "Take me to the Church of San Berlingo." The gondolier fell into a brown study, and answered after a while, " Signot, I don't know where the church is." The Englishman pretended to get very angry, and went in search of another boat, repeating the same proposal and receiving the same answer, and thus four or five times in succession. At length one' gondolier received his orders in silence, and, plying his oar, laboured on and on for over an hour, drawing the boat to land opposite to some distant church, when he said to the passenger, "Hero you are, Signor." "And is this really the Church of San Berlingo?" inquired the latter, in great surprise, well knowing that there existed no church of that name. "Oh, certainly !" added the boatman. "This is All Saints' Church; so, if your San Berlingo is really one of them, this must be his church too."

STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETIES. FORMATION OF A SOCIETY IN WARRINGTON. On Monday evening a largely-attended meeting was held in the Workmen's Club in connection with the Starr-Bowkett Building Society (826), which has just been formed in Warrington( .The chair was taken by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who was supported on the platform by Mr. E. J. Collings, of Bolton (who was present in place of Mr. Starr), Mr. Noah Legge, Mr. J. Titchett, and other gentlemen. The MAYOR said he was glad to see so much in- terest taken in that question. There was a much larger audience present than he expected, and that showed that the interest taken in building societies was not altogether extinguished by the bad trade they had experienced for a considerable time past, and by the fact that, he was afraid, there was no very brilliant prospects of improvement. When he was asked to take the chair that night he readily assented, because he considered that not only Starr- Bowkett but all kindred societies have a tendency to and do inculcate habits of thrift, and therefore if it were only for that alone he thought it was a sub- ject he might very properly identify himself with. (Hear, hear.) If he could be of the least aid, he considered it was one of the collateral duties of the office he held to place himself at the dis- posal of the gentlemen who invited him to come there. He ought to say that he was already a trus- tee of a kindred society to that called the Permanent Benefit Building Society, and although there ap- peared to be advantages about the Starr-Bowkett societies over any other, still he could testify that the Permanent Benefit Building Society had been of verygreat advantage to many people in Warrington. (hear, hear.) He himself had been twenty-two years in the house in which he at present lived, and he made out that if, twenty-two years ago, instead of becoming the tenant of the house, he had entered into an arrangement to purchase it, and had.fol- lowed out the system of that society, he should have been in possession of the house years ago, whereas he had paid rent for twenty-two years and there was not a brick of thd house belonged to him. Yet he calculated that he paidqlouble the value of the house. (Hear, hear.) He saw no reason why every man should not be able to prepare for himself a comparatively comfortable time in his old days. He could conceive of nothing more wretched. than to see a man pass through life and in the latter end of it become the recipient of parochial relief or have to depend upon the charity of his friends. - There was no more pitiable object, and in his (the Mayor's) opinion in the great majority of instances it was brought about entirely by the person's want of that valuable quality, thrift. (Applause.) Mr. E. J. COLL.INGS then gave an address explana- tory of the objects and methods of Starr-Bowkett Building Societies. Having referred to some of the means adopted to encourage thrift by the late Right Hon. H. Fawcett, when postmaster-general, Mr. Collings said he had not come there to attack per- manent building societies, being a member of one of these societies himself. Permanent building societies had done a vast amount of good. They had worked upon certain lines and were at present, and had been for some years in low water, but if the present movement in trade was to last, if they were to again see brighter times, permanent build- ing societies would do a vast amount of good in the future. Starr-Bowkett societies had done a vast amount of good in the past and were doing it now. They were meeting to a certain extent the wants of a class which permanent building societies could not reach, and while they wished the latter socie- ties god-speed in their work they asked for only fair treatment from them on the part of the Starr- Bowkett building. societies. These societies were first organised by Dr. Bowkett, but for some twenty years or so they hung lire, but were then taken up and improved by Mr. Starr, and the number of the societies was now 826 the vast majority of which were in full working order. The number of mem- bers of a society was limited to 500, and when a person entered he received a number, for instance 20, and that was called his registered number. Under that number he might take one, two, three, or four shares, but they could not hold more than four shares under one registered number. If they wanted to hold more than four shares they must take more than one registered number. A person could be entered as a member at any age, and it was not so long since a man entered his child as a member a few hours after its birth. That was an exceedingly important provision, and he had known cases in which parents had taken shares for their children merely for educational purposes in order that their children might have an inducement to train themselves in habits of thrift and economy, and that was one way in which parents might assist their children. On entering the society is per share entrance fee was paid, and if they took one share they afterwards paid Gd per week, two shares is, four shares 2s. That 6d per week per share is calculated to run on 21 years, when it amounted to 1'27 Gs, and that was the amount of money they were required to pay into the society. That £27 6s they lent the society for a comparatively long period, he had said 21 years, but as a matter of fact it would be nearer 18 or 18. years, and the society in return undertook to lend them the sum of £lOO on each share for 124 years, free of interest. They must not imagine, however, that they were not going to pay that £lOO back. The £lOO was termed their appropriation, and of course they were allowed 12i years to repay it, and they went on at the same time paying their 6d. per week on each share. For the purpose of deciding who should have the appropriation, they had the ballot, which four of her Majesty's justices had said was perfectly fair and honest in its opera- tion. The lecturer then explained the manner in which the ballot was worked, and he added that everything was done in a perfectly fair way, and he had never yet heard of a single person who objected to the'ballot after he had seen it work. If they supposed that the number 421 was drawn, the per- son whose registered number that was—if he was perfectly clear on the books, that is, paid the previous week's subscription—was entitled to an appropria- tion. Having got an appropriation of £4OO, what were they going to do with it? Suppose they could not do anything with it—having decided to go to America or some other place—they might sell it. Then they might ask him what price they would get for it. He could not tell them that, but he could tell them rhat prices had been got. He knew of a case in which a member had an appropriation of £4OO drawn, having paid on his book £l7, which, when the society wound up, he would be. entitled to take again. In that Case the appropriation was sold for £75, and he himself was the person who sold it. (Applause.) But in these cases the person sell- ing the appropriation was really to some extent selling other people's money, and clearly they had a right to Some share of the profit; hence the rules saidthat a member who sold his appropriation must pay to the society £2 per £lOO. Mr. Collings also mentioned other cases in which appropria- tions had been sold for substantial sums, and he remarked that after he had sold his own appropriation he went back into the society, and now stood good to get another appro- priation. As a rule the appropriation was drawn about three months before the money was ready, and the money when obtained must be spent on property, leasehold, freehold, or copyhold, so that it might be mortgaged to the society for the repayment of the appropriation. Suppos- ing they wished to buy a piece of pro- perty with their appropriation, they had to apply to the secretary for a form containing a number of questions which were to be answered, the form was put into the hands of the society's surveyor, and he visited and wlueel the property, and after he had reported that the pro- perty was worth the amount of the appropriation, say £4OO, the society advanced every penny of the value. Now that was their weak point, and be would claim, paradoxical as it appeared, that therein also lay the strength of the society. It was a weakness for this reason. The surveyor said the property was worth £4OO, and the society was consequently advancing the full extent of the risk. Therefore it was their weakness, but he was going to claim that it was also their strength. First of all they must remember that the society did not advance more than £4OO upon one appro- priation, and if they wanted to purchase a bigger property and spend £BOO or £1,200, they must either buy somebody else's appropriation or find the remainder in some other way. In these societies there was no advancing £117,000, as was done by one society on collieries. They did not enter upon responsibilities of that character, because they knew the vast majority of their members were working•men and women who depended upon small and to a certain extent fixed incomes, and could not afford to lose their money on foolish speculations. Their directors would have no power to advance more than £4OO on one appropriation, and they must have security for the full amount. This point was their strength, because • they met the wants of that very class of people who could not afford to find any ready money. (Llear, hear.) An ordinary building society would not advance them £4OO on property valued at £4OO, but only something like £320, and they themselves would have to find £80: But the majority of the members of Starr- Bowkett societies could not find £BO, and therefore they met the wants of that class. But there was a safeguard for risk in the fact that directly the advance was made repay- ment commenced at the rate on a £4OO appropriation of 123 4d per week, and this was continued week after week, and year afVr year. Referring to the profits of the society which were distributed amongst the members on the wind-

NORTHWICH. SPEECH BY MR. BRUNNER. On Saturday afternoon, the Gladstone Liberal Club, Northwich, was opened by the President, Mr. T. Brunner, who in the course of his address re- ferred to the death of Mr. G. W. Latham. Mr. Latham had done his work in this world, but he had left the Liberals of Cheshire a legacy, and that legacy he. (.Mr. Brunner) trusted would grow, and grow until it was a mighty fortune for the Liberals of the county. (Applause.) The opening of that club was the result of the election last July. (Hear, hear.) To that election a good many of them looked back with feelings of regret and discern- for,—(hear, hear,)—and las had not found a man who was proud of the result. Who was successful at that contest? Our member had since declared "We hare wiped out a minority of 1,028 and created a majority of 468." Who was the "we "? (Hear, hear.) Ile had propounded this question, but he did not think they would expect him to give a definite answer. They would wait and see. Those laughed bast who laughed last. The net result of that election up to that day was that Mr. Robert Verdin had been made a Wearer trustee—a position he considered Mr. Verdin had been more. entitled to than 90 per cent. of the men who were on that trust—(hear, hear,)—by his property, by right of his special knowledge, and by right of his abilities. He was sorry indeed that Mr. Verdin should only have attained to that position when he sold himself to the Tory party. (Laughter and applause.) Up till that day that had been the net result of the election, but he welcomed their presence that day as a proof that they were going to have other and better results. (Applause.) Since July there had been activity and .increased thought amongst the Liberals of that Division beyond what he had ever known. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner then declared the club open. In reply to .0. . letter from Mr. Brunner, asking for permission to use his name as the title of the club, Mr. Gladstone wrote as follows: Ilawa.rden Castle, Chester, October 9, 1886. My dear have received, and I at once agree to your flattering request, while I regret that my name will be but an enipty token and that some one more effective has not been chosen. I sin- cerely regret that you have been among the many victims to public duty on the occasion of the late election. But I trust their time will come, and I feel confident it will be found their only offence has been out-running some of their fellow-citizens in the discernment of justice and necessity.—Believe me, faithfully yours, W. E. Gladstone." The two pages upon which the letter was written, together with the envelope and a vignette portrait of Mr. Gladstone, had been mounted and framed by Mr. Birtles, photographer, Warrington; for the purpose of being displayed on the wall of the Club.

ing up, Mr. Collings said he had in his hand a balance sheet of the South London (262) society, which showed a prospective profit of £1,014 14s 4e„-1, and he also mentioned several other similar instanced. In answer to persons who might ask where the prefits 'came from, he said they had first of all the entrance fees, which weie is per share, and sometimes there were as marly as 1,00 shores tlic.n up in one society, then there was the profit in the Sale of anpropria. tions referred to above, tines, and, besides, the society had a right to buy an appropriation and sell•it again, and some- times a very respectable amount of profit was made by tkat means. The fines in Starr-Bowkett societies were a very small source of profit, because when a person fell back a week in his payment he was not fined if he was willing to make up for it by paying a week in advance. (Hear, hear.) He then pointed out that the whole management lay in the members' hands. Some of the older societies took the pre- caution of electing five respectable gentlemen, not members of the society, to act as arbitrators to settle disputes if any arose, but never in the whole history of these societies had it been necessary to call in the arbitrators. Some person might ask if he would be breught before the magistrates in case of any dispute, but he might say that no legal proceed- ings whatever could be taken against any member except by the consent of the whole body of the members, so that they might feel satisfied they would not be unfairly treated. (flear, hear.) All the solicitor's and other charges in con- nection with the buying of property were fixed according to rule, so that each member knew exactly what he was going to pay, and, if need be, these charges were advanced by the society. In case of a member being sick or out of work, on notice being given to the secretary, he was not fined if he did not keep up his payments, and after he was well again, or obtained work, he was given time to make up the arrears. Never in the history of these societies had a bona-tide rnet-n- -her had his mortgage foreclosed and his property sold over his head. (Applause.) The lecturer then made several calculations to show the advantages of obtaining property through ihese societies over the ordinary methods. The working expenses of the society were met by the payment of is 3d per share annually, but very frequently the members were not even called upon to pay this Is 31. In conclusion, he remarked that Starr-Bowkett building societies were mutual self-help co-operative societies, and in Lancashire, the birth-place of co-operation, they would not decry the principles on which these societies were founded. (Applause). After his lecture Mr. Collings answered several questions put to him by Mr. Diggle and others in the audience. The following directors were also provisionally elected :—Messrs Noah Legge, P. Worthing!on, T. Burton, John Walker, G. Lea, W. Crampton, J. Griffiths, 0. Hillidge. The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the Mayor.

DEATH OF THE CITAMPION BOWLER—Tom Hart, of Westhoughton, near Bolton, the champion bowler of Eng- land, died on Thursday week. He was born at Lostock in 1856 or 1857, and came out as a bowler ten years ago, meet- ing "Old Kay," from Yorkshire, at Bolton. for £25 a side, and beating him easily. From that time Hart had a suc- cession of victories over well-known bowlers, until in 1881 he offered to give any man in England ten in a game of 101 up. Barlow, of Pendlebury, took up the challenge, and was beaten. He then agreed to meet Hart at Pendlebury for £5O a side, the champion to concede 20 points. Hart ran out an easy winner. Towers, of Hollinwood, who about this time was the reputed champion, was beaten on four euccessive occasions by Hart, who conceded ten points in the last match. Latterly, however. Hart, had given way to intemperance, and on more than one occasion suffered defeat. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON,. THURSDAY. Affairs in the East of Europe are drifting on no one can say whither, though for the moment things look more peaceful than they did a week ago. A report comes to-day from Vicnna, whi..:th somewhat enigmatically points to the establishment of a secret understanding between Germany, Austria, and Russia, according to which Rw_sia has engaged not to occupy Bulgaria, but is to be allowed to take any steps short of occupation to recover the posi- tion held in the country under the treaty of Berlin. Quite a new feature in the case is the appearance upon the scene of Turkey, who is working hand in hand with Russia to regain the supremacy of the Czar. This is undoubtedly a rebuff to British dip- lomacy at Constantinople, where efforts have been persistently made to keep Turkey straight'. Had Mr. Gladstone chanced to be in power just now, we would have heard a good deal about the loss of British prestige, of national humiliation, and of the good old flag being dragged in the mud. Happily a more sensible, not to say a more patriotic course, is taken in Liberal circles. It would undoubtedly have been better if Turkey could have been kept out of the arms of Russia at the present junctme. But beyond doubt Lord Salisbury and Lord Iddes- leigh at home, and the British Emmisaries abroad, have done their best to accomplish the desirable end, and failure is neither a treason nor a crime. Lord Randolph Churchill's speech at Bradford next week is looked forward to with perhaps more curiosity than has marked any previous occasions. Everyone is anxious to see how he will take up the thread of his memorable. discourse at Dartford. He cannot very well leave matters as they now stand, and to successfully retouch them will require great skill. He must either stultify himself by ex- plainino• away much he said at Dartford, or he must deliberately and resolutely take issue with a con- siderable and influential section of the Conservative party. The consternation and indignation aroused by his adoption at Dartford of the Radical pro- gramme has been faithfully mirrored in the Conser- vative press. Some leading representatives of it have been ominously silent. Others have muttered discontent and avowed disbelief in the natural ex- planation of Lord Randolph's sentences. He must say something to the. point at Bradford, and they must declare themselves on the following morning. There cannot possibly be another epoch of masterly silence in the Conservative ranks. The announcement of the death of the Marquis of Aylesbury recalls a figure once familiar in the House of Commons. This was Lord Ernest Bruce, who up to 1878 sat for Marlborough, a now extinct borough, which he represented uninterruptedly for nearly half a century. Lord Ernest was, of course, Conservative, and had taken his seat in the first re- formed Parliament, under the apprehension then common among Conservatives, thaT the country had finally gone to the dogs. It nevertheless Jogged along pretty comfortably, and before Lord Ernest Bruce was called to the Upper House by the death of his brother, the second marquis, he had seen and beard a good many strange things. He saw a great deal more than he heard, for he was almost stone deaf. In their way there were few things that amused the House more than occasional conversa- tions between Lord Ernest Bruce and Mr. Gladstone across the table. Lord Ernest was one of Mr. Glad- stone's few remaining contemporaries, and was al- ways treated.hy him with the special courtesy he reserved for such veterans. When Lord Ernest had anything to say to the then leader of the Opposi- tion, he was wont to come down to the Treasury- Bench and whisper across the table after the man- ner of deaf men. Mr. Gladstone had a difficulty in hearing what Lord Ernest said, Lord Ernest could not catch the remotest whisper of Mr. Gladstone's observations, and between the two there was an in- terchange of incoherent courtesy which greatly amused the House. The death of the "Marquis" endows us with one _ _ __ _

of those hereditary legislators of whom the country is justly proud. The late Marquis is succeeded by his grandson, the famous Lord Severnake. The new Marquis is only in his twenty-fourth year, but he has already succeeded in making a name for himself. For several years he has beer 'a man about town, and chiefly about the.stables. However much :we may desire to extol him, it cannot be said that he has a soul above buttons. On the contrary, some of the higher instincts of his mind have been devoted to buttons, with the result that he has the most remarkable collection known; either in Kent or the civilised world. He loves to present himself in the park in an overcoat with broad seams grow- ing outside, and buttons the size of cheese plates adorned with sporting figures. His outward ap- pearance, in fact, is of the kind that might have been designed by the inventor of Dick Swiveller or Bob Sawyer. But he is the Marquis of Ailesbury, and will now begin to make laws for us, and throw out measures passed by the Liberal majority of the representatives of the people. It is only a few years since the new Marquis took to himself a wife. She was Miss Dolly Teste, of the Empire Theatre, Leicester Square, and is now the Marchioness of Ailesbury. The Pastor of the City Temple has been running through one of the morning papers a correspond- ence which has come to be known as "Dr. Parker's puzzle." It is now explained by the fact that to- (lay Mr. Haweis preached from the pulpit of the City Temple to a congregation which filled every seat. The significance of this event is of course i found n the fact that Mr. Haweis is a clergyman of the .Church of England. It was anticipated that the Bishop would interfere and prohibit a proceed- ing which is, it appears, shocking to some minds. Somewhat, I fancy, to the disappointment of the divines immediately concerned, the Bishop has as yet made no sign, and the event would have passed over without attracting much attention except for Dr. Parker's cleverly constructed advertisement. Mr. Haweis probably would not be accepted by The great body of his brethren as a representative clergy- man of the Church of England. Regarded either as a preacher or a writer, he is what Mr. Carlyle would call "a puir creature." Yet he manages to keep himself before the public and make both ends luxuriously meet. He is a clever man after the style of Mr. Augustus Harris, of Drury-lane. His church is most comfortably appointed, the pews being rather like stalls at the Lyceum than the ordinary sittings of a church. In winter the church is particularly snug, with thick curtains and skilful arrangement of hot water pipes". In fact, the only thin item in the pro- gramme is the sermon. But it pleases the audience, who are further gratified by the unfailing flowers displayed from the pulpit and the cambric handker- chief flashed to and fro to emphasise the string of glittering common-places. The Rev. Charles Honey- man was not a patch on the Rev. Mr. Haweis, who, on the whole, manages things much better. Within the last few months a new avocation has sprung up, and is just now in a highly flourishing state;, It consists of taking a word, such as "ward- robe. or " aster," or "acrostic," and offering prizes for the largest number of English words formed i from t. This, or something else like it, is familiar i enough n the weekly papers. The peculiarity of the new development is that a preliminary condi- tionto taking part in the game is a contribution of a shilling. This makes a pool out of which the prizes are provided,th e balance going into the pocket of the enterprising promoter. It was started first by a private soldier of fortune, who made a i good thing out of t. Its remarkable extension within the last few weeks arises from the fact that it has been taken up by the clergy. Rectors, vicars, and canons who want new organs, stained-glass windows, or extension of their churches have dis- covered their opportunity. Lotteries are forbidden by the state, but there is at present no edict against this form of gambling. Accordingly there are to- day before the public about a score of these little games. Their attraction for the public is extraor- dinary. I happen to know the particulars of a case
OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. LFROSI OUR OWN ( DRRESPONDENT 1. 23, Old Broad-street, E.C.

There have been a series of puzzling fluctuations in the Stock Exchange prices this week, which after dodging up and down left off at a fairly intelligible position. Home railways have considerably improved, and the falling market in Brighton A's has been changed for a decided rise, and Bulls of this stock are a•nin hopeful. I was among the first of the few critics who foretold the gold mining mania which is now simply raging, and with- out departing from the opinion I have expressed from the first, I feel that the time has arrived when I can honestly advise speculators to indulge in a modest dabble in these most erratic of all investments. To investors pure and simple, my advice is emphatically, "Don't," but for pur- poses of speculation the gold mine market just now offers advantages which, with caution, might be turned to profit- able account. There are a large number of small mining shares to be had for a few shillings, which by virtue of this fever are almost certain to go up, but they must not be held beyond the first sign of a profit, for the fall will assuredly be as rapid as the rise. As an instance I may mention "Ruby's," which went up in twelve hours from ten to four- teen shillings. But unless buyers can sell out promptly it would be the height of folly to purchase at any price. The Colonial Exhibition has had the effect of drawing attention to some of our neglected colonies, and the sudden and enormously increasing demand for Ceylon tea has brought about the Ceylon Pure Produce Company, who are now inviting subscriptions. This undertaking seems to have had the good fortune to secure a practical monopoly of the tea trade there. and the enterprise shows promise of a lucra- tive career. The much adveKifed Forder Cab Company has been recognised, and are asking for money. Considering the disastrous failure of two or three such attemprs to float London cab companies, the promoters must be bold men in- de,-d. In these days of express speed busy men don't wait till a particular kind of cab comes along; they take the first that comes.

After a I,earing of three days duration, the magistrates at the Mansion House have settled the cause celeb)e of the day in financial circles, the libel action on the manager of the London and Leeds Bank against the Financial N,103. The opinion I have so guardedly expressed about the bank has been emphatically and unequivocally emphasised by the magistrates of the Mansion House, and the bogus institu- tion which was to have reformed banking principles in the North of England has been officially stigmatized as an im- pudent fraud. The Financial News, through its plucky editor, has saved the public thousands of pounds, but the reward is not calculated to inspire journalists with an ardent desire to serve their fellow men The editor has won his Case, but at a cost of hundreds of pounds. It is stated that the leading bankers in the city are- inaugurating a testi- monial to the editor of the Financial News, and certainly no one has done more to uphold the integrity of the binking world.

theatre going. Well, then, I say the music hall is bad; the singing at the conversazione created a desire in the audience for going to the music hall—in fact, "the only difference was dress and scenery "—therefore no singing should have been allowed at the conversazione. To argue like this is to argue all pleasure out of life, and no rational being will support it. If "W. E. S.' will endeavour to raise his mind out of the narrow groove in which it now lies, by reading classic dramas and enjoying dramatic performances, we shall perhaps see no more published evidences of bigotry and darkness.

As I was a leading performer in the piece about which "W. E. S." writesp and as I coasider the charge of leading the young to the places of the ungodly a serious one, 1 shall be glad if you will publish the above reply.—Yours truly, Liverpool, Oct. 16, 1883. WM. BROADHURST.

Sir,—ln regard to the presumption which 'R. P." ac- cuses me of for writing in respect to the concersazione in the Wesleyan Schools, simply on the assumption that I was not present, I ask him, were not two dramatic pieces acted (not recited), and were not the actors highly compliminted on their Effutti, and was not the acting in every sense such as is seen in thpatres, except the scenery and dress? If so, which is not denied by anyone, have I not a perfect right, as a Wesleyan Methodist, to write upon such a matter, and Wive to nip in the bud anything which is contrary to Methodist laws and usages. It is very evident from the w bole tenour of "R.P.'s " letter that h 3 is not a" Methodist," and, therefore, assuming his own line of argument, it is pre- sumption on his pat to write on a question which is purely Methedistical.

I quite agree with "R.P." of the need of opportunities for social enjoyment; and let them be as high intellectuallV and as pure morally as they can possibly get them, but as regards what will make them so, from the tone of his letter, I can see we should entirely differ. Noticing his remark as to ‘:cholars reciting for the amusement of scholars, would it not be better if he would put it in its true sense and, in- stead of reciting, say "acting"? I am glad he acknow- ledges the evil influence attached to theatres. I would ask him the question, is it the walls or the drama that gives it the evil influence? We sometimes have the gospel preached in theatres—is there an evil influence then? I think it is generally admitted that it is the drama as acted which gives the evil influence, no matter in whet kind of a place it may be produced. Bat supposing that because it was acted in a Funday school, in the presence of the ministers, there was no evil influenle, he must admit that it is a questionable amusement and is an appearance of evil, which is a matter of importance to Methodists, it being emphatically laid down in their rulus to "abstain from all appearance of evil."

SANITARY SCIENCE AND LONGFORD WORKS. Sir,—Being, in common with most of your readers, an inhabitant and ratepayer of the borough of Warrington, I naturally take an interest in those matters which pertain to the health of the inhabitants and the pockets of the rate- payers. But as we cannot separate the inhabitant from the ratepayer, his personality and responsibility not being like that of the old German archbishop, who swore in his capacity of elector and not in that of archbishop, it must be that our interests as ratepayers mast be in harmony with our necessities as inhabitants. Financially considered, it may be a harmony of subserviency, for whatever may be the apparent monetary gain or loss, it must remain an in- controvertible fact that our health as a community as well as individuals is paramount, having a pre-eminence above all considerations of money value. The persons are not all dead who think our forefathers left us a legacy of profit in the old asbpits and cesspools which formerly existed in such profusion in this and urban districts in general. The sale of their contents formerly yielded a small perquisite now and again which I can re- member was keenly relished by menY of the old inhabitants, and especially, where the neighbourhood was rich in the pos- session of an ashpit of more than average capacity. But in Warrington we have been educated, and if not by scientific treatises or lectures, by the persistence of a few men, the chairman of the Sanitary Committee leading, in giving practical demonstration of the superiority of the pail closet with its organized system of removal over the old ashpit and cesspool. How many of our aneestors these have poisoned it would be ,im- possible to say, but by a comparison of the death rates and the averages of duration of human life in the early years of the present century and the lest few years, we must come to the conclusion that in former days health and life were squandered with a prodigality which is now matter of astonishment to those who will take the labour to acquaint themselves with the stern facts and deductions of modern sanitary science. To breathe an nnvitiated atmosphere is among the greatest pleasures of human life, and when thirsty te think from au unpolluted fountain is not the less, but these cannot be en- joyed if festering heaps of refuse and night-soil are left for months tegether to defile the atmosphere and pellets the water, the invaluable elements of physical life and comfort. If there can be a utilization of these destructive agents that shall be profitable financially, so much the better for us as ratepayers. Not having a practical knewledge of the value cf the manure manufactured by the Corporation at Long- ford, I have anxiously wished to know the opinion of an un- biassed and practical man derived from intelligent and im- partial trials of its use in agriculture. Happening to have a friend in whose judgment and integrity I could rely, and ole who has had the opportnnity of fairly testing the re- sults of the use of the Longford manufact,nred manure—l don't know if it is a patent—l asked him the other day to give me his candid opinion. His statement he reply was that he had found it effective and cheap, but that svch was the prejudice of farmers in fayeur of two-horse loads of night-soil, that if the ratio of value of the concentrated manure to the crude article were as two to one, it would yet in many cases be utterly impossible to prevail upon them to take the best.

In 1854 Mr. Samuel Brookes offered to lay £l,OOO in the hands of the Manchester Corporation for the purpose of making inquiries and experiments on the question of utili- zation. lam not acquainted with the immediate re,ult of this offer, but I do know this, that the effects prodnced on Carrington Moss, although no older than the current year, have beea such as to excite the wonder, and admiration also, of all who have heel the opportunity of witnessing them, and I do not see why we, without purchasing a moss or a moor, may not, if th. Corporation are liberal and enter- prising, so compel attention from the agricultural- interest in this neighbourhood to the value of the product they have for disposal, that there may be not only good sanitary work don. at Longford, but moreof financial success than many have expected. W. T.
WESLEYAN METHODISM AND THEATRE GOING.

Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last there appears a letter on the above subject, signed "R. P.," the last paragraph of which reads thus—" I hope 'W. E. S.' will reconsider the matter, and not needlessly hareper Sunday school managers who are trying to interest as well as instruct their young people." Any one reading this will naturally conclude that the performances in question were under the auspices and approval of the managers of the Bold-street Sunday school, whereas the Sunday school authorities had nothing what- ever to do with it, neither the committee, superintendents, nor teachers, and as one of the superintendents I may say that we are not likely to resort to any such questionable tactics to interest our children. The present managers will strive to conduct the school on lines laid clown in 2ad Cor. 6th, 17v., and 2nd Thess. sth. 22v. As one of the speakers complimented them upon their " bravery " for introducing such things, it is only fair the public should know that the honour of such " bravery " be- longs to the "Young Men's Mutual Improvement Society," ana not the Sunday school.—l am, sir, yours truly, J. B. ISAAC.

Sir,—ln your issue of the 9th inst. there is a letter by "W. E. S." on "Wesleyan Methodism and Theatre going." The writer would have you to understand that all that he wants to ao is to point out the inconsistency of the minis- ters. But who would employ the newspapers for such a purpose? It needs no keen observer to see that he is one of those good, intelligent, open-minded individuals whose moral rectitude has prevented them all their lives from go- ing to a theatre or reading dramatic works, and which creates in them an abhorrence of such thinge as if it were an inherited instinct. Almost all savages are afraid of, and shr;nk from, things that they have never before seen, like "W. E. S." shudders and closes his eyes at the thought of dramatic performances.. Yet his knowledge on such matters appears to be very profound, for he passes a criticism on the acting, and says two pieces were performed, one from "Henry VIII.," the other from "William Tell," and they were "just like life;" while only one piece was performed

• —two -scenes from "Richard III." What schoolboy of twelve would have displayed such ignorance? After this I need not say whether "W. E. S." is competent to say —as he has said—that the theatre is a place where we see inculcated "the fashions and customs of the ungodly." Did the piece which was performed inculcate any ungodli- ness?" "Oh no! " says" W. E. S." "but it created a de- sire in some to go to the theatre." That may be, but would they be any worse for seeing it performed in a theatre? "It is the niece and not the walls that makes the theatre." " Ah !" says "W. E. S ," contradicting his previona argu- ment, "they would see bad company there." Possibly, but you see bed company in every crowd. If you go to political meeting you see blackguards; if you go to the Salvation Army you see drunkards; if you go to chapel von see—and this is worst of all—a hypocrite turning up the whites of his eyes and bowing and groaning and weeping—a business advertisement—and when this has amassed him sufficient wealth to make him as he thinks an oracle, and the threaten- ing to draw away his purse a power in the place, you see him holding high office—a tyrannous paged—commanding that no theatrical performances shall he given, and dictating what meetings shall be held. But because a person sees at political meetings a number of blackguards is he t.a shrink from politics? Because at the Salvation Army a person sees drunkards is the Salvation Army to be con- demned? Because at chapel a person sees a hypocrite is he to neglect his soul? Most decidedly no! Then if at the theatre a person sees bad company is he not to have his mind refreshed and edified by seeing the performance of a drama?
But admittmg, for the purpose of argument, that theatre going is demoralising, bow does it affect the performance in question? "W. E. S." says that it creates a desire for
Silence is the happiest course a man can take if he is diffident of himself.

COURTSHIP IN ULSTER.—The Ulster man is not rapid in his love-making. Courtships extending over ten, fif- teen, even twenty years, are not uncommon among the people, but frequently marriages are made up by the friends and relatives of the contracting parties. 'l'm savin', Joe, will ye tak' our Susy ?" was the openi chapter of a little romance which ended very happily not long since. Or the young man's mother goes a-court;ng for him, and, as in a case which occurred not many months ago, comes home and tells her son. "Go up till Allie (Alexander) —'s; I've axed his Ellen for ye, an' she'll tak' ye." "But I'm no' wantin" Ellen, an' I've no' thought to change my life," quoth the reluctant swain. 'Man, dear, ye maun go up. I've axed the wee cutty (little girl), an' ye'll no' shame her an' me," said the mother. The youth looked perplexed, rubbed his curly head, then rose to his feet and said sheepishly, "I sup- pose I'd better be goin', I'm no' sayin' but tak' her." In a month they were married. "An' the never a word o' courtin' there was at all," said the proud Tootle'', as she told the tale. •

It is a grievous blunder to try to attract young people to the religion of our Lord by making concessions to their worldly t :stes. Such an attempt must defeat itself, for those whom we would thus seek to allure Are keen to I discover the meaning of the bait held out to them, and the practical insincerity of the faith which thus acknowledges that it hopes to succeed by false pretences. The Wesleyan Conference notices this very point in one of its pastoral ad- dresser., and says :—" Inasmuch as we have heard, with great sorrow, that in some placesour chapels and school premises, set apart as they are for the worship and service of &id, have been unlawfullyabuqed by holding therein of enter- tainment:3 which were not only utterly devoid of religious ten- dency, but seemed to enter into undisguised competition with music ball and theatre, brethren, we call upon you every- where to stand by us in an uncompromising opposition to this mistaken and dangerous policy. Success gained by it is too dearly bought to be worth having." Surely there are perils sufficient in the ways of our youth, without add- ing to them this altogether needless danger. "R. P." hopes I shall reconsider the matter, a-trl not hamper our school managers, ctn. lam glad to say our school manavrs (or superintendents, as a Methodist would ill them) had nothing to do with the affair. They are to a man against such proceedings; is fact, it was not a echo.' affair at all, but got up by the Young Men's Mutual Improve. ment Class, of whom many are not Methodists, and the majority of the remainder only nominal ones.. I am sorry that one of our ministers should so far forget his calling as to pander to the worldly tastes of a few ambitious young men, and thus sacrifice the sympathy and good wishes of the majority of the Methodist people of Warrington. It came as a shock upon them. In a quiet way I have got to know that most real Methodists are one with me in the sentiments exoressed in my letter To an outsider my views may seem narrow, but they cre Methodistical, and as a Methodist I have discussed ton. lam sorry t 3 have had to write upon the subject, but it is my only means of getting listened to, and if I succeed in any measure in stopping such question- able things in connection with our church, I shall have done good service.—Yours,
W. E.. S.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

Sir,—Your readers would be surprised at :he intimation conveyed to them last Saturday morning respecting the coming Municipal Electioes, and the modeat proposals of the Conservatives. I think it is high time the town awoke up to the danger it is running in allowing a political party to assume to itself the right Is dictate what shall he the composition of so important a body as tbe Town Council. Hitherto the Conservatives have had a decided and over- whelming majority in the Council chamber, and what has been the result? Why, if report speaks truth, scarcely a transaction in the town has been carried out on purely business principles. Ratepayers can hardly be satisfied to see the improvements in Bridge-street carried on in such a lachlyneome manner, and there are those who rouedly assert that in the buying and selling of land the ratepayers are suffering in consequence of "jobs." It is perfectly right that Bevrsey-street should be widened, but it is possible that, if a little care and forethought had been exercised in dealing with the Cheshire Lines Committee, a great saving of money nsight have accrued to the ratepayurs. Not the least important question on which the attention of the town is just now fixed is the department over which Alderman Burgess presides, and if it should turn out that the rather elaborate schemes out forward by the borough surveyor, and supported by the Sanitary Committee, should prove sncceseful, well, we must render a full measure of praise to these gentlemen. The sanitary condition of the town is, without doubt, the most important question with which the Corporatism can interest itself. That we stand well in comp at ison with other towns in our bill of health is doubtless true; but the ratepayers must not forget that, with one exception, we are the heaviest-rated town in the kingdom. I draw attention to these matters, sir, because I think them of such great importance, and that it is not de- sirable the town should be allowed to lose its head entirely, and become lost in every sense of the word. Is it because' at the two general elections we have had, in which the Tories have been successful, that they now want, in an indecent and brutal fashion, to thrust themeelves and their chameleon-like politics to the front ? Are they so hungering after the spoils of office that they are willing to see toe "tag rag and bob-tail "of their party placed in I positions were only men of tried capability are required?' It would be invidious to give the names of gentlemen be- longing to both parties who have served the town well and faithfully, and who have'never allowed the question of party to interfere with their duties as townsmen. Are these gen- tlemen willing to star 1 by now and see a clique carry out a caucus-arranged programme that must result in mere petty- fogging ignorance being placed in the Council chamber? The Liberals are willing to acknowledge that under ex- isting circumstances they are in a minority in the Town Council. I think they are also willing to allow November to pass over quietly, that the Conservatives shall continue in a majority, and the town be a gainer in respect of peace and the swing of expenses. Shotild it happen that the Conservatives should be so blind and lost to all patriotic sense, to all the rules of ordinary prudence, as to insist upon their insulting terms for a compromise, there is but one course for the Liberal aldermen and councillors to pursue— that is the one already suggested—resignation in a body; and if the townspeople are so enamoured of Toryism let them have their fill. We may rest saisfied that it is but another example of the saying—" Whom the gods wish to destroy, they first drive mad." I think the most important part of the question, however, is—What do the leaders in the Tory ranks think of it all? Are they satisfied that the tail end shall wag the whole body? I know they are not satisfied with their own mem- bers in the Council Chamber; that they are not satisfied with their leading alderman's magnanimity in nominating a Liberal Mayor a short time since, and now putting one for- ward who is sufficiently honest and intelligent enough to point out to them their stupid courses. I know all this., and I know it was pointed out to them years ago teat they were puttine such ignorant men forward as Councillors that in- telligent townsmen would refuse to allow themselves to be nominated; they were warned of all this, but according to their wont they refused to be advised. What is the result? The Tories have now in the Council Chamber men of whom they are ashamed, and others are thrusting themselves for- ward of whom the whole town may indeed be ashamed. The Tories are never tired of praising "Unionists," in national matters, when they have something to gain. Let them practice what they praise in municipal matters, when their forbearance will be the town's gain. If two or three of the leading Tories will only refuse to give the screaming or starts amongst them any support, or recognition, the town may be spared one of the most humiliating sights ever recorded. If not, then let the Liberal, stand on one side, and they will soon see a new version of the Kilkenny cats episode, and may, before long, be invited to take part in their obsequies. CLIFFORD DIX. October 20, 1830.

AN AIDE-DE-CAMP KILLED BY THE CZAR. A Central News telegram, dated Vienna Friday, says : Advicea from St. Petersburg leave little doubt but that the Czar has killed his aide-de-camp, Baron Reutein, in a paroxysm ot Year. The most reliable information tends to show that the Czar, alarmed ttt:his aide-de-camp's sudden ap- pearance. and fearing another attempt upon his own life, cut him down with a sabre. killing him on the spot. WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB. A special meeting of the members, of the War- rington Liberal Club was held in the large billiard room on Saturday evening to receive and consider the report of the Special Committee: appointed to investigate the affairs of the ChiN.ancl to report thereon. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., and there was a good. attendance. The report was presented, the proceedings through- out being unanimous. A vote of thanks. was paid to the special committee for their services;, and also to the chairman.

The annual general meeting of theraembers was held on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. McMinnies, J.P. The meeting was well attended. On the motion of Mr. George Walling- ton, seconded by Mr. S. Barlow, Mi. Wm Pierpoint was unanimously elected president, and on the motion of Mr. McMinmes,, seconded by Mr. D. Tinnion, the following gentlemen were' elected vice-presidents Thomas Jones. Mr. Thomas Morris, Mr. J. H. Fleming, Mr. John Harrison, Mr. Joseph Garner; Mr. George Plumpton, Dr. J. H. Gornall, J.P., M. S. Barlow, and Mr. F. A. Roberts. Mr. John Cresfidd, J.P., was unanimously elected treasurer on the motion of Mr. J. G. McMinnies, seconded by Mr. S: Barrow. Mr. S. Bbirlow was appointed honorary, secretary. The following gentlemen were elected; upoii the com- mittee :—Messrs. Arthur Browne, James Strange, Joseph Albinson, Samuel Barlow; Noah Legge, S. Kenyon, J. Critchley, J. It. CalVert,. W. Gilbert, G. Wallington, George Clay, T. Pemberton, and J. Whitehead. A vote of thanks to the chairman con- cluded the meeting.

The opening conversazione of the ninth session of the Padgate Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society was held in the Wesleyan School at, Padgate, which has recently been enlarged, on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance of members of the society and their friends. The inaugural address was delivered by Dr. MAcKIE, whose remarks were especially directed to the young,. They were based on the text, "It is good for a man to bear the yoke in his youth," taken from the lamentations of Jere- miah, who, he said, was himself an excellent speci- men of the bearing of the yoke. Ire often looked with uneasy feelings on the gap that death was making in Warrington and the neighbourhood, and had thought of the difficulty which had existed, did exist, and he feared might long do soi.in the obtain- ing of men willing to be baptised for-the dead—to fill the places, religious and secular,, of those who were dying off. Personally he had seen nearly every pulpit in the district filled more than once, and changes of all; the public officials with the exception of the borough treasurer. Of nearly 40 borough magistrates living, all had been appointed since 1852. besides a large number who had died. The county magistrates having jurisdiction over the district that Padgate and Warrington was included in num- bered nearly a score, and half of them were not included amongst the borough justices, so that nearly 50 were en- gaged in dispensing justice. They were dying off at a cer- tain rate, and they wanted to bring up young men who could fill their places. There were 36 aldermen and coun- cillors required, and of those new in office only some half- dozen had served the comparatively short Period of fifteen years. He mentionci this to show that the town of Warring- ton required 59 magistrates and 3t3 members of the Council, and, including Padgate, a half-a-ocore of Poor Law Guar- dians and 20 or 30 va-ious.officials. There were also a large number of people holding high office in Societies for the bene- fit of working-men, and engaged in Sunday school work, but they were dying off, and the great thing was to get young men to bear the yoke in their youths, so as to be able to fill those places as they became vacant. " It is the mind that is the stature of the man," and what mind one had should to laid under tribute greatly, especially in youth. Daniel was a yoke bearer in his youth. In Dante and Michael Angelo they found men, whose youth was a time of yoke bearing, and so it was also with Shakespere, Milton, and with the noble army of great men who had suc• ceeded them. But he wished to refer more particularly to the youth of that particular district,who should be fit to replace such men as Mr. W. Beamont and :cores whom he could name. Mr. Beamont was a representative man who had long been in the front. There were also Lords Win- marleigh and Cross, who both had their advantages in youth, but had they not borne the yoke in their youth they might never have gained the honourable positions they now occupied. Mr. Peter Rylands—(cheers)—was another who bad botne the yoke front his earliest youth. Who was to replace such men—who would be willing to be baptised for the dead? They wanted men who cauld go to their families and friends, and say what religion bad done for them. They must catch them in their youth; yoke them in their boyhood. It might be said that he waslset, ting too high an ideal, but he exhorted all young men to prepare to be as useful as they could, and take care not tobe classed amongst "Those that are unstable in their ways," During the evening refreshments were dispensed, and a programme of songs and readings was gone through. The centributors to it were Mr. 'W. Wellington, songs; Miss Podmore, song; Mr. A. Bennett,'reading; Mrs. Pearson, song ; Mr. J. J. Nield, songs; Mr. W. H, J. Jenkins, reading; Miss H. Bennett, pianoforte solo Miss E. Turner, song; Mr. J. E. Richardson, reading; and Miss Harding, song. Mr. 'I. C. London also gave some chemical experiments. In various parts of the room there were on view—misce/laneous curi- osities, lent by Mr, Arthur Bennett; Indian curiosities, lent by Mr. Thomas Bennett; illustrations of the abbeys and castles of England, lent by Mr. Theodore C. London' kaleid- oscope And panorama of the history of the world, lent by Dr. Mackie ; galvanic battery, lent by Mr. W. J. Dunn ; and microscope, lent by Mr. H. Whithana.—Dr. Mackie was ac- corded a very hearty vote of thanks for his services in de ,- Uterine the inaugural address, on the motion of Mr. Ben- nett, senr., seconded by Mr. Wright, and supported by 31r. A. Bennett.

- -- At the Warrington County- Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Street. a Croft, was sum- moned by his son. Thomas Street, a railway servant, who complained that defendant detained Mary Jane Street, four years of age, with, intent to deprive him, the father, of its custody. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant; and, MT; P. Davies for the defendant. Mr. Browne, in,stating.the circum- stances of the case, said that it was a. painful one, as defendant was the father of the complainant, and therefore it was a family matter: Complain- ant married four or five years ago,. and his wife soon afterwards died. About: fOur yeara ago com- plainant went with his child to live with his mother and then got married a second, time. Eve:. since then h 3 had been trying to regaimpossession of the child, and aboat a month ago endeavoured to ob- tain it by force; he was at that time ratherroughly handled; pushed out of the house,.and assaulted in several ways. All that' he- wants& was to have his child back, and if defendant would consent to give it up to him the case would be withdrawn. -- Mr. Davies•said that the defendant would not give up the. child. The magistrates had not power to 'deal with, the case. Mr. Browne had fairly stated 'the facts,. with one exception. He said that the son of the defendant had endeavoured to obtain the , child, for the last three years, which defendant denied. Complainant, who was 24 years of age, was married early in life to a girl who was 21 years of age. The child was born at Bolton, and the mother took it from Bolton to complainant's mother, to whom she gave it, say- ing "I am going to die." She died about four6een days aftel-wards. The son did not claint the child, and admitted that its mother.bad'yiten it to the grandparents, as he was not in a .position to. keep it. The grandparents claimed the child as a.matter of right. The complainant's present, wifx3- was of a different religious persuasion, and it was-the Church to which she belonged that, claimed the child.— Mr. Browne : That is not true-- Alter the complainant had been examined, Mr.. Nichol- son (magistrates' clerk) said tfiat he thought there was no evidence of a detaining by force on the part of the defendant, and he con- sidered that the best plan would be to, withdraw the summons, and see what 'arrangements could be made. If an arrangement.could not be arrived at additional proof might be obtained, and another summons taken out.—Mr. R. Houghton, the only magistrate on the bench, . told defendant that he was acting under a misapprehension in keeping the child; he was not legally entitled to do so.—Mr. Davies: They are determined to carry it to the bitter end; they say they will nevergive it up.— Mr. Houghton : I quite admit it is a.very hard thing. —Mrs. Street (grandmother of the child) : The child was given to me when it was three weeks old.—Mr. Houghton: I think it a very cruel thing on the part of the father: the child looks healthy and well cared for, but the law says you must give it up.—Mr. Nicholson: There can be no sympathy extended by any one to the • complainant.—The, summons was then withdrawn, on the understanding, that further proceedings would be taken if renewed efforts to gain possession of the child were Unavailing. On leaving the court complainant made a. formal demand for his child, which was not complied with.

PRESENTATION AT HAYDOCK. An interesting gathering was held in the Haydock Read- ng Room on Wednesday evening, when Mr. John Fair- hurst, an old ond respected resident of the district, was the recipient of a tangible token of the esteem in which he is generally held. There was a good attendanae, amongst those present being Mr. Thomas Jackson (who presided), Mr. Arthur L. Evans, Dr. T. E. Hayward, Messrs. Edwin Jackson, R. M. Prescott, John Jackson, Beilhy, Bradshaw, Taylor, Forrest, an& others. The Chairman stated that his duty of presenting their old friend, Mr, Fairhurst, with a mark of their regard, and with a more substantial token in the shape of a purse of gold, as a slight recognition of his kind services and obliging manners, was a very pleasant one. He had never known Mr. Fairhurst refuse oa decline an act of kindness to anyone, and his willing and genial manner had gained hiva hosts of friends. The secretary (Mr. R. M. Prescott) then read the following testimonial :—"ToMr. John Fairhurst. We, the undersigned, acting as a committee on behalf of the sub- scribers, beg to ask your acceptance of the accompanying purse containing the sum of 27-guineas as a small token of tLe esteem and regard in which you are held in this district. We have observed how yon have ever studied to render good service to those with whom you have from time to time come in contact. Your courtesy, kindness, and good offices have become proYerbial, and the genial and unassuming,, manner whi,eh has distinguished the faithful discharge of env functions you have taken in baud has made it a pleasure to those availing thems-lves of your services. 111 the pursuit of your dai)y avocation it has been a able feature feature to us to know how zealously you have laboured to gain V..e confidence and good will of every one in what we are assured has been a faithful discharge of your dotr. We can but offer you our sincere and hearty thanks for all/the favours you have done us, and express the hope that your valued life maybe long spared to labour amongst,ns anti' that afterwards yen will enjoy a wen- earned and merited repose. We are, sir, yours wry faithfully (signed) Arthur 'vans, ;John Jackson, B B. Glover, Richard Bradshaw, Edwin 'Reilby, Edwin Jackson, Wiliiam Halharrv, John Balton, James Taylor, John Wright,,committee ; Thomas Jackson, chairmen; R. N. Prescott, secretary." The address was the work of Mr. R. M. Prescott (clerk to the Havdock Local Board), and vas in old. Euglish text, nicely coloured, and illuminated. It was a splendid piece of penmanship and was enclosed in a massive gilt frame, with a six inch gold mount. At the ton of the address was a portrait of the engine "Newton," showing Mr. Fairhurst ((hirer) and his stoker. Mr. Fairhurst, it may be added, has driven that engine for a considerable number of Years under Messra. Richard Evana and Co.—Complimentary addresses to Mr. Fairhurst were delivered by Messrs Arthur Evans, E. Beilby, B. Jacason, R. M. Prescott, J. Taylor. John Jackson. and Dr. Hayward. In handing the testimonial and purse to Mr.Fairhurst the chairman expressed the hope that the red-. pleat would be long spared to enjoy the confidence and good will of all his friends. (App)atlSe.)—Mr. Fairhurst feelingly acknowledged the gift, and said what he had dene had been from a sense of his duty.—On the motion of Mr. A. Evans, seconded by Mr, John Jackson, cerdial thanks were paid to Mr. Prescott for his active interest In the matter, and a hearty vote of thanks to the oha'rman, on the motion of Beilby, seconded by Mr. Bradshaw, closed the proceedings,
